The Peak: the pitch

A pitch, from the Second Director to Parker. Seven biomes, 78 places, one slide each.

The Peak of DeGayo: how the first seven biomes should look

You told me the Peak looks blocked out and unfinished, and that every place on it should be a little diorama: a background that plays into what you climb, the play space, and a sparse foreground. This is my proposal for how to do that from the station to the top of the chimney.

Each biome gets one slide first: what the place is, how it is built, and what it reuses. Then one slide for every place in it. On each slide I tell you what the place is, show it to scale, say why it works and what it would take to build, and list anything I still need from you.

Nothing here is built. No model is made and nothing in the game has changed. Where a design would need the course to change, the slide says so.

This viewer cannot save your feedback. Open this file in your own browser (Chrome, Edge or Firefox) so what you type is kept.

How to use this

  • Left and right arrow keys, or the buttons at the bottom, move between slides. The menu at the top jumps to any slide.
  • Every slide has a feedback box at the bottom right. Pick a verdict if you like, and type what you think. It is saved as you type, in this browser.
  • When you are done, the last slide (or the Save button at the top) gives you all of it as one file, or copies it, to hand back to me.
  • Each picture is a diagram, to scale, drawn from the game's own numbers. It is not concept art. The numbers on it match the list beside it. Blue-grey is proposed background, yellow is added to the play space, pink is foreground, and the rest is the game as it is today.

What you should know before you judge it

  • I wrote the seven biome sheets. A helper for each biome drew its places from the sheet, then redrew them after your answers of 11-13. I have looked at some pictures from every biome, not all 78.
  • The view from above on each slide was mostly not checked by eye by anyone.
  • Where a slide says a jump or a reach is untried, it is: nothing was run in the game for this.
  • A few calls on these slides are the helpers' or mine and you have not seen them. Each one is flagged on its slide.

Before the biomes

The rules every slide follows

These hold on the whole mountain. The second one is yours, from 11-13. If you disagree with any of them, say so here and I will change every slide it touches.

  1. What you can hold is dry, pale and matte. What you can't is dark, glossy and wet. This is the mountain's first law and no design breaks it.
  2. Where a thing stands tells you more than its colour (Parker, 11-13). If it is in the play space you can generally hold it. Scenery stays out of the play space, behind or in front, and is greyer, darker and cooler than the things you climb.
  3. Everything you touch is the near end of something real that carries on behind it, like a ladder and its rungs.
  4. Nothing thin hangs in the background near the climb: it reads as a rope (notes 4 and 18). A hanging thing is a real rope, or thick, or far back.
  5. The foreground is sparse: thin posts and low lips, in front of solid rock or below the lowest floor, never over the open space you climb through (note 40).
  6. Every moving thing shows its machine: what drives it stands in the background (notes 19, 36, 57).
  7. Every danger shows where it comes from and warns before it acts (notes 12, 21, 23, 56).
  8. Every breakable thing wears the game's one breakable look: cracked already, with a corner gone (notes 16, 24, 31, 53, 64).
  9. The painted back wall never stops inside the frame, so there are no black holes (note 51). The insides of small pits can't be held (note 52).
  10. One frog is hidden in every biome (note 60), in a little room you can walk into. A room you can enter is cut away at the front: floor, back wall and roof, no front wall.
  11. Far backgrounds are flat facade pieces (Parker, 11-13): one cut-out card standing well back, painted in a few broad rows that haze toward the horizon, with a few bold silhouettes cut into its ridge. Never modelled terrain, and never an empty plane running to a ruled horizon. The station's dry hills are the worked example.

Biome 0 of the first seven · 5 places · 0 open questions

La Estación

The trailhead at the edge of town, and the cart ride into the mountain. The only biome in the open air until the cliffs.

The station is the handshake. It is the only place the player sees the whole mountain, in full sun, before going under it. I want it to say three things without a word: this is the edge of town, people come here to climb and do not come back, and that red lever is the way in. You gave me a free hand here, so this is a second, bolder pass: a walled yard, the station house up on the dock, your Missing posters, a frog on the windowsill.

What this place is

This is where the mine's ore used to come out and where the town ends. A loading platform, a siding with one cart on it, a tunnel mouth, and the Peak standing over all of it. The mine shut long ago. The station is kept up now by nobody in particular, for the luchadores who come to climb: somebody still hangs bunting, somebody still oils the cart's brake.

It is the last place that looks like the town: plaster, tiles, paint and noon sun. From the tunnel mouth inward, everything is the mine's.

The ride is the way in: 115 m of track, a dip, a banked drop, a broken rail the cart really hops (with dust off its wheels as it lands), one look at the waterfall cavern through a gap, and the buffer that tips you out.

How it is built

  • Town building: thick plastered walls in cream, terracotta roof tiles, painted woodwork, all in the plaza's own painted-cardboard look.
  • Station gear in honey timber and red paint: the loading platform on posts, ore crates, barrels, a hand crane, the cart, its red brake lever.
  • The tunnel mouth is the first timber set of the mine: the same posts and cap as every set inside, here whitewashed, with a painted pug over the cap.
  • Down the tunnel the same sets go from whitewashed, to bare, to grey and wet. That is the whole of the change from town to mine, and it happens while you ride.

Colour and light

Noon sun, the brightest place in the game: cream walls, a blue sky, short hard shadows. In the tunnel the daylight shrinks to a dot behind you and the lanterns take over, one every twenty metres, each a little dimmer and more amber than the last.

How it tells you what a thing is

You can hold itHoney timber, crates, barrels, pale dry rock, the cart's wooden sides, rope.
You can'tAlmost nothing here: one streak of black mud in the tunnel, so the first slick thing you ever see is seen from a moving cart.
It movesThe cart. You start it by pulling the red brake lever, whether you are in the cart or not: your hand takes the lever the way it takes a chair, for as long as you hold that limb's button. Red means: this does something.
It is sceneryThe town and the mountain: far, flat and sun-bleached. Near scenery (the station house, the fence) is plaster and tile, which nothing you climb is made of.

The three layers here

BackgroundNear: the station house, the crane, stacked ore sacks, the back posts of the platform. Far: the Peak filling the west half of the sky, with the tiny bell at the top, and the town's roofs to the east. In the tunnel: the back wall's timber sets, side passages bricked or boarded, and once, the waterfall cavern.
Play spaceThe crates and barrel, the platform, the cart and its track.
ForegroundOutside: one fence post with a tail of bunting at the right edge of the first screen, a clump of agave at the bottom edge. In the tunnel: the front post of every fourth set, sweeping past the cart.

How you come in, and how you leave

In: You start here, standing in the sun at the edge of town, facing the mountain.

Out: The cart's tunnel is the join with the mine. The timber sets go from whitewashed to rotten as you ride, the lanterns go from bright to amber, the bunting stops, and the gap shows you the waterfall cavern before you are in it. It is designed as its own page: the join from the station to the mine.

La Estación · Challenge · place 1 of 5

0.1-0.2 El Primer Paso and Súbete

This is where the town stops and the mine's ground starts.

You come out through the town's gate into a walled yard, and the Peak fills the sky ahead. On the yard wall behind you are the Missing posters: the masked faces of the ones who went up and did not come back. Across the yard stands the ore dock, a timber platform 2.2 m high and 31 m long that runs to the tunnel mouth, with a siding along it and the little station house built on its back. Ore came out of the mountain in carts and was swung down off the dock's end by a hand crane. The last load is still where the crane put it down, and it is your first steps: a barrel, then two crates. On the siding one cart is left, held by a tall red lever, and somebody still oils it. The frog is asleep in the station's ticket window.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The Peak and the town, far off. Far cut-outs, the plaza's own. The Peak stands whole in the west half of the sky with the tiny bell on its top: the only time you see all of it until the ending. The town's roofs show over the yard wall. Both are flat and sun-bleached, so nothing near is mistaken for them.
  • 2The yard wall, the town gate and the arrow sign. A plastered wall 2.4 m tall with a tiled top closes the yard on the town's side, 3.6 m behind you. In it is the gate you came out of: an arch 2.4 m wide with the town's street going away behind it. It is why you can't walk back east: the way to town turns away from you, through the wall. The pug arrow sign stands by the wall's end where it does today, moved 0.4 m further back so it is out of the play space.
  • 3The station house. Built on the back of the dock, behind the cart: cream plaster, a terracotta roof, a narrow porch on two slim posts, a shut door, a ticket window, and a small bell on a bracket at its west corner. Its wall is 1.5 m behind you, so you walk and ride along its front. On the wall, straight above the lever's handle, a red arrow is painted, pointing down.
  • 4The Missing posters. Four here (Parker, 11-13). Two fresh ones side by side on the yard wall, right behind where you start: the stripe and the fangs. An old copy of the stripe further along the same wall, by the arrow sign: sun-bleached, creased, one corner gone. And the star, on the station house wall beside the ticket window. Each is 0.5 m by 0.7 m and hangs at face height. The fifth is on the tunnel mouth's post, on the next page.
  • 5The posters, drawn large. A key, not a thing in the scene: the three posters at 6 times their size, square by square. They are made the way the lock-in money is made. Each is 16 squares by 22, a square 3.1 cm across, in four inks of one of the money's six colours (lavender, green, rose): the colour, a lighter one, a darker one and a darkest. Round the edge runs the money's two-line border. Across the top, the money's woven band. In the middle, where the money has its sun, is a masked face: an oval with a dark rim, two diamond eyes and a slot of a mouth. Each mask has its own mark: a stripe down the middle, two fangs up the cheeks, or a star on the brow with a dot on the chin. Under the face, the money's dotted trim stands for the lines of print. No words and no numbers. The paper curls and creases the way the bills do. In this sketch the four inks are drawn pale blue, yellow, slate and black.
  • 6The frog. Asleep on the sill of the ticket window, 1.1 m above the deck and 1 m west of the cart, in plain sight (Parker, 11-13). The cart carries you past it at arm's length as it pulls out. It is the first frog, so it is not hidden: it teaches you there are frogs to find (note 60).
  • 7The hand crane and the rest of its load. On the dock's back corner beside the house, 3 m tall, its arm swung out over the steps. The hook block is wound right up under the arm's tip, so nothing hangs from it. On the road behind the steps lies the rest of the load: a second barrel on its side and a heap of ore sacks, too low to look like another step.
  • 8The dock's back half and the second cart. The dock is 5 m deep and you climb only its front edge. Behind runs the rest: a second row of posts, set between the front legs so both rows show, and a rail along the back edge west of the house. Against that rail a second cart stands on blocks, its wheels gone. The cart you ride has been kept running with parts from this one.
  • 9The bunting. Torn papel picado from the gate's head to a pole on the wall's end, on to the crane's head, and from the house's roof west from pole to pole along the dock, all the way to the tunnel. It points the way before the sign does. It is high, it is 2.3 m or more behind you, and its flags are 0.5 m deep, so it can't be taken for a rope.

Play space

  • 10The barrel and the two crates. The first step is drawn as a standing barrel, 1.1 m tall and 1.2 m across, banded with iron. It is the same box to stand on. The two crates above it get the mine's pug stencilled on their faces. All three are scuffed pale on top, where hands and boots go.
  • 11Sawn ends along the deck's edge. The deck's cross-beams show as a row of square sawn ends along its face, one every 2 m. They say the deck carries on back. The mine uses the same mark on its rock.
  • 12The lever. As tall as you are: 1.7 m, standing in an iron quadrant bolted to the deck 0.2 m east of the cart. At rest it leans towards the cart, so its handle hangs right over the cart's east end, 1.65 m above the deck and 1.1 m above the cart's floor: at shoulder height from the deck, at chest height from inside the cart, and within 0.7 m of your shoulder either way. The shaft is red. The top 0.4 m is a pale wooden grip, because that is the part your hand takes. Take it as you take the chair, with the hand whose button you are holding, and draw it east: after 0.7 m it drops into its second notch and the cart is off (the dashed line). A rod along the deck ties the lever's foot to a chock under the cart's wheel, so you can see what it lets go. Pull it from the deck and the cart leaves without you unless you are over its end within a second. It comes back to the siding 25 seconds later, as it does today.

Foreground

  • 13A fence post with a tail of bunting. The last post of the town's fence, with a torn tail of bunting tied to it. It stands on the low ground in front of the road, and its top comes only 0.3 m above the road, so it never covers you.
  • 14An agave clump. On the low ground at the bottom of the frame, in front of the road's face. It is below your feet wherever you stand.

  • The cart on the siding at x -9, with its low sides.
  • The start: on the road at x 6, 8 m east of the steps, facing the mountain.
  • The lever changes: see the notes at the foot of this page.

What it would change in the game

  • COURSE CHANGE, a thing you touch: the lever's foot stays at x -7.6. The lever grows from 1 m to 1.7 m, comes forward from 0.9 m behind you to 0.45 m behind you, and leans so that its handle is at x -7.95, 3.86 m up, over the cart's east end. Pulled, the handle is at x -7.25.

Small effects, no models

  • The lever goes over with a heavy clunk, the chock is kicked out from under the wheel, and the cart starts to roll.
  • The frog croaks now and then, loud enough to hear from the steps. It does not wake, even when the cart goes by.
  • The bunting stirs, and one corner of the old poster lifts and settles.
  • Short hard shadows under the dock and the steps: the noon sun is straight overhead.

Notes

  • Parker, 11-13: the station may be completely reworked. This is the second pass. The station house moves up onto the back of the dock, behind the cart. The road gets a yard wall and the town's gate. The first step is drawn as a barrel, as the challenge list has it.
  • Parker, 11-13: Missing posters, made the way the lock-in money is made, take the place of the board of crossed-out masks. Four hang here and one at the tunnel mouth.
  • Parker, 11-13: the frog sits in plain sight. It is on the ticket window's sill, beside the cart (note 60).
  • Parker, 11-13: the lever works. COURSE CHANGE, the play: pulling the lever starts the cart whether you are in the cart or not, and getting into the cart no longer starts it. The lever becomes a thing your hand takes and keeps while you hold that limb's button, like the chair.
  • Nothing you stand on moves: not the steps, the deck, the legs or the rails. The first crate keeps its size and is only drawn as a barrel.
  • Scenery that is in the play space today and moves out of it: the pug arrow sign, 0.4 m further back.

La Estación · Challenge · place 2 of 5

0.3a El Descenso, part one: the dock, the tunnel mouth and the first drop

The ride starts in the open.

The cart runs 27 m west along the dock, in the sun, with the Peak's foot coming up to meet it, and goes into the mountain through the tunnel mouth. The mouth is the mine's first timber set, the same two posts and a cap as every set inside, whitewashed here because this end belongs to the town. Inside, the tunnel tips downhill at once. For the first 26 m the sets and the plank lining are still white, the first lantern is bright, and one last string of bunting follows you in and stops. This was the haulage way. Full carts were hauled up it by mule to the dock, and the empties ran down by their own weight, as yours does.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The mountain's foot. Pale dry rock coming down to the road behind the dock's last 6 m. Above the mouth it becomes the Peak's east face, which the course already has. It is what the dock runs into.
  • 2The dock's back half, the ore hopper and the mules' trough. The back posts and the back rail carry on from the station. Against the hill stands a timber hopper on legs, where carts were tipped, with a chute down behind the dock to where the wagons stood. Beside it is a water trough, for the mules that hauled the full carts up.
  • 3The pug over the mouth. A round painted board, 1.2 m across, on an iron bracket above the cap, turned to face the camera like a shop sign. A pug painted flat over the cap would face the town, and from the side you would see only its edge.
  • 4A Missing poster on the mouth's post. The fifth and last poster (Parker, 11-13), on a board nailed to the mouth's back post and turned to face you, 1.2 m above the deck. It is an old copy of the fangs, sun-bleached, with its lower third torn away. It is the last face from the town before the dark.
  • 5The tunnel's back wall. Plank lining, limewashed white as far as the second lantern. The planks are nailed on level while the floor falls away under them, so the wall itself shows you how steep the track is.
  • 6A bricked-up side passage. Between two sets, 19 m in. Bricked up and whitewashed, which is town work. Further down, a closed passage is boarded, which is the mine's way.
  • 7The timber sets, whitewashed. A set every 2.6 m: a back post against the lining and a cap across the roof, posts 0.3 m square. Eleven in this stretch, counting the mouth, all whitewashed, the wash a little thinner on each one.
  • 8Two lanterns. Each hangs under a set's cap at a place where the track changes slope, so a lantern always marks a bend in the grade. The first is nearly white. Each one after it is a little dimmer and more amber.
  • 9The bunting's end. From the last pole on the dock to the pug's bracket, and one string more inside, from the mouth's cap to the cap by the first lantern. There it stops. The town comes 10 m into the mountain and no further.

Play space

  • 10Whitewash on the roof. The rock roof is limewashed for the first 10 m, fading out. It is paint on dry rock, so it is still pale and matte.
  • 11The sill. Where the dock's deck meets the rock: a timber sill shod with iron, worn hollow in the middle by wheels.

Foreground

  • 12Three front posts. The front post of every fourth set, so one every 10.4 m. Each is 0.3 m wide and plain. At the cart's speed one sweeps past about every 1.2 seconds, and there are never more than two on screen. The back post of the same set stands behind it, so you pass between the two. All the other sets have a back post and a cap only. Here: the mouth's own post and two inside, all whitewashed.

The tunnel's floorThe haulage way's rock bed, cut on a gradeThe level planks of the lining, which show the grade
The tunnel's roofRock, held up by a timber set every 2.6 mThe back posts and caps, and the front post of every fourth set
The cart, rollingAn empty, running down by its own weightThe trough of the mules that hauled the full ones back up

  • The cart's speed: it is at its full 9 m a second by the time it reaches the mouth.
  • The mouth at x -36, 5 m tall. The roof stays 5 m above the bed all the way down.
  • The bed grips, so you can get out and walk the tunnel.
  • The lantern lights at x -46 and x -62.

La Estación · Challenge · place 3 of 5

0.3b El Descenso, part two: the dip, the crest and the banked drop

The miners drove this tunnel along a soft seam of rock, and the seam wandered.

So the track runs down to a low point 42 m in, climbs 2 m over a rib of hard rock that was not worth cutting through, and then drops down the far side at 17 degrees, the steepest grade of the ride. Water gathers at the low point, so a hand pump stands there. The rib needs no timber, so for two sets' length the roof is bare rock. Carts always went light over that crest, and in the end the rails past it tore out. So the cart leaves the track at the top, flies, and comes down 7.6 m further on, in a burst of dust. This stretch is also where the town lets go. The whitewash has stopped, and a small shrine in the wall at the bottom of the dip is the last thing in the town's paint.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The tunnel's back wall. Bare plank lining, the limewash gone. Behind the landing the planks are pale with old dust. Further down the drop the first planks are missing and wet rock shows in the gaps: two dark patches, the first wet you see on the ride.
  • 2The hard rib. A slanting band of harder, bluer rock, 3 m wide, crossing the back wall at the crest. It has old drill holes in it and no timber on it: two sets are left out here, because this rock holds itself up. It is why the track climbs.
  • 3The timber sets, bare. Bare wood, dull and dry, greyer than anything you can hold. At the low point the feet of three posts are stained dark to knee height. Past the crest the wood starts to go grey.
  • 4The shrine. A small arched niche in the back wall at the bottom of the dip, whitewashed, with candle stubs in it and a scrap of papel picado over it. The miners touched it on the way in. From here down, nothing is in the town's paint.
  • 5The hand pump and its trough. At the low point, against the back wall: an iron hand pump, 1.4 m tall, with its handle up. A wooden trough runs from it along the foot of the back wall, up over the crest and on down the tunnel. It is why the dip is not a pond.
  • 6Three lanterns. Where the course has its lights: at the low point, at the crest and at the foot of the drop. The one on the crest hangs from an iron spike driven into the rib, since there is no cap there. It lights the place where the rails stop, so you see the break coming.
  • 7The skull-pug sign. The mine's own danger sign, on a post against the back wall half way up the climb to the crest. It is the warning before the hop, and the first of these signs you see. The kit has it.

Play space

  • 8The broken rail. From the crest at x -90 to x -94 both rails are gone and only the sleepers are left. The near rail's stub is bent up at the crest like the lip of a ramp. The far rail lies in the ballast beside the sleepers. The kit has the broken piece.
  • 9The hop. The cart leaves the rails at the crest, where the track turns from 9 degrees up to 17 degrees down. Thrown at its own 9 m a second, it flies 7.6 m in 0.9 seconds, is 0.9 m clear of the sleepers at its highest, noses over in the air, and comes down at x -97.6. The line drawn is the cart's floor. These are the numbers of a real throw, as a place to start: the feel is for the thread to tune. You are light in the cart while it flies, so hold on.
  • 10The landing. Where the cart comes down, from x -97 to x -100, the rails are scraped bright and the sleepers are doubled, two side by side, because this is where they always broke. Pale dust lies thick between them. It is the dust that jumps off the wheels. The bed under it is unchanged and still grips.
  • 11Banked sleepers. Below the landing the track is laid banked: the far rail 0.2 m higher than the near one, so the tops of the sleepers show. It reads as a track built to be run fast. The bed under your feet is unchanged.

Foreground

  • 12Four front posts. The front post of every fourth set, so one every 10.4 m. Each is 0.3 m wide and plain. At the cart's speed one sweeps past about every 1.2 seconds, and there are never more than two on screen. The back post of the same set stands behind it, so you pass between the two. All the other sets have a back post and a cap only. Here: four, in bare wood, and none on the rib. The fourth is moved one set down the hill, to x -101, so that nothing crosses in front of the cart as it lands.

Why it works

Each thing you touch is the near end of something real behind it.

The landingThe place every cart has come down sinceThe lining behind it, pale with old dust
The banked dropThe steepest grade, laid banked for speedThe lining with its first planks gone and wet rock showing
The tunnel's roofRock, held by a set every 2.6 m except on the ribThe back posts and caps, in bare wood

What I am not touching

  • The track's line: down at 4 degrees to the low point at x -78, up at 9 degrees to the crest at x -90, then down at 17 degrees to x -104.

  • The lantern lights at x -78, -90 and -104.
  • The bed grips all the way: dry and pale, even at the low point.

La Estación · Challenge · place 4 of 5

0.3c El Descenso, part three: the wet tunnel and the gap

The lower tunnel runs along the edge of the waterfall cavern, and the cavern's water is getting in.

The sets are grey, the lining has planks missing, and a seep of black mud has come through the back wall. It is the first slick thing in the game, shown where you can't touch it. Then, for 8 m, the back wall is gone. It fell out into the cavern and took one timber set with it. Through the hole you get one look at where you are going: the far wall of a very big room, the long white line of the waterfall, and a few lantern specks on the workings beside it. Then the wall closes again.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The tunnel's back wall, wet. Grey plank lining with planks missing and wet rock behind. The trough along its foot carries the water on down. Drips fall from the caps.
  • 2The gap. 8 m of the back wall broken out, with a ragged edge and a low sill of rubble. One whole set went with it, so the roof is bare there. The back posts of two other sets still stand in the opening, dark against the view. At the cart's speed the gap is on screen for about 3 seconds.
  • 3The waterfall cavern. Seen through the gap, 14 m back and more: the cold grey-violet far wall, the waterfall as one pale line from above the frame to below it, mist at its foot, and five lantern specks on the workings beside it. It is a far cut-out, like the Peak at the station. It is the only cool light on the ride.
  • 4The black streak. A seep of glossy black mud down the back wall between two sets, 2 m wide at the floor, with pale drips on it. The lanterns either side light it. It is on the back wall only, never on the bed.
  • 5A boarded side tunnel. The mine's way of closing a passage: two planks nailed across a dark opening. The mine's kit has it.
  • 6The timber sets, grey. Grey and wet, some leaning a little. One cap just below the gap is cracked and held up by an extra prop. From here on these are the mine's sets.
  • 7Two lanterns. Amber now, and dim. The gap sits half way between them, so their light does not fight the view. The second is the tunnel's seventh and last.

Play space

  • 8The dry bed. With all this wet behind it, the bed and the rails are drawn dry: pale rock, rust-orange rails, dry sleepers. Nothing dark or glossy is put on the floor here, because the floor grips.

Foreground

  • 9Two front posts and a stump. The front post of every fourth set, so one every 10.4 m. Each is 0.3 m wide and plain. At the cart's speed one sweeps past about every 1.2 seconds, and there are never more than two on screen. The back post of the same set stands behind it, so you pass between the two. All the other sets have a back post and a cap only. Here: two, in grey wood, and the one that would stand in front of the gap is a 0.5 m stump. It went when the wall did. So from x -119 to x -140 nothing stands in front of you: the longest clear stretch of the ride, placed where the look is.

La Estación · A join between two biomes · place 5 of 5

0 to 1 The station to the mine: the end of the line

The end of the line.

The tunnel levels out for its last 16 m and stops at a buffer, 2 m short of the door into the mine. By here everything the town sent in has dropped away. The bunting stopped 10 m in, the whitewash at 26 m, the shrine in the dip was the last paint, and the daylight is long gone. What is left is the mine's: grey wet timber, smashed lining, amber light. The door is one timber set that belongs to both places. The first thing beyond it is honey-coloured timber you can hold, the first since the dock, and under that timber is the first black mud you can touch.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The tunnel's back wall, the last 16 m. The lining is smashed here and the rock behind it is wet. This is the same back wall the mine's galleries have.
  • 2The mine's first gallery. Drawn here only so the two back walls meet at the door. What is in the gallery is on the mine's own page, 1.1 La Galería: the mud pit, the posts over it, the cart the mud took.
  • 3The last five sets. Grey, wet and rotten, 2.6 m apart. One cap is cracked and held by a prop. After the fifth comes one wide bay, 4.2 m, with the buffer in it.
  • 4The door set. The timber set at the door, which the course already has. It is the tunnel's last set and the mine's first: the same posts and cap, no whitewash, nothing painted.
  • 5The buffer's braces. The buffer is a timber baulk laid right across the track. Its far end is held by two braces that rake back to the floor against the back wall. What you see in the play space is the near end of it.
  • 6The miners' pegs. A board of six pegs on the back wall, where the men hung their lamps and coats when they got out of the carts. Five pegs are empty. One still has a hat on it, and a dead lamp.
  • 7The trough's end. The trough along the wall's foot ends at the door, and its water runs over the sill and on towards the gallery's mud pit. The tunnel's water is what made the mine's first mud.
  • 8The mine's first lantern. Where the course has it, just inside the door. The tunnel's last lantern, 18 m back up the track, is the same amber and just as dim, so the light does not change at the door.

Play space

  • 9The buffer's iron face. The iron block becomes the near end of the timber baulk, faced with an iron plate that is dented where carts have hit it. It keeps its size.
  • 10The sill at the door. The tunnel's floor is 0.6 m higher than the gallery's, and today it ends in a bare step. The step gets a worn timber sill along its edge, so it reads as the end of a loading floor.

Foreground

  • 11The last front post, and the door's broken one. One whole front post, at x -140. The door set's front post is broken in the middle: a length hanging from the cap and a stump on the floor. The gap between them is where the cart throws you, so nothing covers you as you land.

Biome 1 of the first seven · 15 places · 0 open questions

La Mina Vieja

The old mine, 30 m under the trailhead to 90 m above it. Timber, rails and mud, round the great waterfall.

The mine has to teach the mountain's language, so I am giving it exactly one way of building: square timber sets, the same posts and caps everywhere. Everything you climb is what is still standing of a working mine, and behind every hold you can see the rest of the thing it was part of. Honey-coloured wood means you can hold it. The waterfall shows up only where it truly is, so when you see it, it matters.

What this place is

The town's grandparents cut this mine by hand for gold. It is one big cavern with a 113 m waterfall down its middle, and the workings climb round the fall: galleries, ladder ways, plank catwalks, a bucket lift, a cart track on a ledge, roof beams, the winding wheel, a hoist shaft. Then the water got in and the roof started to fall, and the miners walked out and left everything where it stood.

Since then the only people through here are the ones who came to climb the Peak. They left lanterns, bunting from town, and one of themselves, sitting by a cold lantern with tally marks scratched on the wall beside him.

So every place in the mine is two things at once: a piece of a working mine that made sense on the day it was left, and the same place eighty years on, wet, rotted and half fallen. What you climb is what is still standing.

How it is built

  • Square-set timbering. Posts 0.35 m square, a cap across the top, a sill at the foot, a set every 1.3 m in a shaft and every 2.6 m in a gallery. The same posts and caps everywhere: this is the mine's one way of building.
  • Plank lining between the sets, nailed on. Where the lining is gone, wet rock shows.
  • Iron only where the miners needed it: rails on sleepers, strap brackets, chain, bolts, the rims of wheels. All of it rust orange.
  • Rock cut by hand: flat pick-marked faces, old drill holes, and slanting seams of gold ore.
  • Hoisting gear: the winding wheel, buckets, a hand winch, pulleys. Every one stands on a timber frame of the same posts.
  • Nothing is painted, nothing is carved, nothing is brick. Paint and brick belong to the works above; carving belongs to the temple.

Colour and light

Almost dark. Warm amber pools round the lanterns, and between them you see little. The one cool thing in the room is the waterfall: pale blue-white, always somewhere in the picture, and brighter than anything else in the background. Far rock is a cold grey-violet, so the warm timber of the climb stands out in front of it.

How it tells you what a thing is

You can hold itHoney-coloured timber, pale chalky rock, rust-orange iron, rope. Dry and matte.
You can'tBlack wet mud and wet rock, glossy, with pale drips running down it.
It will breakGrey rotten wood, already cracked, with a corner gone. It creaks and sheds dust before it goes.
It movesIron and timber like the rest, but it always hangs from or runs on something you can see: a cable over a wheel, a chain, a rail.
It is sceneryThe same timbering, but greyer, darker and cooler than the timber you climb, never honey-coloured, and never inside the play space. Nothing thin hangs in it near the climb.
It will hurt youIt comes out of a dark hole you can see, and dust falls from the hole first.

The three layers here

BackgroundThe rest of the working, carried on behind you: the back wall with its timber sets, ladder ways, boarded side tunnels, ore chutes, and further back the far wall of the cavern and the waterfall.
Play spaceThe beams, planks, rungs, rails and rock that are still standing. Each one is the near end of something that runs back into the background.
ForegroundThe front post of a timber set, in broken lengths, and a low lip of rubble along the bottom of the frame. Only in front of rock, never in front of the open space you climb through.

How you come in, and how you leave

In: On the cart, down the tunnel from the station. The tunnel's timber sets have gone from whitewashed to grey and wet by the time the buffer tips you out, and you have already seen the waterfall cavern once, through a gap, on the way down.

Out: Up beside the top of the waterfall to its lip. The fall turns out to be the works' river going over a brick weir: the last timber set of the mine stands against the first brick arch of the works, and the amber lantern light gives way to cold teal.

La Mina Vieja · A place to rest · place 1 of 15

1.0 The Sump and the frog's cave

This is the bottom level of the mine, and it is under water.

When the mine worked, a watchman and a line of buckets kept this level dry, and a timber staging crossed it on piles. Then the water won. What is left above the surface is the heads of the piles, the caps of the drowned timber sets along the back wall, and the foot of the great waterfall, which lands here white and loud. Everything that falls far, from anywhere on the mountain, ends in this pool. At its west end, past the foot of the fall where nobody would think to swim, a doorway in the rock leads to the watchman's little room. It is dry, a lantern is lit in it, and the mine's frog lives there now.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The frog's cave. A dry room cut in the rock behind the west wall: 4.2 m wide and 2.7 m tall, with a doorway 1.2 m deep and 2.1 m high. Its floor and doorway come forward through the play space so you can walk in, and its front is cut away. Further back in it: a little stove with a kettle, an upturned ore bucket with the frog sitting on it, a shelf of boots and masks that the water has brought in, and one lit lantern, the only warm light at the bottom of the mine. Scratched up the door post are the watchman's marks of the water rising. The last one is level with the doorstep.
  • 2The rock the cave is cut in. The course's west wall is a skin of rock 4 m thick with nothing behind it. The room needs rock all round it, so the wall is carried on to the west and back. It is black and running with the fall's spray.
  • 3The foot of the waterfall. The fall lands here after 113 m. From the pool it is a white column 6 m wide going up out of sight, and it is the brightest thing in the picture. Where it hits, the water is white and the mist hides the west wall, so you find the cave's doorway by its warm light. The sheet of water itself comes forward through the play space: you swim through its foot.
  • 4The drowned level. Along the back wall, 3 to 4 m behind you: the timber sets of the bottom level, under water to their caps, and a side tunnel boarded shut that you see through the water. A barrel from the works above is wedged against one cap. What goes over the fall ends up here.
  • 5Carts on the bottom. Lying on the floor of the pool behind you, seen through the water: three old ore carts, one on its side. The cart from El Carrito Loco sinks here every time it goes over, so it has company.
  • 6The staging's back row. Behind each pile you can hold stands its twin, with a stub of the deck beam that joined them. The staging was a walkway two piles wide. Its deck is gone.
  • 7The way out. The mine's pug arrow, nailed to a back pile and pointing east along the piles. It is the only thing down here that tells you which way to swim. The kit has it.

Play space

  • 8The doorstep. New, from note 71: a rock step at the doorway, 0.8 m out from the wall, its top half a metre above the water and worn hollow in the middle. It is pale dry rock, so it reads as a thing to hold, and it is how you pull yourself out. The cave's floor behind it is the same pale rock.
  • 9The piles. Each pile gets a dark stain up to the old high water mark and a rusted iron band round its head, so it reads as the leg of something built and not as a pole in the water.

Foreground

  • 10The near bank. A low lip of black wet rock along the bottom of the frame, below the pool's floor. It is the front card that is there today, kept, because it covers only rock.

The waterThe flooded bottom level of the mineThe drowned timber sets, the boarded tunnel, the carts on the floor
The doorstep and the cave's floor (new, note 71)The step and the floor of the watchman's roomThe room itself: stove, shelf, lantern and frog
The falling waterThe foot of the great waterfallThe white column going up out of the frame, and the mist at its foot

What I am not touching

  • The pool, its water level and its floor, and the piles, each where it is.
  • The falling water's push, and the 6 m of calm under it just above the pool.
  • The way out is still the long swim east to the landing stage. The cave leads nowhere.
  • The only new things you can touch are the doorstep and the cave's floor, both from note 71.

What it would change in the game

  • Course change: a doorway is cut through the west wall at the water line, a rock doorstep 0.8 m wide is added in the water in front of it, and the cave's floor is 5.4 m of new ground to stand on. Nothing else you touch moves.

1.0b The landing stage and the incline

The east end of the Sump, and the way back up.

When the bottom level was dry, ore was hauled from it to the main gallery up a steep track, by a hand winch at the top. The rails are gone, but the sleepers are still spiked to the slope, and they are your steps. At the foot is the landing stage, the one dry plank at the water's edge, where the miners tied up the flat boat they used once the water had come. To reach it you swim under El Diente, through what was the bottom level's tunnel through the foot of the pillar. Everyone who falls into the Sump comes out here. The waterfall is 50 m behind you by now: a noise, and a cold light on the water.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The cavern's wall. The same hand-cut wall as behind Los Tablones, 20 to 34 m below the walk. Down here it is black and wet, and the lower walk's row of empty sockets is far overhead.
  • 2The tunnel through the pillar's foot. The space you swim through under El Diente was cut by the miners: the bottom level's road, 11 m long, with four timber sets. Their posts stand in the water and their caps are just under the rock. So the pillar stands on a timbered tunnel, not on a gap.
  • 3The back rail, and a cart left on it. Behind the sleepers one rail of the old track is still spiked down, from the water to the gallery's mouth, and a grey ore cart sits on it a third of the way up, where the winch let it stop.
  • 4The winch at the head of the incline. In its cut beside the gallery's mouth, as on the camp's page. Its drum is bare.
  • 5The drowned level. The bottom level's timber sets, carried on east of the pillar along the wall, under water to their caps.
  • 6A lamp post and the pug arrow. At the back of the landing stage. The lantern that hangs in the air here today gets a post to hang from. Under it the mine's arrow sign points up the incline.
  • 7The miners' boat. A flat boat 3 m long, sunk at its mooring behind the landing stage, with one end still out of the water.

Play space

  • 8Spike plates and rust lines. Each sleeper gets two iron plates where the rails were spiked, and the slope between gets two faint rust lines. The slope reads as a track with its rails taken up.
  • 9The landing stage. A plank deck on two short piles, with an iron mooring ring at its end.

Foreground

  • 10The near bank. The same low lip of black wet rock as at the Sump's west end, along the bottom of the frame and below the pool's floor.

1.1 La Galería

This was the mine's main road: the gallery the ore carts ran along to the tunnel and out to the station.

It is 5 m tall and timbered in two storeys, with a set of posts every 1.3 m because the miners knew this stretch was bad ground. They were right. Mud burst through the back wall, took 10 m of the floor down with it, and the lower posts of four sets went down too. What you cross on is what stayed up: the cross pieces of the sets either side of the hole, hanging from their upper posts, and the heads of the four sunk posts standing in the mud. It is the first place the mine asks you to tell honey-coloured timber from black mud.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The gallery's back wall. Plank lining from floor to roof, held by the timber sets. A long tie timber runs along it at head height, at exactly the height of the beams you hold: they are one row. Over the pit the lining has burst outward and the tie is gone. That black hole is where the mud came from.
  • 2The back posts. Behind every beam stands its back post, with an iron strap where the beam is let into it. Over the pit the lower halves of the posts are gone and the beams hang from the upper halves. Where four sets went down altogether, two stubs are left under the roof. Today a post in hold-coloured timber hangs in the middle of the play space above each beam. It moves back to the wall and goes grey.
  • 3The slump and the cart. The pit carries on back behind you as a tongue of black mud coming down out of the burst wall. In it, half sunk: an ore cart on its side, and the bent ends of the rails, which stop at the brink on both sides. The cart is in the play space today, in iron's own colour. It moves back and goes grey.
  • 4The ore chute. High in the back wall by the door: a dark hole, and a timber chute coming down out of it on two wall brackets, to fill the carts that stood on the rails below. It says what the rails are for, and why there is a cart in the mud.
  • 5A warning sign. The mine's skull-pug diamond, nailed to the lining at the brink of the pit. It is the first one you meet. The kit has it.
  • 6Two lanterns. One over each brink, as today, but each on an iron bracket from the roof timber at the back wall. Today they hang inside the play space. Between them the pit is the darkest part of the gallery.

Play space

  • 7The four sunk posts. Each post standing in the mud keeps the cut tongue on its head where a beam once sat, and is black with mud up to a tide line. You can see they are the lower posts of the four missing sets, gone down 2 m with the floor.
  • 8The beams' torn ends. Each of the five beams shows its end to the camera, splintered where its front post tore away. The front posts are in the pit.
  • 9The mud. Black, glossy and wet from brink to bottom, with slide marks and pale drips, and nothing pale drawn anywhere on it, so the pit reads as a pit (note 52). The floor at the bottom is a slab of the old gallery floor, dry and pale, with a sleeper still on it.

Foreground

  • 10The door set's front post (there today). The door's timber set is the last of the cart tunnel's and the first of the mine's. Its back post stands behind the play space, its front post in front of it, and its cap is under the roof, out of reach, so no part of it is where you can put a hand. It stays as it is, grey and wet. This is the one place in the gallery where something stands in front of you, for one step, at a doorway you only walk through.
  • 11A low lip of rubble. Mud-caked rubble and a length of bent rail along the bottom of the frame, below the floor and below the pit. It stands in front of rock only.

1.1b The frozen climber's camp

The west end of the gallery, between the mud pit and the mouth that opens on the cavern.

The ladder shaft comes down through the roof here, so this was where the miners waited their turn to climb: there is a bench cut into the back wall for them. Long after they left, somebody who came to climb the Peak made camp on that bench, at the foot of the first hard climb. He tried the ladder, came back, scratched a mark, and tried again. He is still here, sitting against the post with his lantern gone cold.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The gallery's back wall. The same plank lining and timber sets as the rest of the gallery, on good ground here, so the posts are 2 m apart or more and all of them stand.
  • 2The miners' waiting room. A shallow room cut into the back wall, 2.1 m wide and 1.2 m deep, with a plank bench. The climber's bedroll is laid out on the bench. Above it is a rail of wooden pegs with one miner's lamp still on it. Today the bedroll lies in the play space at his feet. It moves back onto the bench.
  • 3His things. Against the wall beside him: his lantern, cold, with no light on it. A coil of rope lying flat. A pickaxe leaning on the post. They are the kit's camp pieces, set a little further back than today so that nothing lies where you walk.
  • 4The tally marks. Scratched into the lining above his shoulder, in fives: the count he kept. Pale scratches on grey planks, the brightest marks on the wall. The last row stops part way along.
  • 5The lantern that still burns. The miners' lantern above him is lit, as it is today, but it hangs on an iron bracket from the roof timber at the back wall and not in the play space. His own is not lit. The one pool of amber light at this end of the gallery falls on him and on the marks.
  • 6The bunting. The miners' bunting from town, torn, strung high between the mouth and the shaft. Today it runs 8 m along the gallery and passes behind the foot of the ladder. It is shortened to 3.5 m, so that no line crosses behind the rungs.
  • 7The winch at the head of the incline. In a second cut by the mouth: the hand winch that hauled ore up the incline from the bottom level. Its drum is bare. It tells you that the slope outside was a track, and that the timbers you walk up it on were its sleepers.
  • 8The cavern, first seen. Through the mouth: the cavern's far wall, cold grey-violet, and mist. You can't see the waterfall from here, because the pillar stands in the way. You hear it, and its blue-white light lies on the mouth's west post and along the floor.

Play space

  • 9A worn path. The floor between where he sits and the foot of the ladder is worn pale, a track one boot wide. It is drawn on the floor and changes nothing you stand on.

Foreground

  • 10A low lip of rubble. Along the bottom of the frame, below the floor, in front of rock only.

1.2 Escalera Rota

The men's way up from the gallery to the workings above: a ladder shaft 4 m wide and 13 m tall, lined with planks.

It was always the wet shaft, because the water that gets into the mine runs down its east side, so the ladder in it is iron where every other ladder in the mine is wood. It was built in four lengths, with a timber landing between each length and the next. The iron lasted. The landings did not. Each one rotted, fell, and tore out the ladder's joint as it went, and those are the three gaps you lunge across.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The shaft's back wall. Plank lining on a timber frame every 1.3 m, the same as every shaft in the mine. Here it is whole, but black with wet and green at the seams, with two planks gone.
  • 2Three rotted landings. Behind each gap in the ladder: what is left of a timber landing, its east half still in place and its west half hanging down. Each length of ladder went from one landing to the next. The three gaps are the three landings. On each one lies the bent iron rung that came out of the ladder there.
  • 3A lantern on the top landing. Today it hangs in the middle of the shaft, in the play space, from nothing. It stands on what is left of the top landing, so the longest gap is the best lit.
  • 4The frame at the head of the shaft. Two posts and a cap at the back, 2.6 m tall, round the top of the shaft. You see it from the foot of the ladder, and it marks where the climb ends. The pickaxe that lies in the play space on the ledge today leans against its west post.
  • 5A pug arrow sign. On the ledge at the head of the ladder, pointing west along the catwalk. The kit has it.
  • 6The cavern. West of the rock the shaft is cut in, the cavern opens: 20 m of air down to the Sump's beach, and the far wall a long way back, cold grey-violet. At the head of the ladder you step out into it. The waterfall is still out of sight behind the pillar, but its light is on everything to the west.

Play space

  • 7Torn rail ends. At each gap the ladder's two iron rails end in torn, rusted points, above and below. The ladder is plainly one ladder with three pieces missing. Today a bent rung hangs in each gap, in the play space, and holds nothing. Those three go from the gaps and lie on the landings behind.
  • 8Empty sockets. In the rock beside the two upper gaps: the square socket the landing's beam sat in, empty. From below you can read where the gaps are by the sockets.
  • 9The wet east wall. The wall you can't hold: glossy black with pale drips, because the water that comes down the slope at the top runs down this side. Nothing pale is drawn on it.

Foreground

  • 10The shaft's two front posts. Thin, each in three broken lengths, in front of the rock at the two edges of the shaft and never in front of the shaft itself. The same piece as El Derrumbe's.

1.3 Los Tablones

A plank walk along the cavern's wall, from the head of the ladder shaft towards the bucket lift on the pillar.

It was built the mine's way: a square timber let into a socket in the rock every couple of metres, a strut under it, and planks nailed on top. Half way along it served a side tunnel. Five lengths of the planking are still nailed down and sound. In four places a timber has dropped out of the wall and the plank over it went too, and somebody later bridged each hole with a loose grey board that rests on nothing but its neighbours. Those four are the ones that break. Under the walk there is only air: 20 m down to the beach at the east end, 34 m to the water at the west.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The cavern's wall. Hand-cut rock, flat and pick-marked, 1.7 m behind the walk. It is dry above the planks and dark with wet below them. It is the wall the walk is fixed to. Today there is nothing behind the walk for 5 m, and its braces stand in the air.
  • 2The bearers. Under each end of each nailed length: a square timber coming out of the wall to the walk, seen end-on, with a short strut under it. Nine of them. They take the place of today's slanting braces, which are in hold-coloured timber and lean across the open air under the walk.
  • 3Four empty sockets. Under the middle of each loose board: the square hole in the rock where its bearer was, empty, with a pale scar below where the strut tore off. Before you step on a grey board you can see there is nothing under it.
  • 4A boarded side tunnel. In the wall behind the walk's soundest length, with two planks nailed across it and the stub of a gangway at its foot. It is what the walk was built to reach.
  • 5The lower walk that fell. Six metres down the same wall: a row of sockets, two bearers, and one 3 m length of an older walk still in place. It is out of reach and leads nowhere. It tells you this wall sheds walks, and it gives the eye something to measure the drop by.
  • 6Two lanterns. On iron brackets in the wall, 3 m above the planks: one over the head of the ladder, one over the tunnel's cap. Today they hang inside the play space, from nothing.
  • 7The miners' bunting. Torn, strung along the wall high over the middle of the walk, where it is today. It is 4.5 m above the planks, well out of reach.

Play space

  • 8Nail heads. Each nailed length shows two rows of iron nail heads, one over each bearer. The four grey boards show none. It is a second way to tell them apart, for anyone who can't trust the colour.
  • 9The four loose boards. Grey and rotten, already cracked across, each with a corner gone: the game's one breakable look. They lie a little crooked, because nothing holds them.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.

1.4 La Cuerda del Minero

The plank walk used to go all the way to the pillar.

Its last 5 m fell while the mine was still working, and the miners did not rebuild it. They tied a rope to the arm of the bucket lift, which sticks out over the gap, and swung across. That rope is still there. It hangs from an iron rod under the arm, greased so that its hook would turn, which is why you can't climb past the rope's top. On the far side is the pillar's shoulder, with the socket of the walk's last bearer still in its face. Below is 34 m of air and the water.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The cavern's wall, and where the last span was. The same wall as behind Los Tablones, carried on to the pillar. Across the gap, at the walk's height: three empty sockets and one bearer snapped off short. The gap is plainly a piece of the walk that is missing.
  • 2The foot of the hoistway. Flat against the wall: the ragged bottom of the dark boards that the lift's weight and bucket run in front of. It is there today (note 4) and belongs to El Cubo. From here it is a dark shape at the top right that says a machine is above you.
  • 3The arm's back half. The arm you will walk along is one of a pair. Its twin is straight behind it. A slanting brace carries the pair from the pillar's face, and a cross timber ties them to the rock. Today the brace is in hold-coloured timber in the play space. It moves back and goes grey.
  • 4Two lanterns. One on an iron bracket in the wall over the pillar's shoulder. One standing on the arm's back twin. Today both hang inside the play space, from nothing.
  • 5A warning sign. The skull-pug diamond on a post at the back edge of the walk's broken end. The miners' own notice that the walk stops.

Play space

  • 6The rod's eye and strap. The rope is knotted through an iron eye at the foot of the rod, and the rod hangs from an iron strap round the arm. So you can see the whole chain of what holds you: arm, strap, rod, eye, rope. The rod is black and glossy with grease, with a drip at its foot.
  • 7The two broken ends. The walk's last plank ends in splinters. In the face of the pillar's shoulder, level with it, is the socket and the stump of the bearer that carried the other end.

Foreground

  • 8The lift frame's front post. One thin post in broken lengths, in front of the pillar's rock beside the iron rungs. It never crosses the open air.

1.5 El Cubo

The bucket lift, built up the side of the pillar between the walk's level and the station 12 m above it.

An ore bucket hangs on one side of a pulley and an iron weight on the other, so that a full bucket going down hauled the weight up, and the weight coming down hauled the empty bucket back. It is how the ore from the pillar's top got down to the plank walk. It was left as it stood, empty and in balance, and it still goes: the weight one way, the bucket the other, with a wait at each end. You ride the weight. The iron rungs up the pillar beside it were the lift men's ladder.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The cavern's wall. The same hand-cut wall as behind the plank walk, carried on up. The lift is built against it.
  • 2The hoistway. There today, and kept exactly: a dark frame on the station deck with an arm over the pulley, and the broad dark boards the weight and the bucket run in front of. It is dark, flat and broad, with no rungs and no thin lines, so it does not read as something to climb (note 4).
  • 3The pulley. On the frame's arm, where it is today, but set back against the hoistway and grey. Today it hangs inside the play space. It turns one way, stops, and turns back.
  • 4The station's back half. The deck you land on carries on back to the wall on two bearers, seen end-on under it, with a slanting brace from the pillar. On its back half: three ore crates and a spare bucket on its side. This is where ore from the pillar's top was sent down. Today the brace is in hold-coloured timber in the play space. It moves back and goes grey.
  • 5The lower station's back half. The arm's twin behind it, the brace that carries them both and the cross timber that ties them to the rock. The same pieces as on La Cuerda del Minero's page.
  • 6Two lanterns. One standing on the arm's twin, one standing on the top crate. Today both hang inside the play space, in the open air, with nothing above them.

Play space

  • 7The weight. A riveted iron box of scrap and rock with a lifting eye on top, rust orange. It is the thing you hold, so it is the brightest thing on the lift.
  • 8The bucket. It matches what you touch now (note 3): iron, rust orange, and you can hold it and stand in it. Its handle over the top stays drawn only, so that its mouth stays open.
  • 9The deck's west end. The deck stops 2.1 m short of the pillar. Its end is drawn as a finished edge with a trimmer across it, not a break: the gap was the hatch that the ore went down, and it is the gap you fall through from Vetas de Lodo.

Foreground

  • 10The lift frame's front post. One thin post in four broken lengths, in front of the pillar's rock beside the iron rungs. It stops below the station, so it is nowhere near the ribs of Vetas de Lodo.

1.6 Vetas de Lodo

The east face of El Diente, the pillar of rock the miners left standing to hold up the roof.

The gold in this mine lies in thin slanting seams of hard pale rock with soft wet clay between them, and eight of those seams cross the pillar. On this face the clay has washed out as black mud, and the hard seams stand proud of it as ribs, 0.6 to 1.2 m out. You climb the ends of the seams. The miners dug along the very same seams in the cavern's wall, and their workings are there behind you, at the same heights.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The cavern's wall. The same wall as behind the lift, cold grey-violet. The same eight seams cross it, climbing to the east at the same slant as on the pillar. They are faint lines, greyer than the rock, so that none of them reads as a ledge.
  • 2Two old workings. Where the miners followed the two richest seams into the wall: a dark slot 1.1 m high along each, with short timber props wedged in it. They are level with the two wide ribs, so each long lunge has a dark slot behind its target.
  • 3A lantern in the lower working. It lights the face from the side, so every rib throws a shadow under itself. Today a lantern hangs inside the play space about a metre from the ribs, from nothing, where it could be taken for a hold. That one goes.
  • 4The station below. El Cubo's station: the dark frame of the hoistway, and the crates on the back of the deck you start from.

Play space

  • 5The seams across the pillar. Drawn on the pillar's blank face: each rib's seam, a pale slanting band 0.4 m thick, running back across the whole pillar from the rib's root. You read the ribs as the ends of eight bands, not as eight shelves stuck on a wall.
  • 6The two wide ribs. The two you lunge for get a row of old drill holes along their edge. The miners started on these two and stopped. All eight ribs are pale, chalky and dry, with a broken edge.
  • 7The mud between. Black, glossy clay with pale drips, oozing from under each rib. Nothing pale is drawn on it between one rib and the next.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.

1.7 El Carrito Loco

The top of El Diente was the mine's high road.

Ore came down from the upper works to this track and was pushed east along it to the bucket lift. West of the pillar the track crossed 20 m of open cavern on a deck slung by chains from a long beam under the roof. That deck has fallen and taken the track with it. What is left is the cart on its siding, held by one wooden chock, a stub of track on two slanting struts with boards nailed across its end, and one last chain, hanging where the deck used to be, too far out to reach from the boards. The track points straight at the waterfall, and that is where the cart goes. The chain is the only way off it.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The waterfall. For the first time you see it side-on and whole: a white column 30 m to the west, from the roof down past the bottom of the picture. The track is aimed at its middle. The sheet itself comes forward through the play space, and the cart falls through it.
  • 2Two slanting struts. From the pillar's west face up to the underside of the track's stub: they are what holds it out over the drop. Today the kit's 6 m trestle leg is placed here, inside the play space, and by the course's numbers its feet are in the air. The struts take its place, at the back.
  • 3The beam under the roof. What the chain hangs from. The first of Las Vigas has a hanger post behind it, up to the roof, and behind that runs a second long beam that never broke. No chain hangs from the back beam: a hanging chain in the background would look like one to take. It has empty iron eyes where the deck's other chains were.
  • 4A second cart, off the rails. On the back of the pillar's top, tipped against the wall behind the siding, grey: a cart that never made its last run. With it, the back rail of the track, which is whole.
  • 5Two lamp posts. The two lanterns here hang inside the play space today, 3.4 m over the track, from nothing. Each gets a thin timber post with an iron bracket at the back of the track to hang from.
  • 6The warning sign. The skull-pug diamond before the cart. Today it stands just inside the play space. It moves back 0.4 m, to the back edge of the track.

Play space

  • 7The one chain. Parker, 11-13: one chain, not two. It hangs 2.6 m past the end of the boards, where the far chain hangs today, which is 1.6 m further out than the near one. From the boards it is out of reach, so riding the cart is the only way to it. It is a real chain with links you can see, the kit's chain from higher up the mountain, in the rusty red the chains have now. It hangs from an iron eye bolted through the first beam, and its tail is at chest height over the cart's road. Catch it while the cart is falling and you keep the chain: the cart drops away under you.
  • 8The near chain goes. The chain that hangs 1 m from the end of the boards today is taken away (crossed out here). With the boards solid it could be taken without riding the cart. An empty iron eye is left in the beam where it hung.
  • 9Boards across the track's end. There today (note 6): the miners' own stop, three boards nailed across the last 1.6 m of rail, with the rails' ends bent down past them. A track that ends in the air always gets these. The rails themselves lie flat on the track you walk on and stay as part of it.
  • 10The chock. A wooden wedge under the cart's west wheel. Your weight in the cart rocks it off the wedge. It is why the cart waits, and why it goes. It is drawn on the track and is too small to be a thing to hold.

Foreground

  • 11A front strut's foot. The front twin of the back struts is gone. What is left is its lower end in two short lengths, in front of the pillar's rock and nowhere else.

La Mina Vieja · Challenge · place 11 of 15

1.8 Las Vigas

Under the flat roof of the cavern, 78 m above the water, the miners hung one long beam on four posts bolted into the roof.

It ran from above the track's end to the landing under the winding wheel, and the deck of the track's long crossing hung from it on chains. When the deck fell, its weight snapped the beam in three places. The four pieces are still there, each on its own post, each sagging to a different height, with 2.5 m of air between one splintered end and the next. A second beam at the back never broke, and shows the line the first one had. You go along what is left the only way there is: swing under a piece, let go, land on the next. The waterfall is in front of you the whole way.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The waterfall. Straight ahead, 6 m past the last beam, and you fling towards it three times. From here it is a sheet 6 m wide, white, with the winding wheel turning slowly in its spray at the top left. It lights the beams from in front.
  • 2The back beam. The twin of the beam you are crossing, close under the roof and all in one piece, 18.5 m long. It shows what the four pieces were. Along it are the empty iron eyes the other chains hung from. No chain hangs from any of them.
  • 3Four hanger posts. One behind the middle of each piece, from the piece up to the roof. Today a post in hold-coloured timber stands in the middle of the play space on top of each beam. It moves to the back and goes grey, so the top of a beam is clear to land on.
  • 4Two lanterns. On iron brackets on the hanger posts of the first and third pieces, at the back. Today they hang inside the play space, just over the beams.
  • 5Stalactites, kept off the route. The roof's stalactites hang only east of the first beam. By the course's numbers a 6 m one is placed at the roof between the second and third beams today. That one goes: nothing may hang in the air you fling through.

Play space

  • 6One chain. Parker, 11-13: one chain hangs from the first beam, not two. It is the one you arrive on from the cart: a real chain with links, rusty red, 9 m long. The near chain (crossed out here) is taken away.
  • 7Splintered ends. Every end that faces a gap is splintered. The two outer ends are sawn square. So the four read as one beam, broken in three places.
  • 8Iron stirrups. A rust-orange iron stirrup round each piece where its hanger post takes it. It is what the piece hangs in, and it is the one spot on each beam that looks strong.
  • 9Bolt plates in the roof. Drawn on the roof above each post: an iron plate with four bolt heads.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.

La Mina Vieja · Challenge · place 12 of 15

1.9 La Polea Grande

The mine's biggest machine, at the foot of the throat the waterfall comes down.

It is a winding wheel 6 m across that hauled the big ore buckets up from the bottom level, 85 m below. It was never turned by hand. A trough catches the edge of the fall and tips it onto a water wheel on the same axle, just behind, and the water wheel turns the winding wheel. The water has not stopped, so neither has the wheel: one slow turn every 20 seconds, with nothing left on it to wind. The planks under it are the landing where the buckets were unhooked. The black sloping roof over it kept spray and falling rock off the machine. You take the rim at the bottom, and it lifts you up the side nearest the fall, over the top, and down to the porch of the upper gallery.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The waterfall. Right beside you. The wheel's rim passes within a metre of it, and for a quarter of the ride you are going up with the water coming down at your shoulder. It is white, loud, and the brightest thing here by far.
  • 2The water wheel. On the same axle, a metre and a half behind the wheel you ride: a wheel with buckets round its rim, 5 m across, running with water. It turns with the front wheel, so you can see that one drives the other.
  • 3The trough from the fall. A timber trough from the edge of the waterfall to just past the top of the water wheel, under the sloping roof. Water runs along it and falls onto the wheel's east side. That is why the wheel turns the way it does.
  • 4The frame that carries it. Two long bearers run out from the rock under the axle, on a slanting strut. The staging hangs under them on two posts, and the porch you step off onto is their near end. Today the staging's brace is a hold-coloured timber in the play space. It goes.
  • 5The roof's posts. Two posts at the back, from the bearers up to the sloping roof. They show that the black slab over the wheel is a roof on a frame, not a loose rock.
  • 6The upper gallery. The same back wall as on El Derrumbe's page: timber frames along the gallery and a side tunnel boarded shut. The ore crate that stands in the play space today, where it looks like a step, moves to the back wall.
  • 7A lantern at the gallery's mouth. Today it hangs inside the play space just outside the wheel's rim, where you come down. It moves onto an iron bracket on the back post of the mouth's timber set.

Play space

  • 8The hub. An iron-banded hub with the square end of the axle showing in its middle. The axle is the one thing that goes from the wheel you hold back to the wheel that drives it.
  • 9The staging. One run of planks, as it is now (note 8), with two rows of nail heads where the hanging posts take it.
  • 10The sloping roof and the life ring. The roof is black wet boards with pale drips running down to its lower edge, which spills into the fall. Propped at its foot is the red and white life ring (note 15). It belongs to La Cortina's page.

Foreground

  • 11The mouth's front post. The timber set at the gallery's mouth keeps its back post and its cap. Its front post is cut to two lengths, one below the gallery's floor and one above its roof, both in front of rock. The length between them is gone, because it would stand in front of the porch at the moment you land on it.

The porchThe near end of the bearers that carry the axleThe bearers and their strut
The slick roofThe machine's roof, to keep spray and rock off itThe two posts that hold it up
The gallery floorThe upper gallery, where El Derrumbe startsIts timber frames and the boarded tunnel

La Mina Vieja · Challenge · place 13 of 15

1.10 El Derrumbe

This was the miners' way between two levels of the mine: a timber-lined shaft, 3.6 m wide and 15 m tall, with a hoist in the front half to haul ore up and a ladder way in the back half for the men.

Then the roof came in. The falling rock went down the middle of the shaft and snapped every cross-beam on its way. What is left sticking out of the two walls are the broken ends of those beams, and they are your holds. The ladders behind are still mostly there, out of reach. The roof is still coming down.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The chimney. The hole in the roof the rocks fall out of, black inside, with snapped roof timbers and torn planking hanging round its mouth (note 12).
  • 2The hoist's wheel. Knocked crooked at the head of the shaft. It says what this shaft was for. No cable hangs from it: a hanging line reads as something to hold. The cable is down at the bottom.
  • 3The shaft's back wall. Plank lining held by a timber frame every 1.3 m, some planks gone with dark rock showing. Two pale scars run down its middle where the rocks scrape it: they mark the two lines the rocks fall down, before you have seen a rock.
  • 4A lantern left on a landing. Today a lantern hangs in the very middle of the shaft, in the path of the rocks. It moves here, where it lights the back wall so a falling rock shows up dark against it.
  • 5The ladder way. In the back half of the shaft: a half landing behind every stub, and short ladders between them, one snapped. You can see the easy way up the miners had, and you can't get to it.
  • 6The foot of the fall. The rubble heap carries on back into the scene behind the slope you walk up. Half buried in it: the hoist's crushed bucket and its cable in a heap.
  • 7The lower level's back wall. Timber frames along the gallery, and a side tunnel boarded shut with two planks nailed across.
  • 8A warning sign. Beside the rubble: the mine's skull-pug diamond, for falling rock. The kit has it.
  • 9The upper level. Timber frames, and the hand winch that worked the hoist, standing at the shaft's edge with its handle in the air.

Play space

  • 10The rock between the two levels. The biggest thing on the screen, and today a blank brown face. It gets a slanting seam of gold ore and a few old drill holes, drawn on its face.
  • 11Sawn ends. Each stub's beam runs on into the rock, and its square sawn end shows on the rock's face beside it. You can read where the holds are from the row of little squares up each wall.
  • 12Splintered ends and empty sockets. The stubs get splintered ends, and the walls get an empty socket wherever a beam is gone altogether. The three long lunges across the shaft are at exactly those places.

Foreground

  • 13The shaft's two front posts. Thin, each broken in two or three places. They stand in front of the rock at the edges of the shaft, never in front of the open shaft, so they frame the climb and cover nothing you need to see.
  • 14A low lip of rubble. Along the very bottom of the frame, below the gallery's floor. It covers nothing you can stand on.
