La Mina Vieja · Challenge · place 14 of 15

1.11 La Cortina

The last climb in the mine: 17 m up the back wall of the throat, right beside the top of the waterfall, to the dry shaft that goes up through the roof into the works above.

No timber lasts in this spray, so the miners went up it on iron. They hammered staples into the wet rock, each a U of iron as wide as two hands, in two rows 1.3 m apart: a rung for the left hand and a rung for the right, because one row in that wet was not enough to trust. They are the same staples as the rungs up the pillar at El Cubo. All 28 are still there, rust orange, a few bent. The spray wets them in turn, one slow drip down each row. Five were bound round with pale cord by somebody who came later, with a little board nailed over each to turn the water aside, and those five stay dry. Somebody hung a rope from the lip, and somebody carried a life ring all the way up here and left it at the foot of the slope below.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The throat's back wall. The wall the staples are hammered into: black rock, polished and running with water, straight behind you. The holds float in the dark today. With the wall drawn, they are plainly in something. Inside the dry shaft at the top it is lined with planks on three timber frames, the same as every shaft in the mine.
  • 2The top of the waterfall. You are level with its top now. It comes through a slot in the roof as one smooth dark sheet and turns white a few metres down. It is 2.5 m from the west row of staples at the bottom and 4 m at the top, and the drips that wet the staples are its spray.
  • 3Drip boards. Over four of the five staples that never get wet: a short board nailed to the wall at a slant, grey, 0.8 m long. The drip runs down to it, along it and off its low end. The fifth dry staple is the top one, inside the dry shaft. The boards are why those staples stay dry, and you can see it happen.
  • 4The top drift. Behind the balcony: the same timber frames and hand winch as on El Derrumbe's page. The pug arrow sign in the drift stands just inside the play space today. It moves back 0.4 m, against the drift's back wall.
  • 5An empty camp. Against the drift's back wall: a bedroll, a cold lantern and a pickaxe, and nobody. Whoever it was got this far, looked at the last wall, and is not here. It is the second and last camp in the mine.
  • 6A lantern by the east wall. Today it hangs inside the play space between the rope and the wall, from nothing, like a third thing to take. It moves 0.8 m east and back, onto an iron bracket in the back wall.
  • 7The wheel's roof, from above. Under the slope you slide down if you fall: the two posts that hold it up and the trough from the fall, as on La Polea Grande's page.

Play space

  • 8The staples. Parker, 11-13: every hold is an iron staple, a rust-orange U of iron hammered into the rock, about 0.5 m wide and standing a hand's width out from the wall, in place of today's rock knob. A few are bent down at one end or pulled a little crooked. All of them still hold. Each has a rust streak on the rock under it. Wet, a staple is a shiny blue-grey and drips, as the holds do now, and it is dry for longer than it is wet.
  • 9The five that stay dry. The same staples, bound round and round with pale cord, the way a tool's handle is bound. Cord is pale where iron is orange, so they keep the other colour they have today, and cord is a thing you hold. They are ringed here. They never get wet, and they are the rests.
  • 10The rope and its bracket. There today (note 14): 8 m of rope from an iron bracket under the lip. The bracket gets a strap back to the shaft's last timber frame, so you can see what the rope hangs from.
  • 11The life ring. There today (note 15), propped at the foot of the wet slope. It is the one painted thing in the mine, red and white, from the town: the town follows you up.
  • 12The balcony. The drift's floor timbers, carried out 3.6 m into the throat. Their sawn ends show at its west edge.

Foreground

  • 13A front post on the east wall. In four broken lengths, in front of the rock east of the throat. It is 2.5 m from the rope and never in front of the staples.

Why it works

What I am not touching

  • All 28 holds where they are, the two slow drips, dry for longer than wet, and the five holds that never get wet, in another colour (note 13; Parker, 11-13).
  • The rope from the lip to half way down (note 14), and the life ring's throw back to the balcony (note 15).
  • The balcony you start from and the lip you finish on.

What it would change in the game

  • Course change (note 13; Parker, 11-13): each of the 28 holds becomes an iron staple, a U of iron about 0.5 m wide, in place of a rock knob. Each staple's middle is where its knob's middle is today, and the drips and their timing do not change. A bar 0.5 m wide is a little wider to catch than a knob, so the reaches should be tried again in the game.

La Mina Vieja · A join between two biomes · place 15 of 15

1 to 2 The lip: from the mine to the black waters

The top of the dry shaft, where the mine stops and the works begin.

The miners' shaft came up through the roof here into a river cave. A generation later the company built its water works along that river and laid brick straight on top of the mine: a weir across the river's end, a pier to keep the water out of the old shaft, and a brick arch over the shaft's mouth, standing on the miners' last timber set because it was there. So within one screen everything changes hands. Posts and planks give way to brick and stone, rust-orange pipe appears overhead, the amber lantern is below your feet and the next one is greenish. And you find out what the waterfall is: the works' river, black and fast, going over the edge 6 m from where you stand.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The mine's side: the throat's back wall. Below the roof: the wet black rock of La Cortina, and the plank lining inside the dry shaft. This is the last of the mine's way of building.
  • 2The river going over. At the back, a brick sill with a stone coping holds the river 1 m deep. The water slides over it, bends, and drops into the slot as one dark sheet. Nothing here is a block of water with a flat end (note 22). From the ledge you look straight across the top of the fall you have climbed beside since the mine's first room.
  • 3The works' side: a brick wall in bays. Above the roof: the back wall of the river tunnel, in slate-grey brick, divided by flat piers every 4 m, with a round arch bricked up in each bay. It is the first brick in the game, and round arches are only ever the works'.
  • 4The last timber set, and the first arch on top of it. In the mouth of the dry shaft stands the mine's last set: two grey posts and a cap. The works' first arch springs straight off that cap, brick on timber, with a cast iron pug in its middle. It is lower than every other arch on the wall, because the shaft was here first. This one object is the join.
  • 5Two lanterns. The mine's last, amber, on an iron bracket on the west post of the timber set, lighting the shaft from inside. The works' first, greenish, hung high over the ledge where the works have it today. Climbing out of the shaft you pass from one into the other.

Play space

  • 6The lip ledge. Two layers, and they should look like two. Below: the miners' rock ledge, pale and pick-marked. On top of it: a course of pale stone coping, the first of the copings you stand on all through the works. The ledge's west end, where your hand first lands, shows five courses of dry pale brick under the coping.
  • 7The pier. Between the slot and the shaft: a brick pier with a peaked stone cap, black and slimy with the river's spray. Wet brick is the works' way of saying you can't hold it. Its foot, inside the mine's roof, is rock.
  • 8The rope's bracket. The mine's last piece of iron (note 14), strapped back to the last timber set.

Foreground

  • 9One post, timber below and brick above. In front of the pier's rock and nowhere else: a grey timber post up to the roof line, and on top of it a brick pier half a metre wide. It is the foreground's own version of the join.

Las Aguas Negras

The flooded works, 86 to 176 m. Brick, iron pipe and black water, along the river that feeds the great waterfall.

After the mine's timber, the works should feel richer and colder: brick, cast iron and black water, built to last and half drowned. The pitch here is machines that still run by themselves and pipes that all go somewhere. What tells you a thing can be held is where it stands, not its colour: if it is in front with you, it holds. The dam ends it with your one lift, straight up a shaft.

What this place is

When the mine was rich, the company built a water works above it: a dam, a mill race, a water wheel, an aqueduct, sluice gates, pumps and a boiler house, all to wash ore and drive machines. It is a generation newer than the timber mine and it was built to last: brick and cast iron, not posts and planks.

Then the river took it back. The lower floors are under black water, the current runs through the arches, and the whole works leaks, drips and steams. Some of it still runs by itself: the wheel turns, the gates rise and slam, the pipes are hot.

The river flows east and goes over the lip into the mine as the 113 m waterfall. Anything that goes in the water here is on its way to the Sump.

How it is built

  • Brick, in slate-grey courses, with round arches: doors, culverts, the aqueduct's spans, the windows of the boiler house.
  • Buttresses and piers with a pale stone coping on top. The copings are what you stand on.
  • Cast iron: pipes on wall brackets, with flanged joints and valve wheels; riveted plate; grated catwalks on brackets; chain. Sound iron is rust orange. Pipes and fittings that only carry water are green with verdigris.
  • Every pipe goes from somewhere to somewhere: out of a boiler, along a wall, into a tank. No pipe just stops.
  • The company's pug is cast into the iron: on valve wheels, on gate frames, on the boiler door.
  • Timber only as left-overs from the mine below: barrels, a few planks. No timber sets.

Colour and light

Cold teal. Lanterns here are few and greenish, and most of the light comes up off the water as a pale moving shimmer on the undersides of arches. The far background is blue-black. Hot things are the only warm colour in the biome: the boiler's door, the hot pipe joints.

How it tells you what a thing is

You can hold itRust-orange iron (pipes, rungs, chain, plate), pale stone copings, dry pale brick.
You can'tBlack wet brick with slime and white drips; wet rock; greased pipe.
It will breakRusty plate, brown and cracked, with a corner gone (note 16, note 24).
It is hotA pipe joint that glows orange and shimmers, and flares before it lets go of you. The cool joints are teal valve wheels (note 23).
It movesIt is a machine, and you can see what drives it: a piston rod, a rack and a gear, a chain to a winch (note 19).
It is sceneryPipe and dark blue-grey brick that stand behind the play space, mostly verdigris green. What tells you is where it stands, not its colour: any pipe that is in the play space can be held (Parker, 11-13).
WaterBlack where it is deep, white where it falls or breaks. It pours off edges and it is never a cube (note 22).

The three layers here

BackgroundThe works, running on behind you: the wall the pipes are bracketed to, arches going back with black water under them, tanks, the boiler house, pump engines, and far off the next arcade of arches. In the middle of the biome: the foot of the well, with one dot of light far overhead.
Play spacePipes, copings, arches' crowns, the wheel, gates, chains, barrels, the catwalk, the dam's lift.
ForegroundA railing stanchion or a pipe elbow at a frame's edge, and the near bank's brick lip along the bottom. Drips falling close to the camera. Nothing in front of water you have to read.

How you come in, and how you leave

In: From the mine, at the lip of the great waterfall. The last timber set of the mine stands against the first brick of the works: the fall you have been climbing beside turns out to be the works' river going over a brick weir. Amber lantern light gives way to cold teal within one screen.

Out: At the dam's crest. The top courses of the dam are split by crystals growing down through the brick from above, the water behind the dam is clear, not black, and violet light comes down the last few metres. The grotto above is the first place on the climb that nobody built.

Las Aguas Negras · Challenge · place 1 of 14

2.1 El Borde

This is the tail of the works: the brick tunnel that carries the river its last stretch to the weir, where it goes over into the mine as the great waterfall.

The company ran an iron water main under the tunnel's roof, from the wheel pit above to the dry shaft, to send wash water down to the mine. It is bracketed to the back wall and it is the only way across. Two lengths of it have rusted through. Just upstream of the weir hangs the chain that once held a boom across the river to catch driftwood: it is the last thing you can grab before the lip.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The tunnel's back wall. Slate-grey brick, 6 m tall, with a brick rib every 6 m. Upstream of the weir, round culvert mouths open at the waterline with black water going back under them. On the ledge there is one arch, bricked up.
  • 2The weir, carried on behind. The weir is as wide as the tunnel. Behind the slot you fall through, the same stone lip and the same white sheet of water run back into the scene, so the slot is the near end of a real weir.
  • 3The main's brackets and its two ends. A cast bracket from the back wall under the main every few metres, and a bigger one where the chain hangs. At the west end the main turns up through the roof to the wheel pit. At the east end it turns straight back to the wall. From there on it is scenery: it runs flat along the back wall, 2.6 m behind you, and goes down the dry shaft. Every length of it that is in the play space is a length you can hold.
  • 4What the landing hangs from. Three iron beams out of the back wall carry the brick landing over the river. You see their ends under it.
  • 5The head of the dry shaft. The last timber set of the mine, standing against the first brick of the works. It belongs to the join from the mine and is drawn here only so the two pages agree.
  • 6The first works lantern. On a wall bracket over the ledge, greenish and steady. It is the first cold light after the mine's amber.

Play space

  • 7The two rusted lengths. Already in the game (note 16): brown, cracked, a corner gone. They are drawn here so the page shows the place as it is.
  • 8Flanged joints on the main. A bolted flange every 3 m and at each end of a rusted length, drawn on the main. They say it is a pipe and not a girder.
  • 9The weir's stone lip. A pale stone coping on the edge the river goes over, with white water breaking on it. The pier's peaked top stays black and wet.

Foreground

  • 10A pipe at the frame's east edge. One riser pipe with an elbow, in front of the solid rock east of the ledge. It stands in front of the play space, so it is scenery, and it never crosses open space.
  • 11The near bank's brick lip. A low broken run of brick along the bottom of the frame, below the river's bed. It stops short of the weir, so nothing stands in front of the water or the fall.

2.2 La Rueda

The wheel pit.

The race runs through the bottom of the mill and turns a water wheel, and the wheel turned everything else: it is one of a pair on the same axle, and the axle runs back through the wall to the mill's gearing. The mill is flooded and nothing is geared to it any more, but the race still runs, so the wheel still turns. You come up the wheelwright's ladder well, step on to his landing, and ride a paddle up.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The pit's back wall and the wheel arch. Brick to the roof. Behind the wheel a round arch 5.4 m wide opens in it, with the race coming out of the dark under it. This is where the race's water comes from.
  • 2The second wheel. The same wheel again, 4 m further back on the same axle, turning with yours in the dark of the arch. It is greyer and wetter than the one you ride. On the sketch it is the ring round your wheel's spokes.
  • 3The wheel's frame. A cast-iron frame standing in the race just behind the wheel, with the axle's bearing at its top. Nothing stands in front of the wheel.
  • 4The ladder well's lining. A round brick well cut in half, 1.8 m across, with the iron rungs you climb let into it and a cast ring where it opens at the landing.
  • 5A works lantern. On a wall bracket over the arch. Steady: nothing in this biome's light pulses (note 17). The moving light here is the slow shimmer the race throws up on the underside of the arch.

Play space

  • 6Paddle boards and the hub. Each spoke ends in a paddle board, drawn on its end, and the hub gets an iron boss with the company's pug cast in it. The boards lift water and drop it as they come round.
  • 7The landing's coping. A pale stone coping on the brick landing, like every place you stand in the works.

2.3 El Acueducto

The aqueduct was the wheel's feed: a brick trough on round arches, sloping gently down from the east wall to the top of the wheel.

It was built two arches thick. The back half still stands whole. The front half, the half with the trough on it, has lost three spans into the race, and what is left of it is four pier tops with a stump of trough on each. On the wall above every span is a pair of iron rings: the masons' lifting rings, for the tackle that took the trough's plates out for cleaning.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The standing arcade. The aqueduct's back half: the same four piers, with the three round arches still whole between them, and plain brick above the arches up to the roof. It shows what each gap was. The piers under your pier tops are its piers.
  • 2Black water going back. Through each arch: the race going back under a second, further arcade, lit only by the shimmer off the water.
  • 3The fallen spans. Heaps of brick under the water at the foot of each gap, behind where you swim. You can't stand on them.
  • 4The hatch. The ladder up the east wall goes through the roof by a brick-lined hatch with a cast iron rim.
  • 5Ring pads and plates. Note 18: the six chains are gone. Behind each ring, a short brick pad built out from the arcade's wall with a riveted iron plate on its face, the way a mooring ring sits on a quay. The pad stops at the back edge of the play space. It is scenery because of where it stands.
  • 6Two works lanterns. On brackets on the arcade's piers, not hung in the air between the rings. Steady.

Play space

  • 7The rings' eye bolts. Each ring stands on a short eye bolt that points straight at you from its plate. From the side the bolt is hidden behind its own ring, so nothing new shows in the play space and nothing new can be held. Nothing hangs above a ring.
  • 8Broken ends. Each pier top shows the trough's section on its broken end, and under it the first few bricks of the arch that sprang from it, drawn on.
  • 9Copings. The pale stone rim of the trough along the top of each pier top. It is what you land on.

2.4 Brazo de Molino

The wash house, one floor above the wheel.

Ore was washed here in a long brick channel, the mill arm, with a steady stream sent down it from a culvert at the west end. Along the far bank stand the round tanks the washed ore settled in. A filler pipe comes out of the wall over the landing, runs out over the channel's drain and ends in an open spout, still dribbling. The washers got out of the channel by iron rungs in the west wall: the top two are left.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The wash house's back wall. Brick, with two round arches barred with iron. The far background, blue-black, shows through the bars.
  • 2The inlet culvert. A round arch at the waterline at the west end, with a rack of iron bars across it. The channel's water slides out of it. It is where the current comes from.
  • 3The far bank and the settling tanks. A stone-coped bank just above the water, and on it two round iron tanks, 2.5 m across, riveted, dull blue-grey. A green pipe goes from each tank up into the roof.
  • 4The filler pipe's wall end. Over the landing the pipe turns back into the wall through a teal valve wheel. Two wall brackets carry it out over the drain.
  • 5A works lantern. On a wall bracket at the west end, over the rungs you are swimming for. Steady.

Play space

  • 6The spout. The pipe's west end is drawn as a flared open mouth turned down, with a thin dribble of water falling from it. It marks the place to let go.

  • 8Copings. Pale stone copings on both landings.

Foreground

  • 9The channel's near wall, cut down. One broken course of brick along the bottom, below the channel's bed and in front of solid rock. It says the channel has a near side. It is lower than the water's bed, so the whole swim is in clear view.

2.5 Las Compuertas

The gate hall.

Three sluice gates stand in the back wall, one above the next like a flight of locks, and each let water on to one floor of the mill. A gate is too heavy to wind up by hand, so the company stood a water-pressure ram in front of each one. The works' regulator still runs them: pressure from the lake lifts a ram slowly, holds it, then the valve dumps and the gate's own weight slams it shut. What you ride is the head of a ram.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The gate hall's back wall. Brick, 20 m tall, wet and black low down where the gates leak, paler above.
  • 2The three gates. Behind each ram: a sluice gate in a cast-iron frame, with the pug cast in the frame's head and a rack and gear, seized, beside it. The gate's leaf is yoked to the ram's head and goes up and down with it. While a gate is up you see black water moving behind it.
  • 3The regulator and its pipes. A riveted valve chest high on the wall, and a fat pipe from it down to each ram, all of it flat on the back wall, well behind the play space. This is what drives them, and you can see it.
  • 4A works lantern. On a wall bracket beside the regulator. Steady.

Play space

  • 5Housing, ram and head. Note 19: each rising block is redrawn as a machine piston, the same size and with the same top. A fixed iron housing stands on the step where the block rests today. A broad ram, as wide as the head, comes up out of it carrying the head. Housing and ram stand in the play space but are black with oil and running wet, so they plainly can't be held.
  • 6The heads. The part you hold: a thick riveted plate in rust orange with a raised rim, drawn on today's top.

Foreground

  • 7The regulator's supply pipe. One riser pipe in front of the solid rock east of the hall. It stands in front of the play space, so it is scenery, and it never crosses the hall.

The catch chamber of El Desague, the works' great drain.

A riveted iron pipe 5 m across comes down through the roof, and under it an iron hopper funnels whatever falls into a wider pipe that drops to the river. 2.0 The frog's valve chamber

A dry valve chamber, cut in the brick under the fitters' gallery.

The keeper of the pool worked the outlet valve from here. It is a round brick vault 3 m wide and 2.6 m tall, and you walk into it from the east end of the ledge where El Charco del Pozo starts. Its round iron door was left ajar. You walk the gallery above without knowing it is there. When you drop to the ledge and turn round, the door is behind you. The frog lives in it.

2.7 El Charco del Pozo

The foot of El Pozo del Diablo.

The well was here long before the company: a round shaft of black rock, 12 m across, that goes up through the whole mountain. The company built a brick hall round its foot and used the pool under it as a reservoir, and floated barrels across it from a store in the west wall. So the hall is brick on both sides and bare wet rock in the middle, where the well comes down. Stand under it and look up: the shaft goes up out of sight, and at the very end of it is one dot of light. You will cross this shaft three times higher up, and everything that falls from those crossings lands here. This is the place the mountain sends you back to.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The hall's two brick flanks. Brick, 15 m tall, west and east of the well, each ending in a brick pier against the rock. A bricked-up round arch stands in the east flank. Each ledge sits on iron beams out of its flank: you see the beam ends under it.
  • 2The well's own rock. Between the two flanks there is no brick: black wet rock, the back of the well, from the water up through the roof and on up. Where the hall's roof meets it there is a ring of pale stone, the collar the company put round the well's mouth. The well keeps this width, 12 m, at every place you will meet it.
  • 3The throat. The look up the well, built the way a paper diorama builds a tunnel: five rings of black rock cut out of card, each smaller, further back and higher than the last. The first is 12 m across and touches the roof. The last is under 2 m. Each ring has a thin pale edge on its upper side, lit from above. Today this is one flat black shape. The rings make it a shaft.
  • 4The dot of light. Behind the last ring: one small pale dot, the top of the well, 365 m up. It is the only thing in the biome that is daylight. It does not flicker.
  • 5What has fallen. On a shelf of rock at the back of the pool, under the well, far behind the barrels: a broken crystal point, a rotted mushroom cap as big as a table, a carved stone block with a pug's face, and a coil of rope. One thing from each place above where the well is crossed. All of it grey-blue and dim, like the rest of the scenery.
  • 6The barrels' cove. Note 21: a round brick arch at the waterline in the west flank, black inside, where the barrel store's slipway meets the pool. Each barrel floats forward out of the dark. It can't be touched until it is in your own plane.
  • 7The frog's door. At the east end of the ledge you start from: the round iron door of the valve chamber, left ajar, and the room behind it. It has its own page.
  • 8Two works lanterns. One on each flank, on wall brackets, greenish and steady. There is no lantern under the well. The middle of the hall is lit only by the pale light that comes down the shaft.

Play space

  • 9The lip. A worn stone sill where the pool goes over into the fall, with white water breaking on it. A barrel tips on it before it goes.
  • 10Copings on the two ledges. Pale stone copings, as everywhere you stand in the works.
  • 11Hoops and brands. Each barrel gets two iron hoops and the company's pug branded on its end, drawn on. They are the mine's barrels: timber here is only ever a left-over from below.

2.9 Tubería

The boiler house.

The boiler stands at the bottom, behind the stoker's grating, with its fire still in. Its steam pipe climbs the hall in three flights to the pump engine at the top, which lifted water back up to the works. The hall's floor is the tail pool, so everything stands on three brick piers, each a storey taller than the last, like a giant's stair. The steam pipe itself runs up the piers behind you, wrapped in lagging. At each joint a short bare stub comes forward off it and ends in a bolted flange, and those flanges are hot. Along the top of each pier runs a cold feed pipe, out in front where you can reach it: those are the three level runs where you can rest.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The boiler house's back wall. Brick, 27 m tall, sooty above the boiler and wet at the west end, where the pool above spills down it.

2.10 La Cascada Chica

The weir hall.

The upper reach ends here and goes over a stone-coped weir, 15 m down into a pool. The keepers had a way up beside the fall: a flight of stone treads built into the back wall, then an iron ladder up the wall, then a second flight to the catwalk. Each tread is a long stone with one end in the wall, and it is the free ends you hold. The ladder between the two flights has rusted away to stumps. Someone who came to climb the Peak hung a rope there instead, from the lifting beam under the roof. The fall's spray wets the treads in turn.

2.11 La Presa

The dam: a wall of brick 15 m tall with the works' lake behind it.

Its downstream side comes down in great steps, and those steps are its spillway: when the lake is high, water runs down them to the upper reach. The keeper did not climb the spillway. He walked into the dam. A low brick gallery goes in through the dam's foot to a lift shaft, and the shaft goes straight up inside the dam to its crest. In the shaft is one small iron cage with a hand winch on board. You stand in it and wind, and the winch's pinion climbs a toothed rack on the shaft's back wall. Stop winding and the cage sinks. The dam is cut open at the front, so you see the gallery, the shaft and the cage in section.

2 to 3 The dam's crest

The top of the works, and the end of everything anyone built until the temple.

The crest is the dam's walkway, with the lake on its far side under a brick vault. An iron ladder goes up from the crest through a brick shaft in the roof. But the roof is giving way to what is above it: crystals have grown down through the top courses of the brick and split them. The lake is not black. It is clear, and it is lit from below by crystals on its bed, because this water comes from the cave. Teal lantern light reaches as far as the foot of the ladder. Violet light comes down the shaft to meet it. Two steps above the shaft's rim, the brick is gone.

  • 1The lake's brick vault. Slate-grey brick over the lake, in round-arched bays. Its top three courses are cracked, and pale light shows in the cracks.
  • 2The shaft's lining. Brick, in a round shaft cut in half, from the hall's roof up to the cave's floor. Sound at the bottom, split open by crystal at the top.
  • 3Crystals grown down through the brick. Rough points of the cave's crystal, deep blue-violet because they are scenery, coming down out of the roof and through the shaft's lining, each with split and shouldered-aside brick round its root. One of them, over the crest, is bright white and is the first of the cave's lights.
  • 4The lake's bed. Clear water, and through it small crystal points on the bed at the back, glowing faintly. They light the lake from below. They are behind where anyone would swim.
  • 5Violet light down the shaft. A soft violet light falls down the shaft and lies on the lake under it. Where it meets the last lantern's teal, on the crest, the brick is lit in both colours.
  • 6The last lantern and the last pug. On the crest, far back: the dam's sluice wheel on its spindle, with the pug cast in its hub and a crust of crystal on its rim. Over it, the last works lantern. After this there is no iron, no brick and no lantern until the temple.
  • 7The head of the lift shaft. At the crest's east end: the top of the dam's lift shaft, with its two guide rails and its buffer beam. It belongs to La Presa's page and is drawn here only so the two agree.

Biome 3 of the first seven · 11 places · 1 open question

La Gruta de Cristal

The crystal cave, 176 to 276 m. Glass and light. The first place on the climb that nobody built.

This is the first place nobody built, and after two biomes of things people made, that is the whole effect. You asked for it purely natural, so nothing here has a bolt or a chain. What moves, moves by itself: water turns the geode, a slow draught swings the pendulum. Crystals grow in points out of the wall towards you. Pale and rough means hold, dark glass means no. One place, El Prisma, throws a rainbow.

What this place is

Above the dam the mountain is hollow and full of crystal: points the size of houses, growing out of the walls, the roof and the floor. Water did this, over more time than the town has existed. The mine company never got up here, and nobody else ever built anything here either.

So nothing in the cave is made. What moves here moves by itself: a geode that turns because water runs through it, a great quartz that swings because the mountain breathes, collars of crystal that have grown round a column, with spikes that slide out and in. The cave is strange the way a living thing is strange, and nothing in it explains itself with a bolt or a chain.

The only signs of people are the ones who tried: one frozen climber, and a coil of old rope.

How it is built

  • Crystal grows in points. Six-sided in section, ending in a point, always leaning the way it grew. Crystals jut out of the back wall towards you (note 26), out of the floor and down from the roof. Nothing in the cave is a flat-topped block or a plain hexagon post.
  • Crystals come in clusters: one big point with smaller ones round its root, on a collar of rough dark rock.
  • Two kinds of crystal. Rough crystal is pale lilac, frosted, and looks like rock: you can hold it (note 30). Clear crystal is deep indigo glass, mirror-smooth: you can't.
  • What hangs, hangs on crystal: a thread of crystal as thick as an arm, grown down from the roof like a stalactite and still joined at both ends. What turns, turns in a socket of crystal worn round and smooth. No chain, no bronze, no carved stone.
  • No timber, no brick, no iron, nothing carved. One coil of old rope and one frozen climber are the only things here that came from outside.

Colour and light

Violet and ice-white. The light comes from inside the crystals: big far ones glow dimly, and each area has one or two bright white ones that light it. No lanterns, no torches. The background is deep indigo, and the things you hold are the palest things on screen. One place has other colours: behind El Prisma's shelves a faint fan of rainbow lies on the wall.

How it tells you what a thing is

You can hold itRough pale lilac crystal that looks like rock, frosted and matte; a crystal's tip.
You can'tClear indigo glass faces, mirror-smooth, with a hard white glint. They show your reflection.
It will breakPale crystal crazed with white cracks, a corner gone. It rings, sheds glitter, and goes (note 31).
It movesIt is crystal on crystal: a thick grown thread it hangs by, or a worn round socket it turns in. You can see where it rubs: the crystal there is polished and bright.
It comes and goesThe spikes on the column's collars, which are the collars' only holds: white and rough, they tremble, slide in, and snap back out with a click and a little glitter (note 34). A spike can go in under your hand.
It is sceneryCrystal further back: bigger, bluer and dimmer, with its points turned away from the climb. Never pale lilac, and never in the play space.

The three layers here

BackgroundNear: the wall the crystals you climb grow out of, rough dark rock crowded with smaller points. Far: crystals bigger than houses, dim and blue, and mirror faces that show a small moving reflection of you.
Play spaceThe points, tips, shelves and nubs you hold, each one the end of a crystal that roots in the wall behind.
ForegroundAlmost nothing (note 40). At most two dark crystal points rising from a bottom corner of the frame, below the lowest floor. Never a crystal across the climb.

How you come in, and how you leave

In: From the dam's crest. Crystals have grown down through the top of the brickwork and split it. Two steps up, the brick is gone and the floor is crystal. Teal light turns violet.

Out: By the first crossing of the well, east from a crystal horn on the west rim. On the far rim the garden has already started: roots hang into the shaft and there is moss in the cracks. You leave pale violet and land in green.

Running through it

  • Your own reflection, small, in the mirror faces behind you.
  • Nobody built this: after two biomes of timber and brick, there is not one made thing.
  • The ones who tried: one frozen climber.
  • The well: the first of the three crossings.
  • The frog: inside a split geode, sitting among the crystals.

La Gruta de Cristal · A place to rest · place 1 of 11

3.0 La Geoda de la Rana

The frog's room.

It is a geode: a hollow ball of stone, 3 m across inside, lined with crystal points, that sat whole inside the cave's west wall. At some time the face of the wall broke away here and took a slice off the geode's side. The slice lies on the floor behind. What is left in the wall is a round room with one side open, and the frog lives in it. The room is on the short piece of floor west of the hole you come up through: the side of the hole nobody has a reason to go to. You hear the frog croak as you come off the rungs.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The inside of the geode. A round hollow in the wall rock, 2.9 m across and 2.8 m tall, cut away at the front like every room you can walk into: floor, back and roof, no front wall. Its back is the far half of the same ball.
  • 2The lining. Short crystal points all round the inside, every one pointing at the middle. They are clear and deep violet, with a faint light of their own. The room is the only place in the cave where crystal is on every side of you.
  • 3The frog. It sits on a stump of crystal at the back of the room and looks at itself in one clear face, 0.9 m tall (note 60). It breathes, blinks, turns to watch you, and croaks.
  • 4The room's light. One bright white point hanging from the top of the hollow. There is no lantern: the frog's lamp is a crystal, like every light in the cave.
  • 5The rind. The geode's shell shows on the wall's face as rings of banded stone round the way in, dark blue-grey, the way a cut geode shows its rings. It tells you from across the hole that this is a geode and not a cave mouth.
  • 6The slice that broke off. The side of the geode, lying hollow side up on the back edge of the short floor like a dish 2.4 m across, lined with the same points. It is why the room is open. It replaces the cluster that stands here today.
  • 7A mirror face over the hole. A clear face 4 m wide on the hall's back wall, straight behind the top of the rungs. The first thing the cave shows you is yourself, small, climbing out of the floor. The game has this face today.
  • 8A giant, far back. One of the cave's far crystals, bigger than a house, dim and blue, standing on the hall floor well behind everything. It is there today.

Play space

  • 9The room's floor. New. Crystal has filled the bottom of the geode level, and its top is frosted and pale like the floor outside, so it reads as somewhere to stand. It is the only new thing to stand on in the whole biome, and only the room needs it.
  • 10The way in. Where the wall's face cuts the geode: an opening 2.2 m tall, so you walk in upright. Its edge is the broken rind, rough and pale for a hand's width, then the wall's dark glass above.
  • 11The kerb by the hole. Today a small white box on the east edge of the hole. It becomes a short rough point of pale crystal, the same size, standing up out of the floor.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.

Why it works

Each thing you touch is the near end of something real behind it.

You touchIt isBehind it
The short floor west of the holeThe hall's frosted floor, cut off from the rest by the holeThe slice of the geode lying on its back edge
The room's floorCrystal that has filled the bottom of the geode levelThe hollow, lined with points, and the frog on its stump
The way inWhere the geode's side broke away with the face of the wallThe rind's rings round the opening, and the slice on the floor outside

What I am not touching

  • The hole, the rungs up through it, and the two pieces of floor either side of it stay exactly as they are.
  • The wall above the room stays glass that can't be held.
  • The room adds one thing: a level floor 2.3 m long inside the wall, at the height of the floor outside, behind a way in 2.2 m tall. It is not on the way to anywhere.

What it would change in the game

  • Course change: a room is added in the west wall, where there is solid glass today: a floor 2.3 m long at 176 m, from x -461.3 to x -459.0, behind an opening 2.2 m tall in the wall's face.
  • Course change, look only: the small kerb east of the hole becomes a short rough point of the same size.

La Gruta de Cristal · Challenge · place 2 of 11

3.1 Primer Destello

The foot of the great hall.

You come up out of the hole onto a floor of frosted crystal and walk east along it, under a stair of six crystals, to where the floor ends against La Rampa: one face of glass, 35 degrees steep and 60 m high, the side of the biggest crystal in the cave. Everything that falls anywhere in the cave slides down that face and stops here. The stair climbs back west over your head. It follows a crack in the back wall where water once came through. Along the crack six pointed shafts of crystal have grown out of the wall towards you, all leaning the same way, up and to the west, each one higher than the last. You walk up the sloping top of a shaft to its point, hang from the point, and fling to the next. At the west end of the floor one climber stands frozen with an arm up, under the mirror he fell from.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The crack, and the rib of rock along it. A dark split in the back wall, rising west at the stair's own angle, with a ridge of rough dark rock standing 1.5 m out of the wall along it. Water came through here, and every shaft on the stair is rooted in it. Tiny points fringe the crack all the way up. You can read where the stair goes from the crack before you see the shafts.
  • 2The shafts' lower halves, and their roots. Each shaft is 4 m long. Its lower half runs back and down from the play space to its root on the rib, 1.4 m east of the part you stand on and 1.4 m lower. Round each root is a fan of three or four smaller points on a collar of rock. The lower halves and the fans are bluer and dimmer than the part you touch, and they are behind the play space, out of reach.
  • 3The foot of the mirror crystal. A clear crystal 6 m thick stands on the hall floor behind the top of the stair and leans west and out towards you as it rises. Its top is El Espejo, the next challenge. Down here it is far back, dim and blue.
  • 4A second giant, further back. Leaning the other way, with a faint light inside it. With the mirror crystal it makes the far wall of the hall. Both are there today.
  • 5The bright cluster under the stair. The one bright white crystal of this area: a cluster 4 m tall on the back edge of the floor, under the third and fourth shafts. It lights the stair from below, so the glass under-faces glint and the rough tops stay pale. One small dim cluster stands further along the floor's back edge.
  • 6A mirror face behind the frozen climber. A clear face 4.5 m wide on the back wall behind him. It shows his back, and it shows you, small, as you walk past him. It is the cave's first close look at your own reflection.
  • 7His rope, and the broken glass. A coil of old rope on the floor behind his feet: the only rope in the cave. Round it lie long shards of clear glass, the sheared-off foot of the mirror 14 m overhead, and one stubby pale point: the tip of the sixth shaft, which the falling glass knocked off. He came down with it.

Play space

  • 8The six shafts. New shapes in the old places (note 26; Parker, 11-13: truly slanted). The dark six-sided pods in the sketch are today's steps, which go. Each of the first five is a six-sided shaft 1.1 m thick, leaning 30 degrees, with its point high and to the west. The part in the play space is 3 m long: a top face 2 m long, then a point 0.9 m long. The top face and the whole point are rough pale lilac. The under-face is clear indigo glass.
  • 9Where you stand and where you hang. You stand on a shaft's sloping top and walk up it. At the top you take the point, which juts out into clear air, drop to hang from it, swing, and let go. The lines are the tops and the small circles are the points. From each point the low end of the next top is 2.2 m across and 1.3 m up. A harder fling goes straight to the next point: 4.9 m across and 2.2 m up. The first top starts 1 m above the floor, at La Rampa's foot.
  • 10The sixth shaft, snapped. The rest before the mirror. It is thicker, 1.4 m, and nearly level: its top rises only 0.8 m in 3.4 m. Its point is gone. The west end is a flat glassy break that can't be held, where the mirror's falling foot took the point off. From the fifth point its low end is 1.5 m across and 1.9 m up.
  • 11The one who tried. The frozen climber, where the course has him: standing on the floor straight under the mirror's foot, one arm reaching up at it. Clear crystal has grown up round him in a shell 3.6 m tall, and you see him through it. The shell is glass: it can't be held.
  • 12A drift of chips at La Rampa's foot. Drawn on the floor where the glass slope meets it, under the first shaft: a low drift of crystal chips and glitter, swept down by everything that has ever fallen in the cave. Nothing to trip on. It marks the place a fall leaves you.

Foreground

  • 13Two dark points in the bottom corner. Rising from the bottom left corner of the frame, in front of the floor's own thickness, with their tips below the top of the floor. They cover nothing you walk on. They are the cave's only kind of foreground, and most areas above this one have none (note 40).

Why it works

What I am not touching

  • The first is taken from the floor. The sixth is the rest before the mirror: the west end of its top stays exactly where it is today, so El Espejo's first reach does not change, and its west end still can't be held.

  • Course change: the five flings were 2.7 m across and 2.2 m up, corner to corner. They become 2.2 m across and 1.3 m up, from a point to the low end of the next top, with the rest of each rise walked up the slope. The last, onto the sixth, is 1.5 m across and 1.9 m up.
  • Course change: the sixth step keeps the west end of its top where it is. Its top slopes down 0.8 m to the east, and its body becomes a thick shaft with a broken west end in place of a six-sided pod.

3.2 El Espejo

A giant clear crystal stands on the hall floor behind the stair and leans west, and out towards you, as it rises.

By the top of the stair its upper face has come forward into the climb. That face is the mirror: 9 m of indigo glass at 67 degrees, smooth enough to show you your own face. Glass can't be held. But five ribs of rough pale crystal have grown across the face, one above another like the rungs of a ladder laid on it, and their near ends are the five nubs you climb. The lower third of the face has sheared off, which is why its foot hangs out over nothing, 2.4 m from the last shaft of the stair. The piece that broke lies in shards on the hall floor 14 m below, round the feet of the climber who was on it.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The mirror crystal. The whole of the giant: clear, six-sided, 6 m thick and 30 m long, rooted where the back wall meets the hall floor and ending in a point above the top rest. Far back and dim at its foot, close behind you at its top. The slab you climb is the one face of it that reaches the play space.
  • 2Its broad face, which shows you. Beside the slab the giant turns a flat face 2.6 m wide towards the camera, just behind your back as you climb. It is a mirror too. Your reflection climbs beside you, a little smaller than you, the whole way up.
  • 3The five ribs, running back. Each nub is the near end of a rib of rough crystal 0.4 m thick that lies across the glass and runs 2.5 m back along the face, like a rung. From the side you see only its end. They are the mirror's version of the roots: the thing you hold carries on behind.
  • 4The roots of the two rests and the loose nub. The top rest is the broken end of a fat pale shaft, and the sixth shaft of the stair is below it. Each has its fan of smaller points on a rock collar where it leaves the wall. The loose nub is the tip of one thin point with a small collar of its own.
  • 5The bright crystal that lights the face. One bright white cluster on the back wall, level with the top of the mirror and east of it. Its light rakes along the glass, so each rib throws a short shadow and stands out, and the glass itself shows one hard white glint.
  • 6The hall floor, 14 m down. Straight under the foot: the frozen climber, his coil of rope, and the shards of the piece that broke (all described in 3.1). The camera shows them at the bottom of the screen while you are on the lowest nubs, so you see what a slip costs and who paid it.
  • 7The far hall. One more giant, far back and blue, on the west side. It is there today.

Play space

  • 8The glass face. Deep indigo, mirror-smooth, with a white glint down its length. It is the cave's plainest picture of what can't be held, and it is 9 m of your route.
  • 9The five rungs and the loose nub. Each nub is drawn as the worn end of its rib: rough, frosted, pale lilac, six-sided, standing a hand's width proud of the glass. The loose nub before the foot is the same crystal, by itself.
  • 10The sheared foot. The slab's lower end is a fresh break: flat, bright at the edge, a little stepped. Below it there is only air where the rest of the face used to be.
  • 11The sixth shaft, snapped. The rest you start from, drawn as it will be (it is designed in 3.1): a thick pale shaft, nearly level, in place of today's six-sided pod. Its west end is the flat glassy break where the mirror's falling foot took its point off. The west end of its top is where it is today, so the reach to the loose nub does not change.
  • 12The top rest's wet lip. Water drips onto the west lip of the top rest from the roof crystal above, and the lip has a skin of new clear crystal: glass, where the rest of the top is frosted. It is why this rest is not quite safe.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.

La Gruta de Cristal · Challenge · place 4 of 11

3.3 Candelabros

The top of the start hall, under its sloping roof.

The floor you walked in on is 23 to 30 m straight down. Water still seeps through the roof here along one seam, and where it drips it has grown threads of crystal: each as thick as an arm, hanging straight down, knuckled every half metre like a spine. At the end of a thread, where the drop hangs before it falls, the crystal has flowered into a cluster of bright points. Three of these have grown 8.7 m long, in a row across the hall, and they are your way over. Nobody hung them. A thread bends at its knuckles, so it swings when you swing it, and its top knuckle sits in a cup it has worn in the roof.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The drip seam, going back. The seam the water comes through runs back along the roof, and younger threads hang from it behind the three you use. They are short, 1 to 2 m, as thick as the big ones, and two have small clusters that glow. Nothing long or thin hangs behind the climb: a far thread the length of yours would read as one more thing to catch.
  • 2Roof points behind the threads. The roof behind the climb is crowded with short thick points, clear and dim, 0.7 to 1.5 m long. The three long threads are plainly the longest of many. None of the short points comes near a chandelier's swing.
  • 3A mirror face that doubles the lights. A clear face 5 m wide on the back wall, below the second and third chandeliers. When a chandelier swings, its light swings in the face, and so do you.
  • 4The roots of the two rests. Each rest is the broken end of a fat pale shaft, with its fan of smaller points on a rock collar where it leaves the wall, like the shafts of the stair.
  • 5The points of two giants, below. The top of the mirror crystal, and one more further east. You are level with their points now. They are dim, blue and turned away from you.

Play space

  • 6The three sockets. Today each thread hangs from a glass knob under the roof. Each knob becomes a worn socket: a knob of clear crystal with a round cup in it, polished bright where the thread's top knuckle turns. It is glass, glossy and dark, and can't be held, as today.
  • 7The threads and their chandeliers. What is a chain today becomes a grown thread: rough pale lilac crystal as thick as an arm, in knuckles half a metre long, each grown into the next. It bends at the knuckles and nowhere else, so it hangs and swings exactly as the chain does. At its end is the chandelier: a burst of crystal points 1.2 m across, bright white, the brightest thing in the hall. Thread and cluster are one crystal, and you can hold all of it.
  • 8The far rest's frosted face. The west face of the rest you land on is rough and pale under its lip, so a low catch still holds. It is the same rough lilac as every hold.

Nothing. That is on purpose.

La Gruta de Cristal · Challenge · place 5 of 11

3.4 La Geoda

A geode is a hollow stone lined with crystal.

This one is 6 m across and it grew in a round nest in the back wall. It has come loose in the nest and it turns: three times a minute (note 29). Water turns it. The crack in the wall lets a steady run of water into the top of the nest. The water goes down the west side between the nest and the geode, pushes on the ribs of the geode's rind, and drips out at the bottom. The geode hangs on one knob at the middle of its back, which sits in a socket it has worn smooth. It is open towards you like a bowl on its side, and a wedge has broken out of its rim. You step in through that gap, walk the lining like the inside of a wheel, and step out when the gap comes round to the top, beside a broken spar of crystal that leads on.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The nest. A round hollow in the back wall, 7.5 m across, a little bigger than the geode and straight behind it, like a cupped hand. The geode grew in it. Its inside is dark, and the turning has worn it as smooth as a bowl. You see it as a dark ring round the geode, with a bright polished line where the two rub.
  • 2The water that turns it. The crack crosses the top of the nest, and water comes out of it there in a steady run a hand wide. It goes down the west side of the nest behind the geode's rim, white where it breaks on the ribs of the rind, and leaves the bottom lip as a quick drip. The west side of the geode is the side that goes down. This is the cave's one piece of running water, and it is why the geode moves.
  • 3The geode's back. The far half of the bowl, close behind you as you walk inside it: the same short points as the lining you stand on, bluer and dimmer, all pointing in at the middle. It turns with the rest. One white vein runs across it from the middle to the rim, and goes round like the hand of a clock, so you can read how fast the geode turns and which way.
  • 4The knob and its socket. At the middle of the geode's back is a knob of crystal 1.4 m across, the stump of the stalk it grew on. The knob sits in a round socket in the nest, and both are worn mirror-bright. From the front the geode hides them. They are drawn here so the maker knows what the geode hangs on.
  • 5The roots of the two rests and the spar. The rest you leave, the rest you reach and the spar between are the ends of pale shafts from the wall, each with its root fan. The spar is a thin flat one, snapped off short over the geode's crown.
  • 6The bright crystal over the way out. One bright white cluster on the wall above the spar. The way out is the brightest place in the frame, so your eye goes to it while you wait for the gap to come round.
  • 7A mirror face under the geode. A clear face on the back wall, low and to the east. It shows the geode's underside going round. It is there today, a little higher.

Play space

  • 8The geode's two skins. Outside, the rind: smooth banded stone in dark blue-grey rings, glossy and wet, with low ribs across it. It can't be held. Inside, the lining: a crust of short rough points in pale lilac, which can. The broken front edge shows both skins as rings.
  • 9The gap's two broken lips. The gap is a break: a wedge of the rim has cracked out and gone. Its two edges are ragged and stepped, and the lining's pale thickness shows on each. Nobody cut it.
  • 10The spar's broken end, and the far rest's wet lip. The spar ends in a rough pale break you can hold all round. The west lip of the rest beyond it is glass under a drip, like the lip above the mirror.

3.5 Agujas

The widest gap in the cave.

Past the geode the back wall falls away into a bay so deep that it is dark, and the only things between you and the far side are four needles of crystal: 7, 9 and 11 m apart, each a little higher than the last. The first stands on the rest you are on and the last on the rest you are going to. The two in the middle have nothing under them. Each of those is one crystal crossed with another: the upright one you see, pointed at both ends, and a second that runs straight back from its waist into the wall and holds it up. Only a needle's point can be held: the top 1.3 m, rough and pale (note 30; Parker, 11-13: the point only). Under the needles there is nothing but La Rampa, 30 to 40 m down, and it carries you back to the foot of the first stair.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The crack, and the rib of rock along it. The same crack as the stair's, higher up the wall now and climbing east under the roof. The rib of dark rock along it is the only part of the back wall that is near you here. Both rests and both middle needles root in it.
  • 2The two cross arms. Behind the waist of each middle needle: a second crystal as thick as the needle, running 3 m straight back into the rib, with a small fan of points where it enters the rock. From the front you see its six-sided end as a knot on the needle's waist. It is what holds a needle up in the air.
  • 3The roots of the two rests. The rest at each end is the end of a fat pale crystal with its fan of points, as on the stair. The first and last needles are points that have grown up out of those two crystals.
  • 4Three giants in the bay. Far crystals standing on La Rampa, well back, with their points coming up level with your feet between the needles. They are big, blue and dim, and their points lean away from you, so none of them reads as a place to land. Each has a faint light inside. They are there today.
  • 5The raft's rail. Far below your feet, one long straight clear crystal as thick as a thigh lies along the back wall, running 24 m west and 4 m down to a knot under the first rest, where a second crystal crosses it. The raft of El Prisma rides on it, and its top is polished bright from the riding. From up here it is a thin bright line. It is glass, it is behind the play space, and it is nothing to land on.
  • 6A mirror face between the middle needles. A clear face 5 m wide on the back wall of the bay, below the line of your second fling. It shows you crossing, very small. It is there today.
  • 7Two bright crystals, one at each end. A bright white cluster on the wall above each rest. The two ends of the crossing are lit and the middle is the dimmest stretch of the route, so the pale points of the needles are the brightest things in it.

Play space

  • 8The four points. Each needle's point becomes rough pale lilac crystal that looks like rock: frosted, six-sided, a little chipped, lighter towards the tip (note 30). It is the same crystal as the shafts of the stair. Same size, same place.
  • 9The shafts. Below its point each needle is clear indigo glass, mirror-smooth, with one white glint down its length. No black: the shaft is plainly the same crystal as the point, but polished where the point is rough. Glass can't be held.
  • 10The frosted sides, and the way back up. The first needle's two sides, the last needle's east side, and the nub and face under the first rest are rough pale lilac like the points. They are the places a hand can stop, and they are the only way back up from the raft's berth.

3.6 El Prisma

The Prism is the long clear crystal that lies under this stair: six-sided, 10 m long, on its side at La Rampa's own angle.

A bright crystal behind it shines through it, and the light comes out split into colours, the way glass splits light. Above it the crack in the back wall climbs steeply, and out of the crack have grown eight thin leaves of crystal, like slates sticking out of a wall, in two rows. They are your steps. They are old and full of cracks, and each one snaps off 1.3 seconds after you take it and rings as it goes: eight leaves, eight notes, one scale (note 31). If you fall, the Prism's top face slides you west onto a raft of crystal. The raft has grown round a long straight crystal that lies along the wall, sloping down to the west, and it is loose on it, as the collars are loose on the column. With your weight on it, it slides down that rail and leaves you below the first needle, with the needles and the leaves to do again. Empty, it is light enough for the cave's breath to push home: the breath blows up the hall from the west and catches the raft's tall back like a sail.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The crack, and the leaves' far halves. The crack climbs the wall here at 58 degrees with its rib of dark rock. Each leaf you step on is the last half metre of a plate 3 m long and 0.26 m thick that grew out of the crack edge-on. The plates stand in two rows, one each side of the crack, which is why the steps go left, right, left, right.
  • 2The Prism. One clear six-sided crystal, 10 m long and 2.6 m thick, lying along the wall on its side, with a point at its upper end. The glass plate that catches a faller today is its top face. It is rooted in the wall along its whole back.
  • 3The colours on the wall. Light goes through the Prism and comes out as a fan of faint colours up the back wall behind the leaves, red lowest and violet highest, roughly one band behind each leaf. They are the only colours in the cave that are not violet or white. They are dim, they are on the wall and never on a hold, and they do not move.
  • 4The bright crystal behind the Prism. The one bright white cluster of this area, on the wall under the Prism's lower side and behind it. You see it through the Prism as a blur of white. It is what throws the colours.
  • 5The raft's rail. One long straight clear crystal, as thick as a thigh, lying along the back wall just behind the raft. It starts here and runs west out of sight, 24 m along and 4 m down, to a knot where a second crystal crosses it. Its top is polished bright where the raft rides: the cave's sign for a thing that moves. It is glass, it is behind the play space, and it is nothing to hold.
  • 6The roots of the two rests. The rest at each end is the end of a fat pale crystal with its fan of points on the rib, as everywhere on the route.
  • 7A mirror face, and a giant behind it. East of the leaves, a clear face on the back wall that shows the stair from the side: you can watch the leaves break behind you in it. Below it, the point of one far giant. Both are there today.

Play space

  • 9The Prism's top face. Clear indigo glass with a white glint, and long pale scratches down it from everything that has slid here. The scratches all run west, towards the raft, so the face tells you where it will send you.
  • 10The raft. A slab of rough crystal, frosted on top, with a tall back and a low kerb at its open end, in the places the game has them. The tall back is its sail. Behind it a claw of the same crystal has grown round the rail and holds the raft to it. It hangs level, an arm's length under the Prism's low end.
  • 11The two wet lips. A drip from the roof falls on the lower rest beside the last needle, and the east lip of the upper rest is glass. Neither rest is quite safe.

3.7 Péndulo de Cuarzo

A great quartz hangs here on a thread of clear crystal 13 m long, and swings: 38 degrees each way, six seconds a swing, from the lip of one rest to the lip of the next, 16 m apart.

Nobody hung it. The thread grew down from the tip of a roof crystal, and the quartz grew crosswise on its end, like the head of a hammer. The thread has cracked through at the top and now hangs by a ball in a cup it has worn there. What swings it is the cave's breath. Air moves up this hall from west to east and out by the well, not steadily but in slow pushes, three seconds on and three seconds off, and each push sends the quartz east. You can see the breath in the glitter in the air. Under the quartz there are 17 m of air and then La Rampa. On the far rest, where there is a small white block today, stands a tiny crystal tree (note 32).

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The swept band. On the back wall behind the swing, a curved band 1.2 m wide follows the quartz's path from one rest to the other. Inside the band the wall's small points are short and all lie over the same way, like grass the wind has combed, and the rock between them is polished. Nothing taller has been able to grow in the wind the quartz makes. The band shows you how far the swing reaches before the quartz gets there.
  • 2The roof crystals, carrying back. The crystal the pendulum hangs from, and the long fin east of it, are thick roof points of clear glass that carry on back to the wall. Each is wider behind than the part that crosses the play space, so it reads as a root and not a blade.
  • 3A mirror face under the swing. A clear face 5.5 m wide on the back wall below the lowest point of the swing. It shows the quartz going over, and you on it. It is there today, a little higher.
  • 4The roots of the two rests. Each rest is the broken end of a fat pale shaft, with its fan of smaller points on a collar of rock.
  • 5The bright crystal by the socket. One bright white cluster hanging from the roof just west of the pivot. It lights the socket and the top of the thread, and throws the quartz's shadow across the back wall as it swings.
  • 6A spire on La Rampa, far below. The point of one far crystal standing on the glass slope, 6 m under the east rest. It tells you how high you are. It is there today.

Play space

  • 8The thread. One straight thread of clear indigo glass, as thick as an arm, smooth, with a white glint. It has no knuckles and does not bend. The chandeliers' threads are rough and pale and you hold them. This one is glass and you can't.
  • 9The socket at the roof crystal's tip. The tip of the roof crystal is worn into a cup, and the thread's top end is a ball that sits in it. Both are polished mirror-bright where they rub, the brightest spot on the roof. It is drawn onto the tip that is there today, 10 m above anything you can reach.
  • 10The crystal bonsai. Where the white block stands today (note 32): a tiny tree of crystal, 0.6 m wide and 1.2 m tall. It has a short twisted trunk of rough pale lilac and three flat pads of small points for a crown. It is the size of the block, it still stops what rolls along the ledge, and you can still hold it. What you touch is the trunk and the pads you see.
  • 11The near rest's wet lip. The east lip of the rest you leave from is glass under a drip from the roof crystal above. You take the quartz from the frosted top, not from the lip.

3.8 Techo de Vidrio

One great flat crystal, 21 m long and 1 m thick, grew out of the back wall here and leans across the hall like a lean-to roof, from just above the pendulum's far rest up to a landing of rock.

You cross underneath it. Its underside is clear glass. Six crusts of rough pale crystal have grown across the underside, each a band that runs back to the wall, like the mirror's rungs turned upside down, and they are the only things you can hang from (note 33). The first is reached from a broken tooth of crystal that hangs under the slab's low edge. La Rampa is 7 to 8 m below your feet the whole way. The slab's top face is polished smooth: it is where anyone who falls off the column's collars above slides back down.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The slab's root on the wall. The slab carries straight back to the wall at the same thickness. Where it enters the rock there is a seam of rough dark rock and small points along both its faces, for its whole length. It reads as one crystal growing out of the wall, not a sheet of glass hung in the air.
  • 2The six crusts, running back. Each patch you hang from is the near end of a band of rough crystal 2.5 m long that lies across the underside of the slab and joins the seam at the wall. From the side you see each band's end, a little wider and deeper than the patch in front of it.
  • 3The column, standing behind the slab. The great clear column of the next challenge stands on La Rampa 5 m behind the slab and goes on up past it. Today it is nearer, and its foot hangs in the air at 240 m. Here it goes down to the slope, so it reads as standing on something.
  • 4A mirror face under the slab. A clear face 5 m wide on the back wall, below the middle of the crossing. It shows you hanging from the ceiling, small. One is there today, near the start.
  • 5A bright cluster on La Rampa. The one bright white crystal of this area stands on the glass slope under the slab, well back. It lights the underside from below, so each crust throws a long shadow up the glass and is easy to find, and it lights the slope, so you see what a miss costs.
  • 6The roots of the rest, and the landing's back. The rest you start from is the end of a fat pale crystal with its fan of points. The landing at the top is the hall's own rock, frosted over, and it runs back to the wall with a few small clusters standing on its back edge.

Play space

  • 7The six crusts. Each flat pale plate becomes a low crust of small rough points in the cave's pale lilac, clinging to the underside of the glass, lighter at its edges (note 33). Same size and place. Pale lilac on dark glass: they still stand out at a glance, because finding them is the challenge.
  • 8The broken tooth. A short rough point of the same pale crystal, snapped off, hanging under the slab's low edge. It is the first thing you take.
  • 9The slab's two faces. The underside is clear indigo glass with a white glint, and it shows a dim reflection of the slope below. The top face is the same glass, scored with long straight scratches that all run downhill, so you can read where it will send you if you land on it.
  • 10The landing's frosted face and lip. The last catch is the landing's west face and the lip above it. Both are rough pale lilac for 2 m, where the rest of that wall is glass.

3.9 La Columna

A proposal.

The cave's tallest single crystal is a clear six-sided column that stands on La Rampa and goes up 44 m to the roof. Three collars of crystal have grown right round it, like bracelets on an arm, and come loose (Parker, 11-13). Each is a flat ring wider than the column, so it hangs askew: the first with its high side to the west, the second to the east, the third to the west again. From the side they make a zigzag up the column. Each collar creeps round the column, the middle one the other way, and the column is worn bright where they ride. The collars are glass and stay behind you. What you hold are their spikes. A spike is a long pale point that slides out of a collar's rim as that part of the collar comes round to the front, crosses in front of the column from the collar's low end up to its high end, and slides back in as it goes away round the far side. So each collar carries you up and across. At each corner of the zigzag you leave a spike that is about to go in for one that has just come out, on the next collar up. Below the collars is a landing of the hall's own rock, and from its east end five nubs lead up the corner beside the well's wall to the shelf where the climb starts.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The column. One clear six-sided crystal 2.6 m across, floor to roof, with a dim light running up inside it. It does not turn. It stands 5 m behind you: further back than today, so that the collars can go right round it without coming into the play space.
  • 2The three collars. Each is a flat ring of clear indigo glass 7.6 m across and 0.5 m thick, with a hole 3.2 m across, hanging on the column at 32 degrees. You see it edge-on, as a slanted bar across the column. Its nearest edge is 1.2 m behind you, so no part of a ring is ever in the play space. The three dashed circles in the sketch are today's rings, which go.
  • 3Three worn waists. Where each collar rides, the column is worn into a shallow waist and polished mirror-bright. It is the cave's sign for a thing that moves: crystal rubbing on crystal. Nothing else drives the collars that you can see. They creep, one turn in about 50 seconds.
  • 4The roots of the two shelves. Each shelf is one wide flat crystal that grew out of the wall like a balcony, frosted on top and clear below. Under each, where it leaves the wall, there is a fan of smaller points.
  • 5The chimney's crack. The crack again, climbing the corner beside the well's wall. Each of the five nubs is the tip of a thin rough crystal growing out of it, and the crack's zigzag is why the nubs go left and right.
  • 6The bright cluster on the landing. A cluster 3 m tall on the back edge of the landing, bright white. It lights the landing and the foot of the chimney, and from below it lights the first collar. It is there today.
  • 7A mirror face east of the column. A clear face 5 m wide on the back wall between the two shelves. It shows the collars from their other side: in it you can see a pair of spikes coming round the back before it reaches the front.

Play space

  • 8The spikes. Each collar carries four pairs of spikes. A spike is a rough pale lilac point 2.3 m long and 0.4 m thick that lies inside the ring and slides out through its rim. When it is out, its last half metre reaches the play space, and that is what you hold. The two spikes of a pair are 1.3 m apart. When a spike is in, nothing of it shows but a pale spot on the rim, behind you, and there is nothing to hold. The small circles in the sketch are three pairs, part way across.
  • 9The three slanted crossings. The lines are where spike tips travel in the play space. A pair slides out at a collar's low end, takes 10 seconds to cross to its high end, 6 m across and 3.8 m up, and slides in. The next pair follows 12.7 seconds after. First collar: from beside the lower shelf up to the west. Second: from the west up to the east. Third: from the east up to the west.
  • 10The way up, step by step. One. From the west end of the lower shelf, reach 1.3 m up and 0.7 m out to a spike as its pair slides out. Two. Ride up and west. The two spikes of the pair take turns to tremble for half a second and slide in for a second and a half: when yours trembles, move to the other. Three. At the top west corner the second collar's pair slides out 1 m above you, a second and a half before yours goes in for good. Take it. Four. Ride up and east, and change the same way to the third collar at the east corner. Five. Ride up and west, and at the top reach 1.2 m up to the west horn.
  • 11The west horn. New. The third collar leaves you on the west side of the column and the upper shelf is on the east. So a second horn grows from the root of the great horn on that shelf, the other way: a rough pale shaft 7.7 m long and 0.7 m thick, level, reaching west over the front of the column to a point. You take its underside from the last spike, climb onto it, and walk east to the shelf. All of it can be held.
  • 12The chimney's five nubs. Rough pale lilac, six-sided, a hand's width proud: the same crystal as the mirror's nubs.

Foreground

  • 13Two dark points in the bottom corner. Rising from the bottom right corner of the frame, in front of the landing's own rock and the well's wall, with their tips below the landing's floor. They cover nothing you stand on or hold.

Why it works

Each thing you touch is the near end of something real behind it.

You touchIt isBehind it

What I am not touching

  • The idea: collar to collar to the top, timing each change. Three of them, and the middle one goes the other way.
  • The spikes are the only holds. Each one slides in and out with a shake first, and a spike can go in under your hand (note 34; Parker, 11-13: harder).
  • The landing, the five nubs up to the lower shelf, and the two shelves stay where they are.
  • A fall lands on the glass ceiling's top face and slides back to the pendulum's far rest, as today.

What it would change in the game

  • Course change: the three face-on rings and their eleven studs go.
  • Course change: the column moves from 1.6 m to 5 m behind the play plane, and its foot goes down to La Rampa. The three collars are added round it. Column and collars are scenery and touch nothing.
  • Course change: new moving holds. On each collar, four pairs of spike tips travel a straight slanted line in the play plane: from (-325.0, 250.7) to (-331.0, 254.5), from (-331.0, 255.5) to (-325.0, 259.3), and from (-325.0, 260.3) to (-331.0, 264.1). 10 seconds a crossing, a pair every 12.7 seconds, 1.3 m between the two of a pair. Each spike is out for 3 seconds and in for 1.5, the two of a pair never in together, and both out at the two ends of a crossing.
  • Course change: the arriving pair on the next collar must be out 1.5 seconds before the leaving pair goes in, at each of the two corners. The collars turn at the same pace in opposite ways, so this happens at the same place every time.
  • Course change: a new piece to hold, the west horn, from the upper shelf's west end at x -324.3 to a point at x -332.0, its top at 266.0 m.
  • Course change: the camera for this challenge needs to see 1.5 m further west.

Notes

  • Parker, 11-13: the three rings become collars that wrap right round the column, and the spikes are harder: one can go in under your hand. This page is the plan for how that plays. Every number in it is a first try for the course's author to tune with a climber.
  • Why askew: a level collar's spikes would only carry you sideways, and the 16.6 m between the two shelves would have to be nine or ten reaches. A collar that hangs askew carries you up as well as across, as today's rings do, and three askew collars fill the height with four reaches.
  • Why a spike is only out at the front: a collar goes right round the column, 5 m behind you at its far side. A spike that stayed out all the way round would look like a hold where you can't reach it. Sliding in and out (note 34) is what keeps every spike you can see a spike you can hold.
  • Could not be checked here: whether a climber can make the two changes and the reach to the horn at these numbers. It needs a run in the game.
