3.10 El Salto del Pozo I

The end of the cave, and the way into the mushroom garden.

The well, El Pozo del Diablo, runs up through the mountain just east of here, and at this height its wall has split open: a breach 14 m tall, the cave's door. The longest rough crystal in the cave has grown out through it: a horn 16 m long, rising at 20 degrees from the last shelf, with its tip 1.4 m out over the shaft. From here the well is black. Its walls are wet and slick, there is no bottom to see, and far overhead there is one small dot of light. Across it the far wall is broken open too, and that side is not crystal. A thick root has pushed out into the shaft above the far door, and three thinner roots hang from it like a curtain, 9 m from the horn's tip. You go up the horn, fling from its tip, and catch a root. Behind the roots there is moss, a green glow and the first mushroom. The cave's breath goes out this way: the glitter in the air drifts east along the horn, through the door, and up the well.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The well's far wall. The shaft is round, and its far side curves behind the crossing: black rock, wet, with thin white runs of water and no ledges. It is the darkest thing in the cave. Below the frame it goes on down with no floor in sight, only a little mist. The cave's violet reaches one arm's length into it and stops.
  • 2The dot of light. Far up the shaft, at the top of the frame when the camera pulls back for the jump: one small pale dot, the well's mouth, 210 m above. A faint grey light comes down the middle of the shaft from it and is gone before it reaches you. It is the same dot you saw from the river.
  • 3The horn's root. The horn's thick end is buried in a collar of dark rock and small points that stands out from the back wall across the shelf. It grew from there towards the well, the way the cave's breath goes. A second, shorter horn grows from the same root the other way, west over the column: it is the last step of La Columna (3.9). The shelf's own fan of points is under it.
  • 4The breach, carrying on behind. Behind the doorway the well's wall is whole again: the door is a split a little over 2 m deep. On the cave side its broken edges are crusted with small pale points. On the well side they are bare black rock. The line between the two is where the cave ends.
  • 5The bright crystal at the door. One bright white cluster on the back wall above the horn. It lights the horn from behind, so the horn is a pale spear against the well's black, and it is the last white light before the garden's green.
  • 6East rim: the great root and the curtain behind. The root that sticks out into the well is the end of a root as thick as a man's body that runs back along the top of the far door. Behind the three roots you catch hang three more, each as thick as a thigh, too thick to take for a rope, with moss on them. Together they are the curtain: you fly into its front edge.
  • 7East rim: the garden through the door. Past the roots: glowing moss on the rock, a spore lantern's green light, and the first mushroom, a small one. At the foot of the curtain one last small cluster of crystal stands dull and grey with roots grown round it. Green light falls on the east wall of the well and stops at its edge, as the violet does on the west.

Play space

  • 8The horn. Rough pale lilac from end to end, six-sided, 0.9 m thick, with growth rings across it every few metres and a clean point. It is the palest and longest thing in the cave, and the only crystal that grew sideways along your path and not out of the wall at you.
  • 9The well's two walls. Black, wet and glossy from top to bottom on both sides, with white drips. Nothing on them can be held. The frosted sill stops dead at the well's edge, and the black starts.
  • 10The three roots. Tan, hairy and dry, each as thick as a wrist: the garden's own picture of something you can hold. They hang 12 m from the root above. The dashed ring is where the fling from the horn's tip arrives.
  • 11The root sill. A mat of roots and moss 2 m thick that fills the foot of the far door and stands 1 m out into the well. Dry and tan on top. It is where you step off the roots.

Foreground

  • 12West: one dark crystal point. Standing in front of the well's west wall below the sill, in front of solid rock. Its tip stops 2.7 m under the sill. It is the cave's last piece of foreground.
  • 13East: a clump of fern. At the bottom right corner, in front of the garden floor's own rock, with its tips below the floor's top. It is the garden's first piece of foreground. One side of the frame has crystal in front and the other has green.

El Jardín de Hongos

The mushroom garden, 264 to 376 m. Bounce and breath. Everything here is alive.

The garden is the breather: the prettiest place on the mountain and one of the oddest to climb. Every cap you bounce on has its stalk behind it, every vine hangs from something you can see. The far forest is your second kind of mushroom, tall pale bells, so an orange cap in front of you always means bounce. And the frog has a house with a roof you can land on.

What this place is

East of the well the mountain is warm and damp, and a forest of mushrooms has grown in the dark: caps as wide as roofs, stalks like tree trunks, vines, roots and moss over every rock. It glows a little, all by itself.

Nothing here was built by people and almost nothing was left by them. The things that live here are snails the size of carts, and the frog, who has a house.

The garden is the gentlest place on the mountain to look at and one of the strangest to climb: the floor throws you, the air lifts you, and the walls are slime.

How it is built

  • Mushrooms are the garden's trees. Each has a stalk, a skirt-ring part way up, a cap, and gills under the cap. Big or small, the same four parts.
  • The mushroom you bounce on: an orange cap with pale spots, a cream stalk and cream gills, in every size. No checked or striped caps (note 37).
  • A second kind, for scenery only (Parker, 11-13): tall and thin, with a small pale blue-green cap like a bell, growing in stands. It makes the far forest. It never grows in the play space, and nothing orange grows in the scenery, so an orange cap always means bounce.
  • Shelf fungus grows out of walls in steps, like brackets. Roots and vines hang like ropes. Mycelium, white and stringy, ties things together like netting.
  • Rock is rounded and mossy, never cut. Slime is black and runs down in sheets.
  • The only made thing is the frog's hut: a door and a round window cut into a fat stalk, a cap for its roof, a lantern made of a spore pod.

Colour and light

A green glow from moss and from spore lanterns, with the orange of the caps as the one warm colour. The glow comes from below and from the sides, so caps are lit on their undersides. Spores drift everywhere, slowly. The dark stretch (Los Ojos) is dim, not black, and the light fades in and out of it over several metres (note 45).

How it tells you what a thing is

You can hold itCream gills, tan roots and vines, pale mossy rock, a snail's shell, shelf fungus. Dry and matte.
You can'tBlack slime, glossy, running; wet stalks.
It throws youAn orange cap with pale spots. It squashes and springs when you land (note 36), and puffs a few spores.
It lifts youA column of spores rising fast, with small leaves and motes carried up in it (note 38).
It burstsA puffball: round, pale, tight as a drum, breathing slowly.
It is sceneryThe second kind of mushroom: tall, thin, pale blue-green bell caps, far back, with nothing between them and you (note 37).

The three layers here

BackgroundNear: the stalk of the mushroom whose cap or gills you are on, the wall the shelf fungus grows from, hanging roots too thick to mistake for ropes. Far: the forest of tall bell-capped mushrooms, stand behind stand, fading to blue-green, well back from the climb.
Play spaceCaps, gills, vines, roots, snails, shelf fungus, the mycelium bridge, puffballs.
ForegroundAlmost nothing (note 40). A few blades of fern or a small cap at a bottom corner, below the lowest floor. Drifting spores close to the camera.

How you come in, and how you leave

In: Out of the air: you land from the first well crossing in a curtain of roots on the east rim. The crystal is behind you across the shaft; moss, roots and the first three caps are in front.

Out: By the second crossing of the well, thrown west off the great cap. The far rim is cut stone: the temple's door, with two banner chains hanging into the shaft to catch. Roots and small mushrooms have got into the stonework on that side, so the garden reaches a little way into the temple.

4.1 Sombreros

This is the foot of the garden's west hall, a room 100 m tall beside the well.

You come in out of the air, from the first crossing, into a curtain of roots at the well's rim. One great root comes down the well's wall at the door, lies along the floor, and rears up as a broken stump. Where a root that size lies under moss, mushrooms come up along it in a row, and that is the challenge: four mushrooms of one family, each older and taller than the last. The first three are young and full of spring. The fourth is old: its cap has turned up like a saucer and gone dry, and it is the shelf you rest on. One more, older still, fell off its stalk long ago, and the moss has taken it: it is a soft green mound on the floor. A climber lay down on it and never got up.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The west hall, far back. Two stands of bell mushrooms, the garden's scenery kind: thin stalks 6 to 13.5 m tall with small pale blue-green caps like bells, 6 to 10 m behind you. Rounded mossy boulders stand along the foot of the back wall. The orange scenery mushrooms that stand 2 m behind you today are gone. Nothing orange grows in the scenery, so an orange cap always means bounce (Parker, 11-13).
  • 2A snail, asleep. On a boulder at the back, beside the door, shell 1.7 m across, drawn in. It is the first snail you see, long before the ones you climb.
  • 3The great root. As thick as a barrel. It comes down the back of the door at the well, and lies along the floor 2 m behind the path, half under moss, humping up and down. The knee and the stump you climb are its near end, broken off.
  • 4The four stalks. One behind each cap and one behind the shelf. Each roots on the great root 2 m back and leans forward, so its cap hangs over the path and the floor under it stays clear. Cream, with a skirt part way up and gills under the cap. When a cap throws you, its stalk dips and rocks with it (note 36).
  • 5Glow moss and two spore lanterns. Moss glows green on the great root. Two lantern pods grow on the stalks, low down, so the caps are lit from underneath. Today a lantern floats in the air beside the shelf: it moves onto the shelf's stalk.

Play space

  • 6Three caps, spotted. Orange with pale spots. No checks (note 37). The face you land on stays as flat as it is today. The roundness is in the rim, which rolls down all round, and in the cream gills underneath. Each cap sways a little at rest, squashes when you land and springs back taller, with a puff of spores from under the rim (note 36).
  • 7The shelf: an old cap turned up. Cream and dry, with its gills on top as fine lines running out from the middle. It has no orange left, so nobody expects it to throw them.
  • 8The frozen climber, on a mound of moss. He lies where he is today. The old cap under him is orange in the course, and it does not throw. It becomes a low mound of green moss with a little grey-brown rot showing at its edges: no orange and no spots anywhere, so it can't be taken for a cap that throws (Parker, 11-13). The moss has grown on over his legs and one arm like a blanket, and three pale bell sprouts come up beside him.

Foreground

  • 9Fern and one small bell mushroom. At the bottom right corner, below the floor's edge: a fern clump and one small bell mushroom, both dark. Nothing else stands in front (note 40).

4.2 Lianas

Over your head is the underside of the island: a spur of the mountain that sticks out of the back wall into the middle of the room, black with slime.

Water seeps through it along four cracks, and where each crack opens in its belly a creeper has taken root and let one long vine down. Under the vines the floor tips up into a ramp of slime that runs all the way back to the floor of Sombreros. So this is a wet cave roof hung with creeper, over a chute. The four vines are the creeper's nearest strands, 5 m apart because the cracks are.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The forest, far back. Two stands of bell mushrooms, 6 to 10 m behind you: one on the floor and one on the back of the ramp. Thin stalks, small pale blue-green bell caps. Their tops stay below the vines' ends, so no far stalk is ever seen behind a vine.
  • 2The island's belly, going back. The roof you hang under carries on 6 m back, and from its far part hangs the rest of the creeper as one thick, dim mass. It is far enough back, and solid enough, that nobody takes it for a fifth vine.
  • 3A snail, asleep on the slope. Far back on the ramp, stuck where it stopped.
  • 4Four leaf collars. Where each crack opens in the roof, just behind each vine: a clump of leaves 1.8 m wide with a root as thick as an arm running back along the crack. Each vine is seen to grow out of one.
  • 5The two shelves' stalks. The shelf you leave stands on its thick stalk from the floor. The shelf you land on stands on a shorter one that roots in the ramp behind it.
  • 6Glow from below. Glow moss along the back of the floor, a lantern pod on the first shelf's stalk, and one spore pod glowing on the ramp. The vines are lit from underneath and show pale against the dark roof.

Play space

  • 7Seep cracks in the roof. The island's face is a blank black sheet today. It gets four cracks drawn on it, one rising from each vine, with a line of moss in each and slime running from it.
  • 8Vine knots. Each vine comes out of its crack in a knot with two leaves on it, so its top end is not just a line that stops at the rock.
  • 9The landing shelf: an old cap turned up. Cream and dry, gills on top, the same piece as the shelf you left.

Foreground

  • 10Fern. One clump at the bottom left, in front of the floor's rock face and below where you walk.

4.3 El Ascensor de Esporas

Half way up the slime ramp there is a hollow, and in the hollow grows a bed of spore pods, each as fat as a barrel.

They breathe out in turn, one after another, and their breath is a column of warm air full of pale gold spores, going straight up for 15 m before it thins out. What is left drifts on up to the underside of the island, 9 m higher, where the spores have settled as gold fur. Three vines hang down out of that fur with dust on their ends, into the top of the column. So the lift has a bottom you can see making it, sides you can see, and a top you can see it reach for.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The dust shadow on the back wall. Years of spores have stained the back wall pale gold in a stripe exactly as wide as the column, spreading out where it meets the roof. Even between puffs, you can see where the column is and how high it goes.
  • 2The forest, far back. One stand of three bell mushrooms on the back of the ramp, thin and pale blue-green, well to the west of the column.
  • 3The pod bed. Five spore pods in a row on the ramp, just behind where you step in, under the whole width of the column. Each swells, then puffs a ball of spores upward, one after another, so the bed never stops. This is what makes the lift (note 38).
  • 4The furred roof and the vines' root. Above the column the island's underside is furred pale gold with settled spores. In the middle of the fur is a knot of root as big as a cart wheel, and the three vines hang from it.
  • 5The two shelves' stalks. The shelf you step off stands on a short stalk rooted in the ramp. The shelf you climb onto stands on a tall thin one, 15 m, also from the ramp, well clear of the column.
  • 6A lantern pod. On the tall stalk under the top shelf. With the glow of the pod bed below, the column is lit from both ends.

Play space

  • 7The column, made visible. A thick stream of pale gold spores with soft edges, so you can see where to step in and where you would drop out. The spores rise fast and thick below 285 m and slow and thin above it, so you can see where the lift gives out. Small leaves and motes are carried up in it, and your climber's arms and legs drift upward while you are inside (note 38).
  • 8Dusted vine ends. The last metre of each of the three vines is furred gold, the same as the roof. They are the first thing the spores reach.
  • 9A dusted lip. The east lip of the shelf you step off is gold with spores for its last half metre. It marks the step in.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.

4.4 Rebote Doble

This is the pocket at the head of the slime ramp, where it runs into the room's east wall under the island's corner.

There is no floor here, only slime, so nothing can grow up from below except on a long stalk. One mushroom did: its cap stands out over the pit on 10 m of stalk. One could not, and grew sideways out of the east wall on a bent stalk, tied to the rock with a web of white mycelium. Between them a root from the frog's garden above reaches out over the pit and lets one vine down. Cap, vine, wall cap: three living things that happen to stand in a line across a hole.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The pocket's back wall and a stand of bell mushrooms. Rounded mossy rock closes the pocket 6 m back, with slime running down it and boulders where it meets the ramp. Three bell mushrooms stand on the back of the ramp, thin and pale blue-green. They stand to one side of the vine and stop below its end, never behind it.
  • 2The first cap's stalk. 10 m of cream stalk from the ramp, rooted 2 m back and leaning forward, with its skirt near the top. It dips and rocks when the cap throws you (note 36).
  • 3The root from the frog's garden. As thick as your body where it leaves the east wall, under the garden's lip. It arches out 6 m over the pit, a little behind you, and its tip turns forward and ends in the knot. The vine hangs from a root you can follow back to the wall with your eye.
  • 4The wall cap's bent stalk. A short thick stalk that comes out of the wall below the cap and bends up to it. The wet bracket you see today becomes its elbow.
  • 5The two shelves, from behind. The shelf you step off stands on its tall stalk from the ramp. The shelf you are thrown to is a shelf fungus growing from the snail wall, and two smaller shelves grow under it in steps, further back.
  • 6Three lights. A lantern pod on the root above the knot, one on the first cap's stalk, and glow moss where the ramp meets the east wall. The vine's top, the first cap's underside and the wall cap are the lit things.

Play space

  • 7The two caps, spotted. Both orange with pale spots, rolled rims and cream gills, flat on the face that throws (note 37). The wall cap is the garden's sideways cap: its rim rolls further on the low side. Both squash and spring (note 36).
  • 8The knot. The root's tip, a fist of wood with the vine grown out of it. Today it is a short bar in the air with nothing holding it.
  • 9Mycelium web on the east wall. A white web spread flat on the rock round the wall cap's stalk, 6 m tall. It ties the cap to the wall, and it is the pale patch that shows you from across the pit where the wall cap is.

4.5 La Baba

This is the snails' wall, and the slime is theirs.

Water seeps out from under the moss at the top of the island and runs down its east face, and five snails the size of carts live on that face and turn the water to slime. Each keeps to its own patch. It climbs 2.2 m to a patch of glowing moss, eats, rests, and goes back down to where the wet is. The wall leans out over the pit, and it curves round behind you into a cove where more snails sleep and where they keep their eggs. A snail's shell is the one dry thing on the wall.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The forest, across the gap. A stand of three bell mushrooms on the frog's garden, thin and pale blue-green, well behind the snails and to one side of them.
  • 2The cove. The island's east face does not stop at the play space. It curves round to the east behind you and joins the back wall, so there is slick wall behind the snails all the way up, running with the same slime. Its top edge is the same mossy lip.
  • 3Two more snails, asleep. On the cove wall, 4 m back, drawn into their shells. They show that the five in front of you are part of a herd.
  • 4The eggs. A clutch of snail eggs in a hollow of the cove wall, each the size of a football and glowing faintly green. They are the wall's lamp: the shells show dark and round against their light.
  • 5The shelf's lower steps. The shelf you start from is the top one of three shelf fungi growing from the wall in steps. The lower two are smaller and further back.
  • 6The root arm's root. Across the gap, on the lip of the frog's garden: the knee of root that the root arm grows up from.

Play space

  • 7Each snail's patch. A stripe of fresh slime on the wall, wetter and glossier than the rest, exactly as long as that snail's crawl. You can read where each snail goes, and where the gaps between them are, before any of them moves.
  • 8A patch of glow moss above each stripe. What each snail climbs for. It grows flat on the wall, drawn on like the stripe, small, green and glowing. It is not a thing that sticks out, so there is nothing to reach for. The top snail has none: it eats the moss of the lip.
  • 9The mossy lip. Thick moss hangs over the top edge of the wall, and the water comes out from under it. It is the dry edge you pull up onto.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.

4.0 The frog's hut

East of the snail wall, across the gap, there is a quiet floor of moss at 318 m where nothing happens.

It is where you land if you fly wide off the giant mushroom, and a root arm on its lip is the way back. It is also where the frog lives. The frog has hollowed out the stump of a fat old stalk and kept its cap on for a roof, and the moss has grown right over the cap. The side that faces you is open, like a doll's house: you walk in along the floor, and you are standing in its one room. The roof is solid: you can land on it, stand on it, and pull yourself up onto it by an eave. Behind the hut is a row of bell sprouts in a straight line, the only tidy thing in the garden. A snail sleeps beside it.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The forest. Three stands of bell mushrooms, thin and pale blue-green, 6 to 10 m back, with mossy boulders at their feet. The tallest stand is behind the hut, so the hut sits under a little wood. The big orange scenery mushroom and the two smaller ones that stand on this floor today are gone: nothing orange grows in the scenery (Parker, 11-13).
  • 2Shelf fungus up the east wall. Three brackets growing from the room's east wall in steps, 11 m up. Today one hangs there alone.
  • 3The frog's snail. Asleep beside the hut, 4 m back, shell 1.8 m across. It is the one that stands here today.
  • 4The frog's garden row. Six bell sprouts in a straight row behind the hut, knee high and pale blue-green, on a strip of turned moss. Somebody planted them.
  • 5The hut's back wall. The back half of a hollow stalk, 3 m wide and 2.6 m tall inside, cream, with a round window in it. A round door of bark stands open against it at the west end. This is the only made thing in the garden.
  • 6The roof's back half, and the chimney. The roof carries on 2 m back over the hut's back wall. All of it is green moss, shaggy at the eaves, with nothing orange showing: it is the colour of the garden's floors, which you stand on. A crooked chimney of hollow root comes out of the back half, behind the play space.
  • 7The frog and its things. The frog, 0.3 m, sits on a toadstool stool against the back wall. It breathes, blinks, watches you and croaks now and then. Beside it are a shelf with three jars and a small clay stove whose pipe is the chimney. A friendly thing, and nothing more (note 41).
  • 8The lantern by the door. A spore pod on a hook of root at the west end of the back wall, glowing warm. It is the one warm light on this floor and you can see it from the snail wall.
  • 9The root arm's root. A knee of root on the lip that the root arm grows up from, with the root running on back into the moss.

Play space

  • 10The roof: solid. The old stalk's cap, 4.8 m across, under a quilt of moss. It is a real thing in the play space (Parker, 11-13): a low dome you can land on and stand on. Its top is 3.9 m above the floor and nearly flat across the middle. Its eaves hang out 0.9 m past each end of the room and come down to 2.1 m above the floor, so you can reach one from outside the door and pull yourself up. It is hollow underneath: inside the room the ceiling is 2.6 m up, over your head.
  • 11The rug. A round mat of woven mycelium on the garden's floor, 2.6 m across. It is the room's floor: there is no step and no sill.
  • 12Stepping stones. Five flat pebbles set in the moss from the root arm to the door, level with the floor.

Foreground

  • 13Fern. One clump at the east corner, in front of the floor's rock face and below where you walk. Nothing stands in front of the hut: it has no front wall.

4.6 El Hongo Gigante

The biggest mushroom in the garden stands on the island's mossy top.

Its cap is 19 m across and reaches out past the terrace's edge, over the gap. It is the same kind as every other mushroom here: stalk, skirt, cap and gills, orange with pale spots. But it is very old, and an old cap here sweats slime: its stalk and its whole cap are wet and can't be held, and under the slime its orange has gone to a dark rust, nearly black. Three things on it stay dry. The gills under its east half hang in the open air over the gap. The rim on that side has rolled up into a dry brim. And when the cap opened, the veil that covered its gills tore: most of it is the skirt on the stalk, and one shred still hangs from the east rim with a dried knob on its end. You go out along the gills, swing on the knob, and come up round the rim.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The terrace's far side. A stand of three young bell mushrooms on the terrace, thin and pale blue-green, and mossy boulders along the back. A snail sleeps on one of them. The orange scenery mushrooms that stand on the terrace today are gone (Parker, 11-13).
  • 2The stalk. A real stalk, 5 m thick at the foot and 3 m at the top, standing behind the play space so the terrace stays open in front of it. It is wet and dark green, with runs of slime, so nobody reaches for it. Its skirt hangs 4 m up: a torn frill, the rest of the veil.
  • 3The gill plates, running back. Under the cap, the gills are plates that run from the rim back to the stalk, 5 m deep, cream and dry on this side. Each gill you hold is the front end of one. The underside is lit from below, so the plates show as a pleated ceiling.
  • 4The wet gills of the west half. Under the west half the gills are slimed black and stuck together in sheets. You can see at a glance which half of the underside to use.
  • 5A lantern pod and glow moss. A lantern pod low on the stalk's east side and a patch of glow moss on the terrace. The cap is lit on its underside, which is where the route is.

Play space

  • 6A real cap: dark, wet, and plainly a mushroom. Today it is drawn as brown faceted rock. It becomes a real mushroom cap, rounded, made to the same outline (note 42). It is not the bright orange of the caps that throw you. Under its slime the orange has gone to a dark rust, nearly black where the slime is thick, with a wet green-yellow sheen and slow drips from the rim. Its spots show only as faint ghosts under the wet. Dark, glossy and wet says it can't be held, and nothing about it says bounce (Parker, 11-13). Only raised, dry, cream things on it can be held.
  • 7The crown: dry and cream. The flat top of the cap, where the slime has run off and the skin has dried and cracked into pale scales. It is orange in the course today and it does not throw. It becomes cream, the same dry cream as the gills and the brim, so the three dry places on the giant are one colour and the crown reads as a place to stand.
  • 8The brim. The east rim's edge, rolled up and dry, cream like the gills. It is the pale lip you are aiming for when you let go.
  • 9The veil's shred and its knob. A strip of the torn veil hanging from the rim, wet and dark, with its end dried into a firm cream knob as big as two fists. The knob is the one thing on it you can hold, and it looks like it.
  • 10Two little mushrooms on the shoulder. Two small cream mushrooms, dry, standing on the slick shoulder: the second and the fourth of the five that are there today. The other three go (note 44). That leaves three gaps of about 2.8 m, 3.0 m and 2.8 m, each a short lunge up the slime.

Foreground

  • 11Fern and one small bell mushroom. At the bottom left, in front of the island's rock and below the terrace's floor: a fern clump and one small bell mushroom, both dark.

4.7 Trampolín en Cadena

Over the giant's west shoulder the roof comes down in two masses of rock, both black with slime: a broad stalactite on the east, and on the west a spur that sticks out of the back wall.

Between them is a slot 6.8 m wide with rock at its back. Nothing can root in slime, but mycelium can cling to it, and a white web has spread up the slot's back wall. Its fruit are four mushrooms that grow sideways out of the two walls, one above another, each on the wall the last one left in shade. A fifth sits low on the giant's shoulder. The web's thick cords run from cap to cap in the same zigzag you bounce.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1A stand of bell mushrooms. Three bell mushrooms on the terrace below the spur, their pale blue-green caps just under it. Everything else behind this challenge is rock.
  • 2The slot's back wall. Rounded wet rock that joins the stalactite to the spur 3 m behind you. It closes the slot, so there is no black gap behind the caps.
  • 3The web. White mycelium spread flat on the back wall. Its thick cords run from cap to cap, so the zigzag of the route is drawn on the wall behind it. Thinner strands fill in between. Three knots in it glow green and light the caps from behind.
  • 4Four bent stalks. Each sideways cap stands on a short thick stalk that comes out of the wall below it and bends up, with its foot in the web. The first cap needs none you can see: it grows straight out of the giant's shoulder.
  • 5The root down the stalactite. A root as thick as a leg comes down the stalactite's east face from the roof and goes in under its foot. The three root ends you hold are where it comes out again.
  • 6Mossy stalactites under the spur. Two short thick ones, hanging over the giant's west rim. They make the spur's underside a roof and not a flat cut.
  • 7A boulder and a lantern on the top ledge. A mossy boulder at the back of the ledge with a lantern pod on it. It is the light you bounce up toward.

Play space

  • 8Five caps, spotted. All five orange with pale spots, rolled rims and cream gills, flat on the face that throws (note 37). Each squashes toward its wall and springs back, and its stalk rocks (note 36). The tilt of each is easy to read because the spots tilt with it.
  • 9Three root ends. Tan, dry and knobbed at the tip, each a little lower than the last. They come out of a crack along the stalactite's foot, which is drawn on.
  • 10Slime sheets on both walls. The two walls are blank today. They get glossy black sheets with pale runs and slow drips, and a wet ring round the foot of each cap's stalk.

4.8 Puente de Micelio

Between the spur's top and a loop of root that hangs from the low roof to the west, a curtain of mycelium hangs from the roof like a net left to dry.

Nobody built the bridge. It is the curtain's bottom edge, grown thick: two cords as thick as your wrist, with small shelf fungi along them for treads. Just under the middle, in a pouch of the curtain, sits a nest of spore pods. Two of them are fat. One points east and one points up and west, and they blow in turn. The curtain bellies out a moment before each one blows, so you see a gust coming before it reaches you. Under all of it is 27 m of air and the terrace.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1A ledge of bell mushrooms, below. A ledge on the far back wall, 8 m under the bridge, with two stands of young bell mushrooms on it, pale blue-green. You look down on their caps, which tells you how high the bridge is. Under the ledge the wall drops away to the terrace.
  • 2The curtain. A net of mycelium with holes as wide as your hand, hanging from the roof's stalactites to the bridge. It leans back, 3 m behind you at the top and touching the bridge at the bottom. It is dim grey-green and plainly a sheet, not a line. Before a gust it bellies the way the gust will blow.
  • 3Roof stalactites. Four short mossy ones along the roof. The curtain is draped from their tips. The two long ones that hang here today are replaced by these.
  • 4The pod nest. Two fat spore pods and a few small ones in a pouch of the curtain under the bridge's middle. The east one swells and blows east. Then the west one swells and blows up and west. They are what the gusts come from (note 38).
  • 5The root loop. The shelf you reach is the bottom of a loop of root that comes down out of the low roof, as thick as a leg. It hangs from the roof by this root and is not on a stalk 27 m tall, as it is drawn today.
  • 6The bridge's east anchor. A mossy boulder at the back of the ledge, with the two cords wound round it and a lantern pod on top.

Play space

4.9 Los Ojos

West of the bridge the roof comes down low, and behind you it comes down lower still: a brow of rock that hangs over the top of the west hall like the brow over an eye.

It is the dimmest place in the garden, because the brow shuts out the glow from both ends. The brow's face is full of round hollows, and in each hollow a puffball grows on a short neck, straight out toward you: pale, round and faintly lit from inside. Seven eyes in seven sockets. Roots as thick as legs come through the roof here and run down the brow between the sockets. Their thin ends are the roots you hang from and their knuckles are the knots you hold. Under you there is nothing for 100 m.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1A far ledge of bell mushrooms. Along the bottom of the screen: a ledge on the hall's far wall with three small stands of young bell mushrooms, pale blue-green and dim. It is the only thing under you. Below it the hall goes down 90 m.
  • 2The brow. The back wall under the low roof: rounded dark rock that hangs down to about 357 m, with a ragged lower edge. It carries on up into the dome in the roof. With it there, the dark place has a back, and the puffballs have something to grow from.
  • 3The way out. Past the brow the roof goes up again and the back wall is far and mossy, with the garden's green glow on it. One mossy stalactite hangs clear of the two roots you catch there. It is the light you travel toward.
  • 4Seven sockets. A round hollow in the brow behind each puffball, 1.9 m across, with the puffball's neck coming out of its middle toward you. A puffball that seems to float in the air today sits in a socket. When one bursts, its neck stays, and the new one swells on it.
  • 5Roots down the brow. Thick roots that come through the roof and run down the brow's face between the sockets, flat against the rock. One hangs free as a loop: its bottom is the shelf you start from. In the dome, a knot of root as big as a cart wheel is what the two roots there hang from.

Play space

  • 6The puffballs, as eyes. Each is round, pale and tight as a drum, 1.2 m across, breathing slowly, with one small dark pore on its face like a pupil. Each lights a pale pool round itself, and the light goes out when it bursts (note 45, done). All seven look alike: the two you need are not marked.
  • 7Root knots. The four knots on the ceiling are knuckles of root, tan and dry, each with a root's line drawn on the ceiling running back from it.
  • 8Where the dim place begins and ends. These two lines are the edges of the dim place in the course file. The light fades over the last 7 m on each side of them and never snaps (note 45, done).

4.10 El Salto del Pozo II

The second crossing of the well, and the place where the garden stops.

On the east rim is the garden's last door, a cave mouth of rounded mossy rock. A root arm stands in it like a diving board, and under the board's lip the garden's grandest mushroom has grown out over the drop. On the west rim, 12 m away, is cut stone: the doorstep of the temple of the First Top Dog. A stone beam sticks out 5 m over the well above it, and two bronze chains hang from the beam, each with a long banner of cut paper behind it. Between the rims the well goes down out of sight. The garden has started across: roots have crept round the back of the shaft, and there is moss and a bell sprout or two in the joints of the temple's first blocks. Green light on one side, torch gold on the other.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The well's back wall. The shaft is round, so behind the crossing its wall curves from one rim to the other, 7 m back at the middle. Slick black rock with pale runs, lit green from the east and gold from the west so that it shows. Today there is only black here (note 46).
  • 2Roots round the back of the shaft. A band of thick roots that leaves the garden's rim, follows a crack round the back of the well, and reaches the temple's doorstep. Three small bell mushrooms grow on it, pale blue-green. It is far back and below the chains' ends, and it is how the garden got across.
  • 3The garden's last wall. Rounded mossy rock behind the cave mouth, with shelf fungus in three steps and a patch of glow moss at the floor. Nothing here is cut.
  • 4The great cap's stalk. Short and very thick, 1.8 m. It grows out of a crack in the well's wall 4 m below the rim, behind the play space, and leans out and forward to hold the cap over the drop. Skirt, and gills fanning out under the cap's west lip. Today the cap has no stalk at all.
  • 5The diving board's mother root. A root as thick as a barrel that comes down from the roof at the back of the cave mouth and spreads into the sill. The post and the board are one branch of it, turned toward the well. A lantern pod grows on it above the board.
  • 6The temple's first hall. Inside the door: a back wall of big pale blocks, 6 m back and in brown shadow, with the temple's carved band along it at two heights and one torch in a bronze bracket. It is drawn as the temple's own page for La Puerta has it, and shown here only as far as you can see from the garden.
  • 7The door's side. The side of the doorway through the well's wall: pale fitted blocks, stepping out at the head in three steps under the banner beam. The steps are what carries the beam so far out over the well.
  • 8The two banners. A banner of cut paper hangs behind each chain, 1.1 m wide and 11 m long, whole and bright in the town's colours with the pug's paw on it. Today they hang inside the play space, 0.4 m behind the chains. They move back to just behind it, so that what is in the play space is the chain you catch and nothing else. With the well's wall lit behind them they are the brightest things across the drop: the target.
  • 9Corbels under the doorstep. Three stepped stone brackets that carry the doorstep out over the well, with moss in their joints. The doorstep is the front of a stone landing, not a block stuck on a wall.

Play space

  • 10The great cap, as a mushroom. Today it is a cream wedge with an orange band. It becomes the brightest spotted cap in the garden, with a fat rolled rim that droops over the well and cream gills under it. It is 4 m across the screen, as now, and about 6 m from front to back, most of that behind you. The three faces you land on keep their angles exactly. It squashes deepest of all the caps and springs highest (notes 36, 37, 46).
  • 11The beam, made longer. The temple's stone beam is real stone in the play space, and today it stops at x -303.5, short of both chains. It is made 2.6 m longer, to x -300.9, so both chains hang from it (Parker, 11-13). Under it, at the head of each chain, is a carved pug boss with a bronze ring. The new length can be held like the rest. The throw off the great cap tops out under it and passes below its end: to be checked again when it is built.
  • 12The garden on the temple's doorstep. Drawn onto the stone: one root across the doorstep's face, moss in the joints of its first blocks, and three pale bell sprouts no bigger than a hand. Nothing orange.
  • 13The doorstep's carved edge. The well side of the doorstep gets the temple's carved band, deep and pale: pug faces, belts and bones. Deep pale carving is the temple's sign for stone you can hold.

Foreground

El Templo del Primer Perro

The buried temple of the First Top Dog, 364 to 484 m. Carved stone and stone machinery, by torchlight.

The temple is the one place on the mountain that was built to be climbed, and I want every room to look like a machine somebody set into a wall on purpose. Every moving stone wears a jade band and shows the slot or axle it runs on. Dark bronze marks what hurts. The carvings are pugs, belts and bones and never a hint. It is also where your new notes bite hardest: gears that crunch, champions with broken arms.

What this place is

Long before the town, people built a temple inside the mountain to the First Top Dog: the first luchador to climb the Peak, a pug in a mask. They cut it out of the rock west of the well, hall above hall, and they filled it with tests. To reach the top of the temple you had to get past its machines.

The machines still run. Nobody knows what turns them. Steps slide into the wall, pistons push out, gears mesh, censers swing, a cross sweeps the altar's shaft. The torches are lit. The banners are fresh.

It is the grandest place on the mountain and the only one that was made to be climbed. Every challenge here was put here on purpose by somebody.

How it is built

  • Big blocks of pale stone, fitted without mortar, joints tight. Walls step back as they rise, in a sloped base with a flat band above it. Doorways and passages are stepped arches: two sides stepping in to a flat lintel.
  • A carved band runs along every wall at the same heights: pug faces, belts and bones. It never shows how a challenge is done (Parker, 11-13). Where you can hold the wall, the carving is deep and pale. Where you can't, the stone is polished black with soot and damp.
  • Jade green is the temple's accent: inlaid eyes, a stripe on a banner, a band round anything that moves.
  • Gold caps the things that matter: the mask's teeth, the altar, the censers' lids.
  • Stone machinery. Every moving block has a slot it slides in, and a bronze-shod edge; every wheel has a stone axle in two carved cheeks; every swinging thing hangs by bronze chain from a carved pug boss.
  • Banners of cut paper in the town's colours, whole and bright, hung high. Torches in bronze wall brackets.

Colour and light

Torch gold. A torch every few metres on the walls you climb, so the play space is warm and clearly lit, and the halls behind fall away into brown shadow with far torches as points. Jade and gold catch the light. No daylight, no glow.

How it tells you what a thing is

You can hold itPale dry stone, deeply carved; bone; gold; bronze chain. Matte.
You can'tPolished black stone, wet with soot, smooth, with pale runs. The shaft walls of the pistons are this (note 48).
It will breakPale stone already cracked through, with a corner gone (note 53).
It movesIt wears a jade band, it sits in a slot or on an axle you can see, and it shakes before it goes.
It is sceneryThe same stonework, further back, browner and darker, its carving shallow. Statues in the scenery have their arms down; statues you climb have an arm raised.
It will hurt youIt is edged in dark bronze: the cross's arms, the pistons' faces, the hammers of the gears.

The three layers here

BackgroundNear: the wall the machine is set in, with its slots, axle cheeks and chain bosses, and the carved band. Far: the hall going back, with columns, banners, torches as points of light, and more carved pugs.
Play spaceSteps, the mask's features, pistons, gear teeth, statues' arms, censers, slabs, the serpent's back, blocks, the beam.
ForegroundA column's base or a low stone balustrade at the bottom edge of the frame, in front of solid floor. Never a banner or a chain in front of the climb.

How you come in, and how you leave

In: Out of the air, from the second well crossing: you catch one of the two banner chains hanging down the well's west wall and climb onto the temple's doorstep. Roots and small mushrooms have got into the first few blocks. Green light gives way to torch gold.

Out: By the third crossing, over the well's own mouth, on the two giant censers. The east side is the forge: the same stone, black with soot, then iron grates and red light from below.

El Templo del Primer Perro · Challenge · place 1 of 12

5.1 La Puerta

This is the temple's front door and the hall inside it.

You come through a doorway 16 m tall, cut through the well's wall, onto 33 m of fitted paving. At the far end the floor meets the great stepped platform that the First Top Dog's mask sits on: five tiers, each 2.5 m high and 3 m deep, built for someone much bigger than you. The tiers are the first test. Three of them are false: each is a slab on bronze shoes in a slot, and when weight comes onto it, it draws back under the tier above. Under the platform runs the chute, a slope of polished black stone. The temple was built with a way back down from every test, and they all end on this floor.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The entry hall's back wall. Wall bays of pale fitted blocks, 4 m wide and 5 m tall, one row above another, with the carved band between the rows. It runs the whole width of the frame and out of its top, so there is no black behind anything (note 51). It is 6 m back, in brown shadow.
  • 2Two doorways. Two stepped arch doorways in the back wall, dark inside, each with a small stone pug plaque over it and a cut-paper banner high above. The hall goes on behind you. Today a string of cut paper hangs low across this wall, 1.8 m behind you, and one mask 6 m across hangs above it. Both go. Nothing thin hangs near the floor you walk on, and the first big face you see should be the great mask at the top of the tiers.
  • 3The fall strip. A carved strip 5 m wide runs up the back wall and out of the frame, behind the place where the great hall's drain comes down. It is carved with bones, tumbling, all the way from the top. You walk past it on your way in, before you know what it is for.
  • 4Three broken forearms. Three stone forearms, each 1.9 m long, lie at the foot of the fall strip. They broke off the champions in the great hall, far above, and came down the ramp and the drain (see El Salón de los Campeones). They lie back against the wall, behind the play space, so they are scenery and not something to stand on.
  • 5The platform the mask sits on. The body of the stepped platform, right behind the tiers you climb. Each tier you touch is the front edge of a terrace that runs 4 m back into the scene. On the platform's face under each tier runs the temple's carved band: pug faces, belts and bones.
  • 6Three slots. Each false tier rides in a slot cut along the platform's face and lined with bronze. The slot is 5.7 m long: the 3 m the tier fills, and 2.6 m of empty channel to the west of it. The empty channel shows you, before you step, that this tier moves and how far it goes. The true tiers have no slot.
  • 7The door through the well's wall. The side of the doorway: the same pale blocks. At its head it steps out to carry the stone beam that the two banner chains hang from, out over the well. That beam is made longer, so that it reaches both chains (the garden's page for the crossing shows it). The mushroom garden has reached this far: one thick root lies in the joints of the first few blocks.
  • 8Torches. Four on the back wall along the floor and one on the platform's face. The floor and the tiers are warm and clear, and the wall above them falls away into brown.

5.2 La Máscara

The west end of the entry hall is one carved face: the First Top Dog in his mask, 16 m wide and 21 m tall, standing on top of the stepped platform.

It was made to be climbed. The face itself is a wall, set back behind you and painted in terracotta and jade. The things you hold stand out from it a full metre: the jaw, the fangs, the lip and its teeth, the nostrils, the cheek studs, the lower lids of the eyes and the brow. They are bone white with gold tips, and nothing else on the face is. The jaw is a block that rides up and down in two slots. Behind the open mouth is the gullet, which leads down to the chute.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The hall's end wall. The same wall bays as the rest of the hall, rising out of the frame, with the temple's carved band of pug faces, belts and bones beside the mask.
  • 2The mask's face. The carved face, kept as it looks today: terracotta, jade and cream, with the ears and the crown above the brow. It is scenery. Its flat cheeks and forehead are out of reach behind you, so they are never mistaken for holds. Its colours are a shade browner than the bone white of the holds.
  • 3The gullet. The open mouth, black inside, with a stepped throat going back and down to the chute. Far back in it, the jaw's counterweight, a 1 m stone block on a thick bronze chain, goes down as the jaw comes up.
  • 4The jaw's two slots. One either side of the mouth, cut into the face and lined with bronze, 6.5 m tall. The jaw's ends ride in them. You can see how high the jaw will go before it moves.
  • 5The eye sockets. Two deep sockets, each with an eye of inlaid jade lit from inside. The ledge you stand on under each is the eye's lower lid.
  • 6The nostril pits. Two round black pits in the nose. The pale ring round each pit is what you hold.
  • 7Torches. Two on the wall east of the mask and one west of it. They light the face from the sides, so every hold throws a shadow onto the face behind it.

Play space

  • 8Bone white and gold on every hold. The rule for the mask: if it is bone white with a gold tip or a gold rim, you can hold it. The three teeth and the two fangs have gold tips. The nostril rings and the cheek studs have gold rims. The lower lids and the brow have a gold line along their front edge. Each hold stands out from the face on a stem you can see, with a gap of shadow behind it.
  • 9A jade band on the jaw. The jaw moves, so it wears the jade band along its lip, between the two fangs, and bronze shoes at its two ends where it meets the slots. It shakes before it rises.
  • 10The brow. The brow ridge is the mask's own brow. It carries on west past the edge of the face as a cornice, and that is your walk to the pistons.

Nothing. That is on purpose.

5.3 Los Pistones

Past the mask's brow the walk goes under a great stone pier and ends at a shaft, 5.5 m wide and 16 m tall, that goes up into the temple's works.

The shaft is a machine. A plunger in its floor lifts you to where the walls begin, and then nine stone bolts, each 3.4 m long, slide out of the two walls in turn, bottom to top, like the bolts of a great lock being thrown one after another. The walls themselves are polished black. The only way up is on the bolts, and each bolt, as it comes out, pushes off whoever is still standing in front of it. West of the plunger the floor is missing: that is the throat that drops to the chute.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The shaft's back wall. Fitted blocks, a shade browner than the bolts, 2.2 m behind you. It carries on down behind the throat into the dark, east under the pier behind the walk, and up into the gear room, so there is no black anywhere in the frame (note 51).
  • 2Nine tracks. Each piston is the near end of a long bolt, and its back half runs in a track cut across the back wall and lined with bronze. Five tracks reach out from the west wall and four from the east. Each ends in a bronze stop exactly where that piston's tip stops. You can read the whole ladder, and how far every step will come, before anything moves.
  • 3The plunger's guide. A slot up the back wall behind the plunger, 3.6 m taller than the plunger itself. The empty part above it is the height it will lift you.
  • 4The carved band. Along the top of the wall under the pier, where you pass it as you walk to the plunger: the temple's band of pug faces, belts and bones. It shows nothing of how the shaft is climbed (Parker, 11-13).
  • 5An offering niche. Beside the plunger, at head height: a small square niche holding a bone and a jade bead. The temple's people left one beside every machine.
  • 6Torches. One over the throat, one under the pier, one at the head of the shaft. None sits between the tracks, so nothing bright is behind a piston.

Play space

  • 7Nine sockets. On the face of each wall, the mouth each piston lives in: a dark square in a carved frame. The game draws these today (note 48). A socket with nothing in it is plainly not a hold.
  • 8Polished black walls. Both walls are polished black from the plunger's top to the head of the shaft, with pale runs of damp down them. Nothing on them is pale except the pistons.
  • 9Bronze faces and jade bands. Each piston's end is shod in dark bronze, the temple's mark for what hurts: that is the face that shoves you. Its top is pale stone with a jade band. The plunger wears the same band round its top.

5.4 Engranajes

Above the piston shaft is the gear room: the place where the temple's turning comes from, as far as anyone can tell.

Four stone wheels, each 6 m across with its cogs, stand one above another in a zigzag and turn against each other, once round in 12 seconds. They are built the way a mill's wheels are built: the wheel is one greased disc, and each of its twelve cogs is a separate block set into a socket in the rim. The wheels hang on two tall stone posts on the back wall, two wheels to a post. Where two wheels meet, the cogs close on each other like teeth, and whoever is between them is knocked out. The temple marked those three places in dark bronze. Nobody knows what turns the wheels. The room is 14 m wide and 22 m tall, and it opens at its top corner onto the balcony of the great hall.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The gear room's back wall. Wall bays, 2.8 m behind you, browner than the cogs, with the temple's carved band of pug faces, belts and bones at three heights. At the top right the room is open to the great hall, and the hall's own back wall carries on behind the balcony.
  • 2Two posts. Two square carved posts stand against the back wall from floor to roof, each with a pug capital. The east post carries the first and third wheels and the west post the second and fourth. Each wheel's axle runs back into its post between two carved cheeks. You see the posts above, below and between the wheels, so each wheel is plainly hung on something.
  • 3Three bronze jaws. Between the two posts, right behind each of the three places where two wheels meet, is a plate of dark bronze 2.8 m wide and 1.8 m tall, cast as a pug's open jaws with its teeth showing. You see it through the closing cogs, and above and below them. Dark bronze is the temple's mark for what hurts, and these are the only three plates of it in the room. They say where the bite is before you are near it.
  • 4The grease shelf. Low in the west corner: an offering niche, and beside it a stone trough of black grease with a long ladle. Black runs of grease go down both posts from every axle. It says why the discs can't be held.
  • 5Torches. One on each side of the room, in the gaps the wheels leave, and one by the way out. The cogs catch the light and the discs do not.

Play space

  • 6Hammer cogs. Each cog is its own block in its own socket in the rim, with a bronze pin through it. Its front and its outer end are pale dry stone: that is what you hold. Its two side faces, the faces that close on the next wheel's cogs, are shod in dark bronze, like the two faces of a hammer. So every cog shows the part that carries you and the part that bites. The three dashed rings mark where the wheels meet.
  • 7Running dogs round each disc. A ring of small carved dogs runs round each disc's face, nose to tail, in shallow relief under the grease. They show which way a wheel turns and how fast. A jade band round the rim says the wheel moves.
  • 8A pug's face at each hub. The end of each axle shows at the wheel's centre as a carved pug's face. It is cut in the disc's own dark stone and greased like the rest of the disc, so it does not read as a hold.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.

  • All twelve cogs on every wheel can be held. The disc can't.
  • Parker, 11-13: the wheels turn twice as fast as today, and being caught where two wheels meet knocks you out. No cogs are taken away and the wheels never turn back.

5.5 El Salón de los Campeones

The great hall is where the temple kept its champions: everyone who ever finished the climb, carved 9 m tall, standing in two ranks down the length of the hall.

The far rank stands in niches in the far wall with its arms down. The near rank, the three you climb, stands out in the hall on great pilasters. Each of these holds its champion's belt over its head in both hands: a broad stone belt, behind you, with the hands gripping it from the front. They are very old and their arms have begun to go. The first and the third have each lost a forearm: the arm ends at the elbow, and the gilded hand is still up there on the belt, with nothing between. The second has lost both arms, and only its two hands are left on its belt. The hall has no floor you can use. Its floor is a polished black ramp that falls away to the east and ends at the drain.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The hall's far wall. Wall bays from the ramp to the roof, 9 m back and brown with shadow. The temple's carved band of pug faces, belts and bones crosses it at three heights.
  • 2The far rank. Two more champions, the same size and the same stone, in tall stepped niches in the far wall. Their arms are down and whole, and each wears its belt at the waist. They are 8 m back and browner. They show what the near rank looked like before it began to break.
  • 3Two great pilasters. The second and third champions each stand on a plinth, and each plinth is the top of a great pilaster that rises from the ramp behind you, with a stepped head that reaches forward to carry the plinth. The third pilaster is 16 m tall and goes out of the bottom of the frame. The first champion stands on the balcony and needs none.
  • 4Three belts, held overhead. Behind each champion's raised hands is its belt: a band of stone 8.4 m long and 0.9 m tall with a round bronze plate in the middle, held up over the head. It stands just behind the play space, on a square pillar that runs up the champion's back. This is the background the hands stick out of. A hand whose arm has gone is still gripping its belt. The belts are browner than the statues and are scenery: you pass in front of them.
  • 5The first champion's forearm. The forearm that broke off the first champion lies on the balcony behind its feet, against the wall, 1.9 m of carved stone with a rough old break at each end. It is behind the play space and is scenery. The other three broken lengths fell onto the ramp and went down the drain: they lie at the foot of the fall strip, by the temple's door (see La Puerta).
  • 6Banners. One over each niche, whole and bright, hung high on the far wall. Today three banners hang 1.4 m behind you under the roof, beside the flight of the flings. They move back here, 9 m behind.
  • 7Torches. One either side of each niche and one on the balcony. They sit low, below the line of the flings, so a climber in the air is seen against plain wall.

Play space

  • 8Three gilded hands. The east hand of each champion: a fist of gold, in the play space, with its fingers closed round the belt behind it. It is the only gold on each statue, and it is where you fling from. On the first and third champions you reach it from the elbow's broken end, 1.85 m away.
  • 9What has broken off. The four crosses mark the lengths of arm that are gone: the east forearm of all three champions, and the outer 1.6 m of the second champion's west arm. The first three are drawn in today's course but could never be held. The fourth can be held today and is taken away. Each stump ends in an old break: rough and weathered, with no cracks running back into the arm, so it does not read as a thing that will break under you.
  • 10The second champion's west hand. A stone fist 1 m across, gripping the belt, with no arm behind it. It is what you catch after the first fling. From it you reach the stump at the shoulder, 1.85 m away, cross the shoulders and the head, and go out along the east stump to the gilded hand. This champion gives you two hands and two stumps where the others give you an arm.
  • 11The whole arm. The west arm of the first and third champions is whole: carved deep and pale along its length, with a belt of small pug faces wound round it. On the third it is your catch after the long fling: 3 m of forearm and a fist, the biggest pale thing in front of you as you fly.
  • 12The ramp's polish. Polished black, with long pale scrapes running down it where others have slid, and three deeper gouges where the broken forearms went down.

5.6 Incensarios

The east end of the great hall, over the drain.

This is where the temple burned its incense: one great censer hangs on a bronze chain from a carved pug in the roof and swings out over the place where the ramp ends and the hall drops 38 m to the entry floor. Across the gap is the keeper's balcony, a small ledge on the well's wall where the censer was filled, with a doorway behind it and a chain up to the gallery. The censer still swings and still smokes. Nobody fills it.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The hall's far wall, carried on to the well's wall. The same bays as the rest of the hall. They carry on east behind the balcony and up behind the chain, to the well's wall, so there is no dark band there (note 51). Behind the censer's swing the wall is left plain, with no carved band, so the gold bowl and its smoke show against bare stone.
  • 2The last pilaster. The third champion's pilaster, 16 m of it, rising from the ramp. It is the last solid thing before the drain.
  • 3The fall strip. The carved strip of tumbling bones starts here, at the height of the censer, and runs down the far wall behind the drain's mouth and on down. It is the same strip you walked past at the door. A stone pug's face looks down the drain from beside it.
  • 4The keeper's doorway. A stepped arch doorway behind the balcony, dark inside, with two incense jars and a long ladle beside it. The chain you climb hangs in front of it.
  • 5Two chain bosses. A carved pug with a bronze ring in its mouth for each chain: one under the roof over the censer, one under the stone above the shaft for the chain to the gallery. Each is set just behind the play space and reaches its ring forward, so the boss is scenery and the chain is what you hold.
  • 6The gallery's columns. Above the roof: the gallery you will walk west along, with its square columns and its back wall.
  • 7Torches. One beside the last champion, one either side of the censer's swing and well clear of it, one in the chain's shaft, and one low down beside the drain so the drop is lit.

Play space

  • 8The one censer. A pierced bronze bowl with a gold lid, coals glowing inside, and a jade band round it because it moves. Its chain is thick bronze, link by link, and can be held along its whole length, up to the ring it hangs from.
  • 9The two that go. The first and third censers are in the course today and are crossed out here. They go, with their chains and their bosses (note 50). The banner that hangs beside the first chain today goes too.
  • 10The balcony's edge. The west edge of the keeper's balcony is carved deep and pale. It is what you fling for.
  • 11The ramp's foot. The ramp ends in a lip of polished black, worn into a shallow spout.

5.7 El Contrapeso

From the keeper's balcony a chain takes you up to the gallery: a walk 40 m long on the roof of the great hall, between a row of square columns, with two slots in the floor that look down on the champions.

The gallery ends at the hall's open west end, and there the temple weighs you. On the back wall is a stone scale: one beam on an axle, and a stone pan hanging from each end. Step on the near pan and it sinks 3 m while the far pan rises 3 m. The way on is from the low pan to the high one, and then to a ledge on the west wall, before the scale settles back.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The back wall. Wall bays behind the gallery and behind the open west end, without a break. Under the gallery's floor it is the great hall's far wall, further back.
  • 2The scale. A stone beam 6 m long on an axle between two carved cheeks, with a pug boss on the axle's end. It is drawn as it rests: east end up, west end down. When you stand on the east pan the beam tips the other way. It is thick stone, set against the wall, and it is browner than the pans.
  • 3Two hanger slots. Each pan hangs from its end of the beam by a stone hanger that runs in a slot in the back wall. The slot is as long as the pan's travel, so the empty part of each slot shows how far that pan will go. Today each slab has a thin chain that hangs 0.6 m behind you, inside the play space, and goes straight up through the serpent's back. Those two chains go.
  • 4The serpent's bed. Overhead: the long carved beam the serpent's back rises out of (see La Serpiente). Its east end stands on the gallery's first column.
  • 5The gallery's columns. Square carved columns with pug capitals along the back of the gallery. Each has a base to match it in front of the floor (item 12), so you walk between a column and a column's base.
  • 6Three doorways and a plaque. Stepped arch doorways between the columns, dark inside, and one stone pug plaque. The temple goes on behind the gallery.
  • 7Torches. One on each column, and one on the west wall over the ledge. The pans and the ledge are the brightest things at the west end.
  • 8The side shrine's doorway. A small stepped doorway in the west wall at the ledge. It is the frog's room: see its own page.

Play space

  • 9A jade band and bronze shoes on each pan. Both slabs move, so both wear the jade band along the top edge and bronze at their ends. Each is carved underneath with a shallow dish, so it reads as a pan of the scale.
  • 10The slots' black lining. The inside faces of the two slots in the gallery floor are polished black from just under the lip to the bottom (note 52). The floor's top is pale and carved right up to the edge.
  • 11The gallery's last edge. The west end of the gallery floor is carved deep and pale on its end face. It is the last sure hold before the scale.

Foreground

  • 12Column bases. The base of a column, 1.5 m wide, in front of the gallery floor opposite each column behind. Their tops are level with the floor, so they cover no part of you. None stands in front of a slot.

5.0 The frog's room

A small side shrine, cut into the west wall at the ledge you reach after El Contrapeso, at the foot of the serpent's tail.

Every hall of the temple had shrines like it, where a climber left a small carved pug before a test. This one is 2.8 m deep and 2.8 m tall inside, with a stepped doorway 2 m tall. Its walls are shelves of carved pugs the size of a hand, dozens of them. On the offering table at the back, in the place of honour where the biggest pug should sit, sits the frog. The room is cut away at the front: you see its floor, its back wall and its roof.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The west wall, behind the ledge. The same back wall as the scale's. The torch over the ledge is the one light outside the room.
  • 2The shrine. The room, cut into rock that is solid today. Fitted pale blocks, a stepped roof, and a back wall 2.4 m behind you. The wall here is 3 m thick today, so the rock behind the room has to be made a metre thicker when this is built.
  • 3Shelves of small carved pugs. Two stone shelves round the back wall, crowded with carved pugs a hand tall, each a little different, some with a jade bead or a scrap of cut paper. They are the offerings of everyone who came this far.
  • 4The offering table, and the frog. A stone table 1.2 m wide against the back wall, under an empty stepped niche where the shrine's own carved pug should be. The frog, 0.3 m, sits on the table in front of the niche, facing out. It breathes, blinks and watches you. Two small lamps burn either side of it.
  • 5The scale's west pan and the serpent's bed. What else is on this wall, for placing the room: the west hanger slot of the scale, and the bed of the serpent overhead with the tail's boss.

Play space

  • 6A line of jade paw prints. Four small paw prints of jade, inlaid in the top of the ledge, lead to the doorway. They are the only sign from outside, with the frog's croak.
  • 7The doorway. A stepped opening in the wall's face, 2 m tall at the ledge and 2.8 m inside. Its frame is carved pale. The wall above and below it stays polished black.

5.8 La Serpiente

Over the scale, under the roof, a stone serpent 20 m long lies along the back wall.

Its tail is a bronze chain that hangs down to the ledge. Its head rests on a ledge at the far end. Its body is a long carved bed fixed to the wall, and its spine is nine stone blocks that stand out of the bed toward you, each on its own ram, each in its own slot. The rams rise and fall 3 m, one after another, so a wave runs along the spine from tail to head. Three smaller serpents look down out of the wall above, mouths open, and each has one long black fang that hangs into your way.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The back wall. Wall bays from below the scale up to the roof. Behind the serpent the blocks are carved in shallow relief with its coils and scales, browner than the spine.
  • 2The serpent's bed. A carved stone beam 19 m long and 1.2 m tall, fixed to the back wall just under the spine. It is the serpent's body. The nine rams rise out of its top. At its west end a roller's axle turns in two carved cheeks: that is what works the rams. Its face is carved with scales, and with a belt of small pug faces along its top edge.
  • 3Nine slots. Behind each vertebra, a slot up the back wall, lined with bronze, as tall as that vertebra's rise. The ram runs in it. The empty slot above a vertebra shows how high it will come, so you can see whether there is room under a fang before you step.
  • 4Three small serpent heads. One over each fang, 2.6 m wide, looking down out of the wall under the roof with its mouth open. Each fang is that head's one great tooth. They are the same carving as the serpent's own head, smaller.
  • 5The serpent's head. On the ledge at the east end, against the back wall, 3 m long, looking back down its own spine with jade eyes. You step off the last vertebra and walk past it.
  • 6The tail's boss. A carved pug with a bronze ring, on the back wall at the spine's west end. The tail chain hangs from it.
  • 7The scale, below. The beam of El Contrapeso's scale is on the same wall, just under the bed. Its hangers stop below the bed. Nothing of it crosses the spine.
  • 8Torches. Three under the roof, between the small heads, so each fang is lit from both sides and its black shows against the lit wall.

Play space

  • 9A jade band on every vertebra. Each vertebra is pale stone carved with scales on its top, with a jade band along its top edge and a bronze shoe underneath where it meets its ram.
  • 10The fangs. Polished black, wet, with a pale run down each. They are the only black things hanging in the room.
  • 11The tail. The chain you climb is the serpent's tail: thick bronze links, getting smaller toward the bottom, ending in a carved stone tip.

5.9 Bloques Fantasma

The stair to the altar.

It was built as a ramp of polished black stone, 10 m long, that nobody could walk up. Five blocks slide out of the ramp's face to make steps, and slide back in, to the beat of a drum. The drum stands on a shelf over the serpent's head, and a stone mallet on an axle beats it: four counts to the bar. Each block is out for three counts and gone for one, and the gone count walks up the stair. Nothing on the walls tells you which block goes when. You learn it by watching the stair and listening to the drum. At the top is the altar's threshold.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The stair hall's back wall. Wall bays behind the ledge, the stair and the threshold, and below them the gallery's back wall. Unbroken. The temple's carved band of pug faces, belts and bones runs along it high over the stair, and tells you nothing about the blocks.
  • 2The drum and its mallet. The temple drum, 1.6 m across, on a stone shelf on the back wall above the serpent's head. A stone arm with a bone mallet swings on an axle between two cheeks and strikes it on every count, hardest on the first. You see the mallet lift before each stroke. Today the drum hangs in the air in front of the serpent's head. It moves up onto the shelf.
  • 3The serpent's head. On the ledge where you start, against the back wall, under the drum (see La Serpiente).
  • 4The altar's apse and two columns. At the head of the stair: two square columns, and between them the stepped niche with the altar in it (see El Altar). It is what you are climbing toward, and it is lit.
  • 5Torches. One by the drum, one over the middle of the stair, one at the threshold.

Play space

  • 6Five sockets in the ramp's face. Each block lives in a socket cut into the ramp: a carved pale frame round a dark mouth, drawn on the ramp's face the same way as the piston sockets. When a block is out you see 1.9 m of empty socket behind it. When it is in, its end sits just inside the frame and can't be held.
  • 7Where each block stands when it is out. The course draws the blocks drawn in. The dashed boxes are the steps as you climb them. Each block has a jade band along its top edge and a bronze shoe on its outer end, and it shakes before it goes.
  • 8The ramp's polish. Polished black, with pale scrapes down it. The big face of stone under the stair is the same black, in fitted blocks with tight joints.

El Templo del Primer Perro · Challenge · place 11 of 12

5.10 El Altar

The altar's chamber is the temple's highest room and its holiest.

The altar stands in a stepped niche at the top of the stair, with room in front of it to stand. Past it the floor stops. The chamber is a pit 11 m wide, 16 m deep to the gallery, crossed by one thin bridge of six stone slabs laid on brackets, and every slab is cracked through. Over the bridge a stone cross 10 m across turns on an axle in front of a great carved sun stone. On the far side a column of stone pegs goes up the east wall to the well's sill. The top five pegs are cracked. Three climbers got that far. They hung from the sill, hand to ankle, to reach past the bad pegs, and they are still there.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The chamber's back wall. Wall bays from the bottom of the pit to the roof, 3.4 m back. It carries on down the pit, so the drop is a lit wall going down and not a black hole (note 51).
  • 2The sun stone. A carved disc 9.4 m across on the back wall, right behind the cross: rings of small pugs, belts and bones round a centre. The carving is shallow and brown. The cross is the near end of its axle.
  • 3The cross's cheeks. Two carved cheeks stand out of the sun stone's centre, one either side of the hub, and the stone axle runs between them. You see them between the turning arms.
  • 4The altar in its niche. A stepped niche 4.4 m wide in the back wall, and in it the altar: 3 m wide, with the First Top Dog's face on its front and a bronze bowl of coals on top. It is 1.3 m behind you. Two square columns stand either side.
  • 5Seven brackets. A stepped stone bracket sticks out of the back wall under each joint of the bridge. The six slabs lie on them, which is why the bridge is in six pieces. When a slab falls its brackets stay, out of reach behind you, and the slab comes back onto them.
  • 6The carved band. High on the back wall, level with the sill: the temple's band of pug faces, belts and bones. It is plain here as everywhere, and shows nothing of the way up (Parker, 11-13).
  • 7A banner. One, whole and bright, high in the west corner, as far from the pegs as the chamber allows. Today two banners 5 m long hang here and go up through the roof. This one, 3 m long, takes their place.
  • 8Torches. Two on the back wall beside the pegs, one by each column, and one far down the pit so you see how deep it is.

Play space

  • 9Six cracked slabs. Each piece of the bridge is pale stone cracked right through, with a corner gone: the game's one look for a thing that will break (note 53). The joints between pieces are plain to see.
  • 10Dark bronze on the cross. The outer 2 m of each arm is edged in dark bronze, the temple's mark for what hurts. That is the part that knocks you out. The inner arms are plain stone. The hub wears a jade ring and a pug boss.
  • 11Eight pegs. Each peg is a carved pug's nose on a stone stem set into the wall. The lower three are sound: pale and whole. The upper five are cracked through with a corner gone. The wall between them is polished black.
  • 12The three who tried. Three frozen climbers hang down the wall beside the cracked pegs. The first holds the sill's edge with both hands. The second holds the first one's ankles and the third holds the second's. They are bone pale and dusty, in the pose they died in, and you climb them like carved stone. Their chain stops 4.6 m short of the bridge.
  • 13The place to stand. A ring of jade paw prints 1.6 m across, inlaid in the threshold right in front of the altar. It marks where a climber stands to pay respects (note 54). It is drawn onto the floor and adds nothing to stand on. The figure in the sketch is standing on it.

Foreground

Nothing. That is on purpose.
