El Templo del Primer Perro · Challenge · place 12 of 12

5.11 El Sacrificio

The top of the Pozo del Diablo.

The temple roofed the well's mouth with a stepped vault and hung two great censers in it, and from the sill on the west side it gave things to the well: the stone on the sill is the sacrifice stone, the temple's second altar. This is the third crossing and the last. You go from the temple's sill to the first censer's tassel, from censer to censer in the middle, and off the second onto the east lip, with the whole well under you. The east side is not the temple any more. It is the foot of the chimney, where the temple's smiths had their forge: the same fitted blocks and the same stepped doorway, black with soot, one last torch at the door, and then iron, and red light coming up through the first grate in the floor.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The well's far wall. The round back of the well, 6 m behind you. Down to the level of the sills it is the temple's fitted blocks. Below that it is the well's own rough rock, stepping back into the dark, with a few glints of wet far down (note 51). The dashed line is the far rim, which is dark and far back and does not read as a floor.
  • 2The stepped vault and its keystone. The roof over the well steps in from both sides to a flat cap. In the middle of the back wall, under the cap, is a stone pug's face 3.4 m across. It is between the two chains and well above the bowls. Today a string of cut paper crosses behind the two chains, and a banner hangs in each top corner. All three go. Nothing hangs in the well room but the two censers.
  • 3Two chain bosses. A carved pug with a bronze ring under the cap for each censer, set just behind the play space. The same boss as every other chain in the temple, at twice the size.
  • 4The temple's side. The altar chamber's back wall, and the side of the doorway through the well's wall: pale blocks, the carved band, and a torch on the sill.
  • 5The sacrifice stone. The second altar: a low stone 2.2 m wide in a stepped niche on the sill, with a bronze bowl on it. All of it is at least 1.3 m behind you, and you can stand in front of it. It counts for 'Pay Your Respects' just as the first altar does (Parker, 11-13), and its bowl answers in the same way.
  • 6The forge's back wall. East of the well the wall is the same fitted blocks in the same bays, with the carved band at the temple's own heights. Here it is black with soot and the carving is worn nearly flat. The chimney's first page has all of it.
  • 7The forge's door, a small iron pug, and the last torch. The same stepped doorway as the temple's, seen from the well, with a small pug's face in black iron over it and one torch beside it. That torch is the last of the temple's. East of it the light is red and comes from below.
  • 8The work place by the door. A small anvil, a rack of tongs on the wall over it, and a stone quenching trough. They are the first made things of the forge, and all of them stand behind the play space.
  • 9The great iron mask and its breath pipe. Across the first room of the forge: an iron pug's face 8 m wide and 11 m tall on the back wall, and a fat ribbed pipe that comes up out of the floor behind the grate and goes into its chin. It is the first thing you see from the temple's sill, lit red from underneath. It belongs to the chimney's first challenge and is designed on that page.

Play space

  • 10The two great censers. The same censer as the hall's, half as big again: a pierced bronze bowl with a gold lid, a jade band and coals inside, on a chain of thick bronze links that can be held all the way up.
  • 11The tassels. Under each bowl hangs a tassel 1.5 m long: a string of five bronze bells with a jade bead at the end. The bead is what you reach for from the sill, and what brings you down onto the far lip. It is the lowest bright thing over the well.
  • 12The temple's sill. Pale carved stone with a worn notch at its very end, where the first tassel comes to hand. In front of the sacrifice stone the same ring of jade paw prints as at the altar marks the place to stand. It is drawn onto the sill and adds nothing to stand on.
  • 13The forge's lip. The ledge the second censer drops you on is temple stone: soot black on its face, and worn pale and dry on top and along its edge, where it is held. Its edge carries the temple's carved band one last time. The wall above it and below it is wet black, which you can't hold.
  • 14The first grate. An iron grate of square bars in a raised rim, 3 m long, rust orange where feet have worn it, with red light and a wisp of steam coming up through it. It is the chimney's first challenge and is designed on its own page.

Foreground

  • 15A column base, west. At the bottom edge of the frame on the temple's side, in front of solid rock.
  • 16The forge floor's kerb, east. A low lip of soot-black blocks along the bottom of the frame on the forge's side, below the floor. It is the same kerb that runs the whole length of the forge floor. The two sides of the well get two different front pieces, pale stone and black.

Biome 6 of the first seven · 10 places · 0 open questions

La Chimenea

The chimney, 476 to 588 m. Heat, then the sky. A forge at the bottom of a natural flue that ends in daylight.

The chimney is a journey in one biome: from the temple smiths' forge, where the belt was made, up through their iron, out of everything anybody built, into daylight. The light tells it: furnace red at the bottom, blue-white sky at the top, and no torch above the forge floor. Every machine shows what drives it. It ends at a crack with the whole valley behind it.

What this place is

East of the well's mouth the mountain has a throat of its own: a volcanic flue, hot at the bottom, open to the sky 100 m up. The temple's smiths built their forge in the foot of it, because the mountain did the heating for them. This is where the First Top Dog's belt was made.

The forge is black iron and soot-black stone: steam grates in the floor, a bellows as big as a house, slag pans, three drop hammers on chains, anvils. Above the forge the made things thin out and the flue is bare rock with a few iron rings, and above that there is only a crack with daylight in it.

So this biome is a journey in itself: from the last room that the temple's people built, up through their iron, out of everything anybody made, into the open air.

How it is built

  • At the bottom, the temple's own stonework, soot-black: the same blocks and stepped arches as across the well, with the carving worn nearly away.
  • Then iron. Black riveted plate, thick chain, grates of square bar, round rings on wall pins, pipes with rib bands. All heavy and plain: this iron was made here, by hand. Sound iron you can hold is rust orange where hands and weather have worn it; the rest is black.
  • The big machines stand on stone footings with a pug's face in iron on each: the bellows, the hammers, the slag pans.
  • Above the forge, basalt: grey-brown rock in rough blocky steps, split by heat. The higher you go the paler and drier it gets.
  • No brick, no timber except tool handles and the bellows' boards, no crystal, nothing green.

Colour and light

The light is the story of the biome. At the bottom it is furnace red from below, with black shadows above. It climbs through orange to a dusty gold. At the top a slit of blue-white daylight comes down the flue, and by the last challenge the rock is lit from above and the red is gone.

How it tells you what a thing is

You can hold itRust-orange iron (rings, rungs, chain, plate edges), pale grey-brown basalt, dry and matte.
You can'tBlack glassy slag, soot-wet stone, greased iron.
It is hotRock or iron glowing orange-red with a heat shimmer over it. It flares brighter just before it lets go of you (note 56). Cool holds among it are plainly grey.
It will breakCracked already, with a corner gone (note 64). One rung is a stick of dynamite, and looks like one (note 58).
It blowsA grate in the floor, or a nozzle. Steam wisps and a gurgle first, then the blast.
It movesIt hangs on chain from a wheel you can see, or it is driven by a rod from a crank.
It is sceneryBlack iron and black stone, far back, lit red from below. Never rust orange.

The three layers here

BackgroundLow down: the forge's back wall, with hoods, racks of tongs, quenching troughs, the wheels and cranks that work the machines, and furnace mouths glowing. Higher: the flue's far wall, bare, with old chain stubs. At the top: sky through the crack.
Play spaceGrates, hot rock, chains, the bellows' boards, slag rafts, hammers, rings, the chockstone.
ForegroundA length of heavy chain's last links at a top corner, an anvil's horn or a quenching trough's rim at the bottom edge. Heat shimmer and sparks close to the camera. Nothing in front of a vent.

How you come in, and how you leave

In: From the temple, across the well's mouth on the censers. You land on soot-black temple stone beside the first steam grate. The torches stop and the red light from below takes over.

Out: Through the crack to daylight, onto the cliffs. The rock goes from basalt to pale chalk in the crack's last few metres, the air turns blue, wind comes in, and the whole valley opens with the town tiny below. The cliffs are the next biome and are not in this run; the crack itself is designed here as challenge 6.9.

La Chimenea · A place to rest · place 1 of 10

6.0 The smith's hut

The east end of the forge floor, at the very bottom of the chimney.

Every fall in the chimney ends on this floor, and the floor slopes this way, so this corner is where you pick yourself up. Today it is bare: one small anvil, one frozen climber sitting on nothing, a torch on the wall. After note 59 it is the smith's hut. The last smith built a lean-to against the flue's east wall, out of the forge's own black stone and iron sheet, round his anvil and a small hearth. Only the frog lives in it now, and it has taken over the anvil. The frozen climber in his dog mask stays where the course has him, and the hut is built round him: he looks as if he came in to have a ring mended and sat down to wait. The hut is cut away at the front: floor, back wall and roof, no front wall, and you walk in along the floor. The light: this is the bottom of the journey. It is furnace red, low along the floor, from two banked furnace mouths in the back wall, with black shadow above. The hut's coals and its lamp are the one small warm spot in it.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The forge's back wall, with two banked furnace mouths. Soot-black temple blocks in bays 4 m wide, with the temple's carved band worn nearly flat. This wall is the foot of the stepped pier that carries the three anvils of La Fragua, 44 m overhead. Two furnace mouths are banked low in it, each under a ribbed hood. Their red glow along the floor is the light of this place.
  • 2The hut's back wall. Soot-black temple blocks, 4 m wide and 3 m tall, the same blocks as the forge wall. The hut is black stone and iron sheet, with no timber in it (Parker, 11-13). A rack of tongs hangs on it, and three wall rings on pegs, finished and half finished: the same rings you hold in Tiro de Chimenea, made here. They are black, not rust orange, and out of reach.
  • 3The roof and its two back posts. A lean-to of riveted iron sheet, sloping down from the east wall, on two iron posts. The hut is cut along the line just behind the climber. The roof stops 1.2 m behind the play plane, so somebody who falls here passes in front of it and lands on the floor.
  • 4The hearth. A block of temple stone against the east wall with a bed of coals on it, a small iron hood over it, and a ribbed pipe that goes up the wall and out of sight. The coals are orange. With the lamp they are the only light on the floor that is not red.
  • 5The little bellows. Beside the hearth, on a stand: two boards, leather pleats and a nozzle, worked by a foot treadle and a rod. It is the great bellows of El Fuelle made small, and like every machine in the forge it shows what works it.

  • 7The frog. 0.3 m tall, sitting on the heel of the anvil in a leather apron, with a tiny hammer. It taps the anvil now and then and looks up when you come in (notes 59 and 60). It is friendly and nothing more.

  • 9Quenching trough and coal heap. Outside the hut's west post: a stone trough of black water with a pair of tongs left in it. Further along, between the two furnace mouths, a heap of coal.

6.1 Primer Vapor

The forge's door and its first breath.

The temple's smiths found a vent here, in the floor at the foot of the flue, where the mountain blows steam every few seconds, and they built their forge round it. They put a grate over the vent and cast a face for it: an iron pug as tall as a house, fixed to the back wall, breathing the vent's steam. The ring in its nose, the chain on the ring and the tongue hanging out of its mouth are what you hold. The light: you come in from the temple's torch gold. One last torch burns at the door. Two steps on, the light is furnace red and comes from below, up through the grating, and from the great furnace to the east. This is the red end of the journey.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The forge's back wall. The same wall as the temple across the well: big fitted blocks, a sloped base, the carved band at the temple's own heights. Here it is black with soot and the carving is worn nearly away. It fills the frame from the door to the great furnace.
  • 2The door, a small pug over it, and the last torch. The stepped arch you came through, seen from inside, with a small iron pug mask over it. One torch burns beside it. It is the last of the temple's torches: east of it the light is red and comes from below.
  • 3The great iron mask. An iron pug's face 8 m wide and 11 m tall, cast in plates and riveted, fixed to a pier of the back wall with its chin 5 m above the floor. It is the forge's own copy of the temple's great mask. By Parker's leave to arrange things (11-13) it is remade taller, so that what you hold belongs to it: the ring is in its nose, the chain hangs from the ring down over its mouth, and its tongue lolls out of the east corner of its mouth and flattens into the plate you land on. It is black iron, set back, and it can't be mistaken for a wall to climb.
  • 4The breath pipe. A fat ribbed pipe comes up out of the floor behind the grate and goes into the mask's chin. The grate is the open end of the same steam, so when the vent blows the mask breathes out through its nostrils and its mouth as well. Wisps come from the nostrils first, then the blast.
  • 5The strip of grating, with the fire under it. The grate you stand on is the front bay of a strip of grating that runs back across the floor to the foot of the pipe. Red light comes up through all of it. This is where the red light from below takes over from the torches.
  • 6Anvil, tongs rack and quenching trough by the door. The work place nearest the door: the small anvil that stands here today, a rack of tongs on the wall over it, and a stone trough. The rack hangs 3 m up the west wall today. It comes down to where a smith could reach it.
  • 7The great furnace's corner. The west corner of the furnace of Piedra Caliente, 1 m east of the tongue's tip. Its fire is the red on the right side of everything here.

Play space

  • 8The landing slab. The ledge the censer drops you on is temple stone, soot-black on its face and worn pale on top, where it can be held. Its edge carries the temple's carved band one last time.
  • 9The grate's rim. The kit's steam grate: square iron bars in a raised rim, rust orange where feet have worn it. Every vent on the climb wears this same grate, so after this one you know what a grate does. The rim is drawn onto the grate that is there: where you stand does not change.
  • 10The tongue's rolled tip. The plate you land on is the mask's tongue: riveted iron, rust orange on top, curled under at its east tip. The curl stays inside the ledge's own outline, and it points at the furnace, where the climb goes next.

Foreground

6.2 Piedra Caliente

The forge's great furnace.

It is a tower of soot-black temple blocks standing on the floor, 9 m wide, stepping back three times as it rises, the way every temple wall does. It has burned for so long that its face has cracked, and the climb goes up the crack. The hot holds are the ends of through stones: long blocks laid right through the wall with their far ends in the fire. The three cool holds are on the furnace's three carved bands, which stand clear of the fire. The ledge at the top is its charging step. The light: the deepest red on the climb. It comes from the furnace's mouth, straight below you, and from the hot stones themselves. Everything above the top band is black.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The forge's back wall. Black temple blocks with the worn band, running on behind the furnace on both sides.
  • 2The iron mask's cheek. From Primer Vapor: the east side of the great mask. The iron ledge you start on is its tongue.
  • 3The great furnace. Four tiers of temple blocks, 9.2 m wide at the foot and 20 m tall. A carved band runs round the top of each of the first three tiers, 490.0, 493.6 and 496.1 m up. The iron tongue you start on stops 1 m short of its west corner. The ledge at the top is its charging step, carried on a stone corbel, and its crown is open and glowing.
  • 4The furnace mouth and its hood. Low in the furnace's face, straight below the climb: a stepped arch 3 m wide with the fire in it, under a ribbed iron hood. This is the light of the challenge. It is deep red and it comes from below, so the undersides of the holds are lit.
  • 5The crack. A heat crack runs up the face along the line of the holds, and the stone is burnt black for a metre either side of it (note 56, built). The fire shows in the crack as a thin red line.
  • 6The air pipe. A ribbed pipe comes out of the wall above the furnace and down into its crown. It carries the air from the three small bellows of El Fuelle, 13 m overhead. The furnace is what all the bellows are for.
  • 7Coal heap and rake. On the floor by the mouth: a heap of coal, and a long iron rake leaning on the furnace.

  • 9The nine hot stones. Each hot hold is the square end of a through stone, and it glows, pulses and steams as the game shows it today. The joint round it glows too, so you can see it is a different stone from the wall.
  • 10The charging step. The ledge at the top is a slab of temple stone with a worn carved edge. The grate of the next challenge is set in it.

6.3 Géiseres Gemelos

The quench pipe.

The slag pan of Escoria hangs 26 m above this spot, and its waste runs off its east lip and falls. The smiths stood a great iron standpipe on the forge floor to catch it, with a hopper on top. The slag drops into the water in the pipe and the pipe blows steam: that is the second vent. A branch of the same pipe comes up through the furnace's charging step: that is the first. They are twins because they are one pipe with two mouths, and they take turns because the pressure can only be in one place at a time. Above them is the lip of the bellows loft, with the smiths' hoist standing on it. The light: red going to orange. It comes from the furnace's open crown, below and to the left, and from the falling slag, which is the first bright orange thing on the climb.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The forge's back wall. The forge's back wall goes on up, black, with one worn band. It is lit from the left and below.
  • 2The furnace's crown. The top of the furnace of Piedra Caliente. The ledge you stand on is its charging step. Its crown is open and glowing, and the air pipe from the bellows loft comes out of the wall and down into it.
  • 3The quench pipe. A standpipe 2.2 m across that comes up from the forge floor, 21 m below, strapped to the wall. It stands here today as scenery. It stays, and it gets its straps and its reason.
  • 4The hopper's back half. The two slick plates you can't stand on are the front edge of a round iron hopper on top of the pipe. Its back half stands behind, lopsided like the plates: short on the west, long on the east, to catch the falling slag. Inside it is black and glassy with splashed slag.
  • 5The branch pipe. A thinner pipe leaves the standpipe and runs under the ledge to the first grate. The two vents are one pipe with two mouths, which is why they take turns.
  • 6The falling slag. Slag falls from the lip of the pan above into the hopper. Today it is drawn as one thin bright strip, 1.5 m from the chain you have to catch, and it could be taken for a second chain. It becomes separate bright drops, set well back. A bigger gob falls 1 s before the second vent blows: the warning you can see.
  • 7The hoist. An iron post, arm and brace standing on the east end of the loft's lip: the smiths' hoist for lowering things to the hopper. The ring is the eye at the end of its arm and the chain is its chain. Today the ring hangs in the air.
  • 8The stair door. In the back wall behind the top ledge: a stepped arch shut with an iron grille. The smiths had a stair inside the wall. You can see how they came up, and you can't use it.
  • 9The stepping bellows' cam wheels. From El Fuelle, at the top left: the first two of the three stepping bellows, each on its iron brackets with its cam wheel under it, and the coupling rod that joins the wheels. Today the bellows hang in the air.

  • 11The slick plates. The two plates are in the play space and can't be held, because the challenge needs nothing to stand on at the second vent. So they are made plainly dark and wet: black greased iron, with runs of glassy slag frozen down them. They are the darkest and shiniest things in the frame.
  • 12The loft's lip. The ledge that ends the challenge is the lip of the bellows loft: a temple slab, sooted on its face and worn pale on top.

6.4 El Fuelle

The bellows loft, the upper half of the forge hall.

The furnace below needs air, and this is where the air is made. The great bellows stands on a stone shelf on the west wall. Three small box bellows step up towards it on iron brackets, each one's pipe going back into the wall and down to the furnace. One steam wheel under the shelf works all of it: a crank and a rod open and shut the great bellows, and a long rod turns three cam wheels that push the small bellows up and let them down. You climb the small bellows as steps, into the great bellows' blast, onto its deck, and up four iron rungs in a stone pier to the slag pan's shore. One of the rungs is not a rung. The light: orange. It comes from above and to the right, off the slag pan, so the tops of the bellows are lit and the furnace's red is left on their undersides.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The loft's back wall. The same black temple wall, here lit orange from above. It fills the frame.
  • 2The stone shelf. A shelf of temple blocks built out from the west wall on stepped corbels. The great bellows stands on it. Today the bellows hangs on the wall with nothing under it.
  • 3The great bellows. Two boards, leather pleats and an iron nozzle box with the pug's face on it, 6 m long, hinged at the nozzle like a real bellows and opening at the west end. After note 57 it moves. Through the 2.6 s of quiet its top board lifts and the pleats spread, so you can read how long you have. Then a stone weight on the top board slams it shut over the 1.4 s of the gust, and the jet comes out of the nozzle along the line the wind blows. It is drawn open. The dashed line is the top board when shut. The deck you land on is a fixed timber deck on the bellows' iron frame, above the moving board.
  • 4The steam wheel, its crank and its rod. What works the great bellows. Under the shelf an iron paddle wheel 3 m across sits in stone cheeks. A pipe comes up the west wall and ends in a nozzle that kicks the wheel round with steam. A crank on the wheel's axle pulls a rod, and the rod goes up through the shelf to the free end of the bellows' top board. Wheel, crank and rod turn once for every gust.
  • 5The long rod and the three cam wheels. What works the three stepping bellows. Each one sits on a pair of iron brackets from the wall, and under it turns an iron cam wheel 2 m across. As the wheel turns, its cam pushes the bellows' top board up 1.8 m and lets it down again. One coupling rod joins the three wheels, each a third of a turn behind the last, which is why the three bellows swell one after another. A long rod runs from the third wheel down to the steam wheel. One wheel works everything in the loft. Today the three bellows hang in the air.
  • 6The rung pier. A pier of temple blocks from the deck up to the iron shore. The rungs are iron staples driven into it. Today they hang in the air.
  • 7The shore's brackets. The iron shore at the top is the front edge of the slag pan's tapping floor: a riveted iron gallery on brackets, which carries on behind you to the smelter of Escoria.
  • 8The open box of dynamite. A small open box on the deck behind the rungs, with the mine's skull pug stencilled on it and three more red sticks showing. It tells you what the red rung is before you touch it, and how it got here. Parker, 11-13: yes to the box.
  • 9The loft's lip, with the hoist and the stair door. From Géiseres Gemelos: the ledge you start on is the lip of the loft, with the smiths' hoist on its east end and the grilled stair door in the wall behind it.

Play space

  • 10Pleats on the three stepping bellows. Each stepping bellows is a small box bellows: a timber top board with a pug's face on its edge, and leather pleats under it that open as it swells and close as it folds (note 57). Its base stays still on its brackets. Only the top board and the pleats move, and the top board's travel is exactly today's. The pleated body is in the play space and can't be held, so it is plainly dark and wet: black greased leather, under a pale dry board that can.

La Chimenea · Challenge · place 6 of 10

6.5 Escoria

The slag pan.

Above the loft the smiths smelted their iron in a round-bellied furnace on an iron tapping floor, and the waste, the slag, ran out of it down a long tilted iron pan to cool. The pan hangs from the hall's roof in two cradles. To keep the slag running they raked it: three iron rakes, their handles worked to and fro by three cranks on one steam wheel at the head of the pan, like oars. The rafts you ride are the heads of the rakes. At the pan's low end the slag runs off a lip and falls to the quench pipe, and the smiths' second hoist reaches over the lip. The light: bright orange, the brightest in the forge, and the slag itself is the lamp. It lights everything from underneath and throws the rakes' shadows up the wall. It is the last place where the light comes from under your feet.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The hall's back wall. The same black wall, lit bright orange from below, with the roof above it left in black.
  • 2The smelter and its spout. A round-bellied furnace of temple stone with the iron pug on its front, standing on the tapping floor behind the iron shore. A stone spout runs from its tap hole to the head of the pan. The slag comes from here, and you can see it pour.
  • 3The pan's back half, its cradles and chains. The pan is 3 m from front to back, and you ride its front edge. It lies in two iron cradles, and each cradle hangs from the hall's roof on a pair of chains with links as thick as an arm. The chains rise behind the two dead crusts, where nobody stands, and well back, so they can't be taken for the chain you want. Today the pan hangs in the air.
  • 4The rake wheel and the three rake handles. What moves the rafts. Each raft is the head of a slag rake. Its long iron handle runs back up the pan to a crank on one wheel at the pan's head, beside the smelter, and a steam nozzle kicks the wheel round. Three cranks, three handles, three rafts going to and fro. The handles pass through eyes on the cradles' hangers.
  • 5The lip and the falling slag. At the pan's low east end the slag runs off a lip and falls, in separate bright drops, 22 m into the hopper of Géiseres Gemelos.
  • 6The second hoist. The same hoist as on the loft's lip, standing on the next ledge with its arm reaching back over the pan's lip. The ring is the eye at the end of its arm and the chain is its chain.
  • 7The foot of the hammer pier. The ledge at the far side is the first landing of the stepped stone pier that carries the three anvils of La Fragua. The pier comes up from the forge floor, 44 m below.

Play space

  • 8The pan's front plate. The front of the pan is black riveted plate with slag frozen in runs over its rim. The slag's surface is bright yellow-orange in the middle of each gap and skinned dark red at its edges, so you can see that it is live.
  • 9The rafts' eyes. Each raft is a thick iron plate with a turned-up edge and an eye at its west end, where the rake's handle hooks on. Its top is rust orange. Its sides are black and crusted where they sit in the slag.
  • 10The two dead crusts. Black glassy teeth of slag that has spat up and frozen round the cradles' hangers. They are in the play space and can't be held, so they are plainly dark and wet: they shine, and nothing about them says stand here.

La Chimenea · Challenge · place 7 of 10

6.6 La Fragua

The hammer shop.

A stepped pier of temple stone rises from the forge floor through the whole hall, each step 4.2 m wide and 4 m tall, like a stair for a giant. One great anvil stands on each of three steps, and over each anvil hangs a drop hammer. Behind each hammer is the wheel that lifts it: a peg on the wheel's rim hooks under the hammer's tail, carries it up and lets it go. A steam pipe under the forge's hood turns the wheels. The chain you climb hangs from the hammer's own lug, so it is only up there while the hammer is. This is the last of the temple's stone and the heaviest of its iron. The light: orange going to gold. The slag's light now comes from behind you and below, and every hammer blow throws white-gold sparks. The hood is a lid over this room, so there is still no daylight in it.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The hall's back wall. The same black wall, here lit orange from the left and below, with sparks on it.
  • 2The stepped pier. Soot-black temple blocks in three giant steps and a head, with the iron pug on each riser. One anvil stands on each step. The ledge you start on is the pier's first landing, and the ledge at the top is its head. Today the anvils hang in the air.
  • 3The slotted towers. Behind each hammer a narrow stone tower rises from the step to the hood, with a dark slot down its middle. The hammer's tail runs in the slot. It is the temple's rule, kept in the forge: every block that moves has a slot it slides in.
  • 4The three lifting wheels. What lifts the hammers. On each tower's axle turns an iron wheel 4.4 m across, with paddles on its rim and one peg. The peg hooks under the hammer's tail, carries it up 4.2 m and lets it go at the top. You can read each hammer's time from its wheel: when the peg comes round to the bottom, that hammer is about to rise.
  • 5The steam pipe under the hood. The slanting black slab over the hammers is the forge's great hood, ribbed with iron underneath. A fat steam pipe runs up under it, and a nozzle drops from the pipe towards each wheel and kicks it round. A puff at the nozzle comes just before each hammer starts up. The same pipe goes on up into the flue and feeds the three vents of El Último Aliento.
  • 6The scorched bunting. High in the corner where the hall's roof meets the flue: one scorched string of the town's cut paper, with three flags left on it. It hangs there today, nearer. It moves to the far back, where a hanging thing can't be taken for a rope.
  • 7The second hoist. From Escoria: the hoist on the pier's first landing, reaching back over the slag pan's lip.
  • 8The last stair door. In the wall behind the top ledge: the last of the grilled stair doors. Above it nobody built in stone.

Play space

  • 9The anvils' bright faces. Each anvil's face is polished bright in the middle, where the hammer lands, and sooty at its two ends. The bright patch is exactly as wide as the hammer. The anvil's foot carries the iron pug.
  • 10The hammers' striking faces. Each hammer is a block of black greased iron with a peaked top and the pug's face cast on its front. Its striking face is a band of bright worn steel, the only pale thing on it, so you can see which edge will hit you. The lug on its east side, where the chain hangs, is rust orange.

La Chimenea · Challenge · place 8 of 10

6.7 Tiro de Chimenea

The updraught shaft: the forge's own chimney.

The great hood over the hammers gathers the whole forge's heat and pours it in here, under the foot of an iron baffle, and it goes up between the baffle and the flue's east wall. That is the wind that carries you. Half way up the baffle has a window with an iron flap, and every few seconds the draught snatches the flap open and sucks sideways through it. The rings on the wall are where the smiths hung their chains to sweep the shaft. An iron grille once capped it: one bar is left, and the last rings are on that bar. This is where the made things stop. The ledge you start on is the last cut stone. Above it the wall is the mountain's own basalt, and the baffle is the last big piece of iron. The light: dusty gold. The red still comes from below, on the underside of everything, and for the first time a pale light comes down from above, down the pipe over the shaft's head.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The flue's far wall. Above the pier's head the temple stone stops. From here up the wall is basalt: grey-brown, in rough blocky steps, split by heat. Low in the shaft the cracks still show a dull red.
  • 2The pier's head, the last door and the last pug. The ledge you start on is the head of the hammer pier: the last cut stone on the climb. Behind it is the last grilled stair door, and over the door the last iron pug. Above this nothing has a face.
  • 3The hood's top end and the steam pipe. The top end of the forge's hood, and the steam pipe that runs up under it. The pipe comes through the hood, goes up the wall and turns in under the next ledge, where it feeds the first vent of El Último Aliento. The hood is what pours the forge's heat into this shaft.
  • 4The flap. The window in the baffle has an iron flap, hinged at the top on the far side. It hangs slack while the air is quiet. It starts to rattle and lift 0.9 s before the gust, and it is flung wide open while the gust blows. It is the warning you can see, to go with the whistle.
  • 5Two chain stubs. The bare flue's only dressing: two short thick stubs of chain on pins in the far wall, three links each. The lower one stands straight up in the steady draught, so you see the wind before you step into it. The upper one is in the gust band, and it lies over to the west when the gust comes.
  • 6The cap grille's last bars. An iron grille once capped the shaft. One bar of it is left whole, slanting from the east wall up to the top ledge, and two more are snapped off behind it. The rings across the shaft's head are eyes on short pins from the whole bar. Today they hang in the air.
  • 7The pale light down the pipe. Straight above the shaft is the slick pipe that comes down from under the chockstone of La Luz, and daylight comes down it. It is the first daylight on the climb: a pale dusty column in the top of the shaft that fades before it reaches the window.

Play space

  • 8The sockets of the three rings that go. Note 61 takes three rings away: the lowest on the wall, the one inside the gust band, and the middle one across the top. Each of the two on the wall leaves an empty square socket with a rust streak under it: dark, flat, and plainly nothing to hold. The one across the top leaves a snapped pin on the bar. The sketch draws the three over today's rings.
  • 9The four rings that stay. The kit's wall ring: a round iron ring 0.5 m across on a pin, rust orange, worn bright inside where hands have been. With half of them gone, the four are the only orange things in the shaft.
  • 10The baffle's window. The baffle is a wall of black riveted iron plate, greased with soot. The edges of its window are scraped bright by everything the gust has pulled through.

Foreground

  • 11A heavy chain's last links. The last three links of a heavy chain hang into the top corner of the frame, in front of the solid east wall. They lift a little in the draught. They are in front of rock, never in front of the shaft.

6.8 El Último Aliento

The bare flue, and the forge's last three breaths.

Above the shaft the flue opens out into a tall leaning cleft of basalt with nothing built in it. One thing of the forge's comes this high: the steam pipe that ran up under the hood. It climbs the far wall in three flights, and at the end of each flight an elbow comes forward and ends in a grate. The steam climbs the pipe, so the three vents blow one after another from the bottom up. The rings are the eyes of the pipe's clamps. Above the third grate there is one ring on a spike, and then only rock. The light: gold going pale. The forge's red reaches about as high as the second grate. A shaft of daylight comes in at the crack and slants down across the flue, and the third grate sits in it. Each breath is lit paler than the one before.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The flue's far wall. Bare basalt. It gets paler and drier as it climbs: grey-brown and cracked at the bottom ledge, with a dull red still in the lowest cracks, and a dry pale grey by the top ledge. Nothing is built on it.
  • 2The steam pipe, in three flights. The forge's steam pipe climbs the far wall: up, across, up, across, and a capped stub. Each grate sits on the end of one flight, where an elbow comes forward to the play plane. After note 62 the two high grates are plainly held up, and plainly part of one machine. The first ring is the eye of a clamp on the second riser. The second ring is on the capped stub.
  • 3The shaft of daylight. Daylight comes in at the crack and slants down across the flue to the west wall. It is painted there today. Low down it turns dusty gold and dies into the red. The third grate and the second ring sit inside it: they are the first things on the climb that daylight touches, and the brightest things above you.
  • 4Two old chain stubs. Two short stubs of chain on pins, both below the second grate. Above it the wall has no iron on it but the pipe.
  • 5The last ring's spike. The last ring is on a single iron spike driven into the far wall beside the top ledge. It is the highest made thing inside the mountain.

Play space

  • 6The two high grates, made plain. Note 62. The second and third grates wear the same raised rim and red grille as the one in the ledge. Each sits on the end of the pipe's elbow, and the elbow stops just behind the play plane, so nothing new is put in the play space under a grate. Steam seeps from them between blasts. The second grate, which daylight does not reach, has a dull red glow in its bars from the steam below, so it is never a dark box in the dark.
  • 7The top ledge. The crack's doorstep: natural basalt, dry and pale, with daylight on it. The frozen climber of La Luz stands on it with one arm raised. From below he is the last thing on the skyline, with light on his hand.

Foreground

  • 8A fin of basalt. A rough fin of basalt standing in front of the foot of the pillar on the right. It covers only solid rock.

La Chimenea · Challenge · place 10 of 10

6.9 La Luz

The crack to daylight, and the way out of the mountain.

At its top the flue narrows to a crack where the basalt of the inside meets the pale chalk of the outside. Nothing here is made: no iron, no cut stone, no soot. Two shelves of basalt step up to a gap, and a block of chalk that fell from the roof is jammed across the gap. Chalk is weak. The block is cracked through and it gives way under you. A band of flint knobs in the chalk is the way over when it has gone. Beyond it is a sill of white chalk, and the opening. One frozen climber stands on the doorstep with his hand up toward the light. The light: this is the top of the journey. It is blue-white daylight, coming level through the opening on the right, and there is no red left in it. The design stops at the opening.

What you are looking at

Background

  • 1The crack's back wall. The crack is narrow. Its back wall is only 1.2 m behind you: the first time on this climb that a back wall is within reach. West of a slanting line it is the flue's basalt, grey-brown and dry. East of the line, for the last few metres to the opening, it is pale chalk: the mountain's outside.
  • 2The gap's black wall. Under the chockstone the gap between the two walls drops away to the updraught shaft, 26 m below. Its back and its sides are black and glassy, worn smooth by the draught, with nothing on them to catch. It reads as a drop, and it is one.
  • 3The flint band. A band of flint runs up through the chalk: a line of knobs in their white rind, slanting from the second step to the opening. The three nubs over the gap are three knobs of this band that stand out far enough to hold. The band goes on past them, so the way out is drawn on the wall before the chockstone ever drops.
  • 4The split in the roof. Right above the chockstone the roof has a split, packed with blocks of chalk that have not fallen yet. The chockstone came out of it. When the stone gives way under you, the next block drops out of the split with a thud and a puff of white dust, and wedges where the last one was (note 64). You can see the next one waiting.
  • 5The edge of daylight. The daylight comes in under the roof, and its lowest edge reaches the frozen climber's raised hand and the top of his mask. The rest of him is in the pillar's shadow.
  • 6The sky through the opening. What you see through the opening, and all you see of the next place. Sky first: a hard clear blue, the first since the station. Under it the far side of the valley, pale and hazy, and at its foot the town, tiny, with the ring a dot of colour in its plaza. One vulture turns a long way off. The opening is 6 m tall and you walk out along the sill.

Play space

  • 7The cracked chockstone. Note 64. The chockstone is a real stone: a rough block of chalk jammed between the two walls, the same size and wedge shape as the stand-in, so the step across plays the same. It wears the mountain's one breakable look: cracked right through, with a corner gone. Grit trickles from under it, and it shifts when you first touch it. It breaks into rough chunks that drop down the gap with white dust.
  • 8The three flint nubs. Three knobs of flint in their white rind, each the size of two fists, standing 0.4 m out of the chalk. Dry, pale and matte. They are natural, and they lie on the flint band's line.
  • 9The one who nearly had it. The second of the chimney's frozen climbers stands on the doorstep exactly where he is today, 1.35 m from the last ring, with one arm raised toward the light. His raised hand and the top of his mask are in daylight. Nothing is put beside him, because nothing was ever made up here: he is the only thing in the frame that is not rock. He got out of the forge, and stopped one easy challenge short of the sky.
  • 10The sill. The two steps are the last of the basalt. The sill is the first of the chalk: white, dry and gritty, with wind-blown dust on it. You change rock as you climb out.

Foreground

  • 11A fin of basalt. The same rough fin as in El Último Aliento, in front of the pillar under the steps. It covers only solid rock.
  • 12A chalk overhang. A dark overhang in front of the roof at the top right, over the opening. With the fin below, it makes the opening the brightest shape in the frame. It covers only solid rock.

Why it works

Each thing you touch is the near end of something real behind it.

What I am not touching

  • The doorstep, the two steps, the three nubs and the sill, exactly as they are.
  • The chockstone's size, wedge shape and timing: it gives way after 1.2 s and is back in 8 s.
  • The gap under it drops to the updraught shaft, two challenges back.
  • The frozen climber, exactly where he stands today.

What it would change in the game

  • Course change, from note 64: the chockstone becomes a cracked block of chalk of the same size and wedge shape. Nothing else you touch moves or is added.
